Security Enhancement for Claude Code

A Practitioner’s Guide to Hardening Every Vulnerability in a Production AI CLI Agent

Tri Doan

22 Chapters + 3 Appendices · ~105,117 words · 2026

Chapter 1: The Security Landscape of Claude Code

The first rule of securing a production system is knowing exactly what you are defending against. Not theoretical threats from a whiteboard exercise, but concrete vulnerabilities with measured severity, documented locations, and quantified blast radii. This chapter presents the results of a comprehensive security source review of Claude Code's 512,000-line TypeScript codebase -- 50 vulnerabilities spanning every layer from plugin ingestion to shell execution. Before writing a single patch, you need this map.

1.1 Scope and Methodology

The security review covered the entire Claude Code CLI source tree: 1,884 files of TypeScript/TSX running on the Bun runtime. Four specialized analysis agents operated in parallel -- a static scanner, a design reviewer, a supply chain scanner, and a patch engineer -- each producing findings that were cross-validated and de-duplicated into the final 50-vulnerability catalog.

The assessment targeted six major subsystems:

Subsystem Files Reviewed Primary Risk
Plugin/Extension System plugins/, utils/plugins/, utils/dxt/ Supply chain, code execution
Credential Storage utils/secureStorage/ Plaintext secrets, TOCTOU
Authentication & Tokens bridge/, services/oauth/, utils/auth.ts JWT forgery, token persistence
Subagent Execution tools/AgentTool/, services/mcp/ Process isolation, privilege escalation
Network & Remote server/, remote/, upstreamproxy/ SSRF, permission bypass, WebSocket
Bash Security tools/BashTool/ Parser differential, injection

The review methodology followed a hybrid approach: automated pattern matching against known CWE signatures, manual data-flow tracing through security-critical paths, and architectural analysis of trust boundaries. Every finding was scored using CVSS v3.1 base metrics with environmental adjustments for CLI tool deployment contexts.

CVSS Scoring for CLI Tools

Standard CVSS scoring assumes network-accessible services. A CLI tool operating on a developer's machine requires adjusted environmental metrics. Consider how attack vectors differ:

  • Network vector (N) applies when the tool processes data from remote sources -- marketplace plugins, bridge sessions, WebSocket connections
  • Local vector (L) applies when exploitation requires filesystem access -- credential files, conversation history, debug logs
  • Adjacent vector (A) applies to same-machine attacks -- cross-process memory access, shared environment variables

The 50 findings distribute across these vectors:

Attack Vector Count Percentage Example
Network 18 36% Plugin download without signature (CVSS 9.1)
Local 26 52% Plaintext credential storage (CVSS 7.1)
Adjacent 6 12% Proxy token on heap after unlink (CVSS 5.3)

This distribution reveals an important truth about CLI tool security: the majority of risk is local. The developer's own machine is both the deployment target and the attack surface. As we'll explore in Chapter 2, these local vulnerabilities chain together into dependency groups that amplify their individual severities.

1.3 The Two Critical Findings

The two CRITICAL-severity findings both involve the same root cause: unsigned plugin code execution.

Finding 1: No Cryptographic Signature Verification for Plugins (CVSS 9.1)

Location: plugins/ (system-wide) CWE: CWE-494 -- Download of Code Without Integrity Check OWASP: A08:2021 -- Software and Data Integrity Failures

The plugin system downloads ZIP archives from marketplace registries and executes their contents with full CLI process privileges. While SHA-256 hash verification confirms the download was not corrupted during transit, no mechanism exists to verify that the plugin was published by its claimed author or hasn't been replaced by a malicious actor who compromised the registry.

The data flow is:

Marketplace API --> download plugin ZIP --> hash verify (integrity only)
  --> extract with path traversal protection --> register plugin
  --> plugin executes with CLI privileges

The hash check answers "did I download what the server sent?" but not "did the server send what the author published?" A compromised CDN, a MITM on the download URL, or a rogue marketplace entry can inject arbitrary code that passes integrity checks because the hash was computed over the malicious payload.

Finding 2: No Signature Verification for Downloaded Plugins (CVSS 8.1)

Location: utils/plugins/pluginLoader.ts, utils/plugins/marketplaceManager.ts CWE: CWE-494 OWASP: A08:2021

This finding is the implementation-level companion to Finding 1. The marketplace JSON is fetched via axios.get() with zero integrity validation. The GCS marketplace ZIP is downloaded without SHA-256 verification against a known-good hash. The .gcs-sha sentinel file is written by the same extraction process, creating a TOCTOU condition.

Together, these two findings represent the highest blast radius in the codebase: a compromised marketplace or CDN can deliver arbitrary code to every developer who installs or updates plugins. As we'll analyze in Chapter 2, this forms the root of the Plugin Supply Chain dependency chain, which cascades through five additional findings.

1.4 The Eight HIGH-Severity Findings

The HIGH tier contains the vulnerabilities most likely to cause immediate damage in production deployments.

Subagent Execution Without Process Isolation (CVSS 7.8)

Location: tools/AgentTool/runAgent.ts:248 CWE: CWE-269 -- Improper Privilege Management

Subagents, including those spawned by third-party plugins, execute in the same Node.js/Bun process as the parent CLI. They share AppState, tool pools, and environment. The only isolation is tool-name filtering at runAgent.ts:465-479 -- advisory, not enforced at the process level. A malicious subagent can read ~/.claude/.credentials.json, exfiltrate tokens via network tools, and fork child agents to establish persistence.

ZIP Path Traversal via Symlinks (CVSS 7.5)

Location: utils/plugins/zipCache.ts, utils/dxt/zip.ts CWE: CWE-22 -- Path Traversal

ZIP extraction validates against .. path components but follows symlinks without validating that resolved paths remain within the extraction root. At zipCache.ts:292-300, the comment reads "Skip symlinked directories (follow symlinked files)" -- but symlink targets are not validated against the extraction boundary. A crafted ZIP with a symlink pointing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys could write files to arbitrary locations.

JWT Decoded Without Signature Verification (CVSS 7.5)

Location: bridge/jwtUtils.ts:21 CWE: CWE-347 -- Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

The decodeJwtPayload() function performs Buffer.from(parts[1], 'base64url').toString('utf8') -- base64 decode of the payload -- without verifying the signature in parts[2]. No JWKS endpoint is fetched, no public key is loaded. The decoded exp claim is used to schedule token refresh timers. An attacker who can MITM the bridge connection could forge a JWT with a far-future exp, suppressing refresh and keeping a revoked token active indefinitely.

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts:21 -- VULNERABLE
export function decodeJwtPayload(token: string): unknown | null {
  const jwt = token.startsWith('sk-ant-si-')
    ? token.slice('sk-ant-si-'.length)
    : token
  const parts = jwt.split('.')
  if (parts.length !== 3 || !parts[1]) return null
  try {
    return jsonParse(Buffer.from(parts[1], 'base64url').toString('utf8'))
  } catch {
    return null
  }
}

Notice what is absent: no call to crypto.verify(), no JWKS fetch, no public key parameter. The function name -- decodeJwtPayload -- is honest about what it does, but the callers treat the output as verified data.

MCP Server Tools Without Process Sandbox (CVSS 7.5)

Location: services/mcp/ CWE: CWE-250 -- Execution with Unnecessary Privileges

MCP server tool calls execute within the CLI process's full security context. While a permission prompt is shown, approved tools run with complete filesystem, network, and shell access. A malicious MCP server registered in a marketplace could define tools that appear benign (e.g., format_code) but execute arbitrary commands when approved.

Plaintext Credential Storage (CVSS 7.1 + 7.1 + 6.5)

Locations: utils/secureStorage/index.ts:9, utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts:57, utils/secureStorage/index.ts:16 CWE: CWE-256, CWE-312, CWE-922

Three separate findings target the same architectural gap: on non-macOS platforms, OAuth tokens and API keys are stored as plaintext JSON at ~/.claude/.credentials.json with only chmod 0600 protection. The code is explicit about this:

// utils/secureStorage/index.ts:9
export function getSecureStorage(): SecureStorage {
  if (process.platform === "darwin") {
    return createFallbackStorage(macOsKeychainStorage, plainTextStorage)
  }
  // TODO: add libsecret support for Linux
  return plainTextStorage
}

The TODO comment has been in the codebase through the review period. Every Linux user, every Docker container, every CI/CD pipeline uses plaintext credential storage.

Conversation History in Plaintext (CVSS 7.0)

Location: history.ts:115 CWE: CWE-312

All conversation history -- including pasted API keys, tokens, and passwords -- persists in plaintext JSONL at ~/.claude/history.jsonl. Small pastes (under 1024 chars) are stored inline. Larger pastes go to ~/.claude/paste-cache/{sha256}.txt. No TTL, no automatic purging, no secret detection. The file permissions are 0600, providing the same insufficient protection as credential storage.

1.5 The MEDIUM Tier: 23 Findings

The medium tier is the bulk of the catalog. These are not individually catastrophic, but they form the connective tissue of the seven dependency chains analyzed in Chapter 2. A selection of the most architecturally significant:

# CVSS Title Location CWE
11 6.8 Shell-Quote Parser as Single Point of Failure bashSecurity.ts:27 CWE-436
12 6.5 dangerouslySkipPermissions Sent to Remote Server createDirectConnectSession.ts:54 CWE-862
13 6.5 Environment Variable Tokens Never Expire auth.ts:1260 CWE-613
14 6.2 Recursive Subagent Forking, Weak Depth Guard forkSubagent.ts:311 CWE-674
17 5.9 WebFetch SSRF via DNS Rebinding WebFetchTool/utils.ts:262 CWE-918
18 5.9 CA Bundle Download Without Cert Pinning upstreamproxy.ts:254 CWE-295
19 5.9 ReDoS in Permission Regex bashPermissions.ts:760 CWE-1333
20 5.5 Keychain Shell Command Injection macOsKeychainStorage.ts:39 CWE-78
24 5.3 Hardcoded Datadog Client Token datadog.ts:14 CWE-798
27 5.0 TOCTOU in FileWriteTool FileWriteTool.ts:267 CWE-367
29 4.8 Short Git SHA for Plugin Versions pluginVersioning.ts CWE-328
30 4.7 TOCTOU in Credential File Write plainTextStorage.ts:57 CWE-367

Finding 11 deserves particular attention. The entire bash security validation chain -- 100+ injection patterns, heredoc analysis, zsh exploit blocking -- depends on a custom shell-quote parser for initial tokenization. If this parser misparses a command differently than the actual shell, all downstream validators operate on incorrect tokens. Six dedicated misparsing validators (validateCarriageReturn, validateBackslashEscapedOperators, validateMalformedTokens, etc.) are reactive patches for known divergences. The architecture is fundamentally fragile: a single unknown parser bug bypasses everything. As we'll see in Chapter 21, adding tree-sitter-bash as a secondary parser for cross-validation is the architectural answer.

1.6 The LOW and INFO Tiers

The 11 LOW and 6 INFO findings are defense-in-depth improvements rather than exploitable vulnerabilities. They matter for compliance coverage and for closing information-leak vectors that support more serious attacks.

Notable LOW findings:

  • Finding 34 (CVSS 4.3): Trusted device token overridable via CLAUDE_DEVICE_TOKEN environment variable at bridge/trustedDevice.ts:46. CWE-473.
  • Finding 36 (CVSS 3.7): OAuth callback listener on predictable localhost port at services/oauth/auth-code-listener.ts:46. CWE-352.
  • Finding 37 (CVSS 3.7): Keychain credentials visible via process arguments on the fallback path at macOsKeychainStorage.ts:118. CWE-214.

Notable INFO findings:

  • Finding 46 (CVSS 3.1): Regex-based security validation has inherent parser differential risk at bashSecurity.ts:1. CWE-78. This is the informational companion to the MEDIUM-severity Finding 11 -- acknowledging that regex-based command validation can never be complete.
  • Finding 50 (CVSS 0.0): PKCE implementation uses correct cryptographic primitives at services/oauth/crypto.ts:1. This is a positive finding confirming that randomBytes(32) and SHA-256 code challenges are correctly implemented.

1.7 Risk Quantification

Raw CVSS scores tell you severity. Risk quantification tells you what to fix first. Three dimensions matter for a CLI tool deployed on developer machines:

Blast Radius

How many users are affected if a vulnerability is exploited?

Blast Radius Vulnerability Users Affected
All users Plugin signature (CVSS 9.1) Every CLI installation
All Linux users Plaintext credentials (CVSS 7.1) ~40% of installations
Bridge users JWT no-verify (CVSS 7.5) Enterprise deployments
Plugin users Subagent isolation (CVSS 7.8) Anyone running 3rd-party plugins

The blast radius analysis reveals that 20% of findings (the two CRITICALs and eight HIGHs) account for approximately 80% of the affected user population. This is not unusual -- it follows the Pareto distribution common in security risk catalogs -- but it has direct implications for remediation sequencing. As we'll detail in Chapter 3, the implementation roadmap prioritizes by blast radius first, then by exploitability.

Exploitability

How much skill and access does an attacker need?

Barrier Level Attack Type Skill Required Access Required Examples
Low Credential theft Script kiddie Same-user process Read ~/.claude/.credentials.json (Finding 7)
Low History exfiltration Script kiddie Same-user process Parse history.jsonl for secrets (Finding 9)
Medium Supply chain injection Experienced CDN/registry compromise or MITM Replace plugin ZIP on marketplace (Finding 1)
Medium JWT manipulation Experienced Network position (proxy/MITM) Forge JWT with far-future exp (Finding 5)
High Parser differential Expert None (LLM-generated payload) Novel shell-quote divergence (Finding 11)
High Targeted collision Expert Significant compute Short SHA prefix collision (Finding 29)

The low-barrier attacks are particularly concerning for CI/CD environments. Container escape or shared filesystem access -- both common in build systems -- provides sufficient access to steal credentials from the plaintext storage path. Organizations running Claude Code in CI pipelines should treat Findings 7, 8, and 10 as immediate blockers.

The medium-barrier attacks require network positioning, making them relevant for enterprise deployments where corporate proxies inspect TLS traffic. Finding 5 (JWT without signature verification) becomes especially dangerous in environments with mandatory MITM proxies, because the proxy is already in position to modify the JWT payload.

Data at Risk

What gets exposed on successful exploitation?

Vulnerability Class Data Exposed Persistence Regulatory Impact
Credential storage OAuth tokens, API keys, refresh tokens Until manually rotated SOC 2 CC6.1, HIPAA 164.312
Conversation history Pasted secrets, code, intellectual property Indefinite (no TTL) GDPR Art. 5, CCPA 1798.100
JWT manipulation Session tokens, org identifiers Until session termination SOC 2 CC6.6
Debug logging Token prefixes, session IDs, URLs Until log rotation PCI DSS Req. 3.4
Telemetry Usage patterns, tool arguments, org metadata Third-party retention policy GDPR Art. 6, ePrivacy

The conversation history risk is often underestimated. Developers routinely paste database connection strings, API keys, cloud credentials, and internal URLs into CLI sessions during debugging. Every one of those pastes persists in ~/.claude/history.jsonl with no encryption, no TTL, and no secret detection. A single compromised developer machine yields not just that developer's credentials but potentially production secrets across the organization.

Aggregate Risk Score

Combining blast radius, exploitability, and data sensitivity into a weighted aggregate:

Risk Factor Weight Score (1-10) Weighted
Blast radius (plugin supply chain) 0.3 9 2.7
Exploitability (credential theft) 0.25 8 2.0
Data sensitivity (OAuth tokens) 0.25 9 2.25
Existing controls effectiveness 0.2 5 1.0
Aggregate Risk 7.95 / 10

An aggregate risk score of 7.95 out of 10 places Claude Code in the CRITICAL risk tier. The existing controls (bash security patterns, hash verification, macOS keychain) provide meaningful defense but leave significant gaps in supply chain integrity, cross-platform credential protection, and process isolation.

1.8 The Architecture Behind the Vulnerabilities

Understanding why these vulnerabilities exist requires examining Claude Code's architecture. The system is a 512K-line TypeScript codebase running on the Bun runtime, using React/Ink for terminal UI and Commander.js for CLI parsing. It is organized into six major subsystems connected through a central orchestrator (main.tsx, 4,000+ lines):

    OAUTH --> STORE
    MCP_SVC --> PLUGIN
    AGENT --> MAIN

Four trust boundaries exist in this architecture:

  1. Input Validation -- bashSecurity.ts (100+ patterns), pathValidation.ts, schema validation for MCP results, SHA-256 hash verification for plugins
  2. Permission & Policy -- toolPermission/ allow/deny rules, shouldUseSandbox.ts, MCP tool approval prompts, policy rate limits
  3. Secure Storage -- macOS Keychain (primary), plaintext JSON fallback (non-macOS)
  4. Shell Execution -- sandboxed shell process with path-validated access

The vulnerabilities concentrate at boundary transitions:

  • Boundary 1 gaps: Plugin downloads cross the input validation boundary with integrity checks but no authenticity checks (Findings 1, 2). ZIP extraction crosses with path traversal checks but no symlink resolution (Finding 4).
  • Boundary 2 gaps: Subagents cross the permission boundary with name-based tool filtering instead of process isolation (Finding 3). The dangerouslySkipPermissions flag can be forwarded to remote servers (Finding 12).
  • Boundary 3 gaps: On non-macOS platforms, the secure storage boundary does not exist -- credentials go directly to plaintext files (Findings 7, 8, 10).
  • Boundary 4 gaps: The bash security boundary depends on a single parser that may diverge from real shell behavior (Finding 11).

Vulnerability Concentration by Subsystem

Mapping all 50 findings to the subsystem that contains the vulnerable code reveals where security debt has accumulated:

Subsystem Findings CRITICAL HIGH MEDIUM LOW/INFO
Plugin/Extension 8 2 1 3 2
Credential Storage 7 0 4 2 1
Authentication/JWT 6 0 1 3 2
Network/Remote/Bridge 11 0 0 7 4
Bash Security 5 0 0 3 2
Data/Telemetry/Logging 8 0 1 4 3
Subagent Execution 3 0 2 1 0

The plugin/extension system contains 100% of the CRITICAL findings. The credential storage subsystem contains 50% of the HIGH findings. The network/remote/bridge subsystem has the highest absolute count but predominantly MEDIUM and LOW severity -- it is a broad surface but not a deep one.

This distribution informs the remediation strategy: fixing the plugin system (8 findings, 2 CRITICAL) and credential storage (7 findings, 4 HIGH) addresses 30% of all findings but eliminates 100% of CRITICAL and 62.5% of HIGH severity issues. This is the efficiency calculation behind Phase 1 and Phase 2 in the implementation roadmap detailed in Chapter 3.

For organizations subject to SOC 2 or HIPAA requirements, the plaintext credential storage findings (7, 8, 10) represent compliance blockers. The absence of encryption at rest for credentials and conversation history means the tool cannot be deployed in regulated environments without compensating controls.

OWASP Top 10 Coverage

The most dense coverage gaps cluster around three OWASP categories:

A02:2021 -- Cryptographic Failures carries five findings totaling a combined CVSS of 36.2. This category encompasses both the plaintext storage issues (no encryption at rest) and the JWT verification gap (no signature checking). For a tool that handles API keys and session tokens, cryptographic failures represent the most fundamental security gap. The remediation spans Phases 2 and 3 of the roadmap.

A08:2021 -- Software and Data Integrity Failures carries four findings including both CRITICALs. The complete absence of code signing for plugins places Claude Code in the worst-case position for this category. Any tool that downloads and executes third-party code without signature verification fails A08 categorically. Phase 1 of the roadmap addresses this directly.

A04:2021 -- Insecure Design carries three findings (3, 6, 14) that together describe a system where third-party code executes with full host privileges. The subagent isolation gap is a design-level issue -- it cannot be fixed with a patch to a single function. It requires a new architecture for how untrusted code executes. Phase 4 addresses this with the process isolation redesign.

Enterprise Adoption Implications

For organizations evaluating Claude Code for developer workflows, the compliance analysis produces three categories:

Deploy now with compensating controls: The bash security subsystem (100+ injection patterns, sandbox enforcement) is robust. The OAuth PKCE implementation is correct (Finding 50 confirms this). The permission system provides meaningful access control for local use.

Deploy after Phase 2: Once credential storage is encrypted across platforms, the tool meets baseline requirements for SOC 2 CC6.1 and HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(iv). This unlocks deployment in regulated industries.

Deploy after Phase 4: Process isolation for third-party plugins and MCP servers is required for environments where untrusted extensions may be installed. Until Phase 4, restricting to first-party plugins is a viable compensating control.

1.10 What Comes Next

This chapter has mapped the battlefield. You know the 50 vulnerabilities, their severities, their locations, and their compliance implications. But individual findings do not exist in isolation.

Chapter 2 dissects the seven dependency chains -- groups of vulnerabilities that interact with each other through shared code paths, shared data, or shared trust assumptions. A fix for one vulnerability in a chain can cascade to reduce risk across the entire group. Conversely, leaving the root of a chain unpatched means downstream fixes provide only partial protection.

Chapter 3 translates these chains into an implementation roadmap: seven phases, ordered by risk and dependency relationships, with resource estimates for the 35 direct patches and 15 architecture solutions.

The remaining 19 chapters of this book provide the exact code changes, test cases, and verification procedures for every finding in the catalog. Each chapter takes one dependency chain or remediation phase and walks through the complete fix -- from understanding the vulnerable code to deploying the hardened version to verifying it works.

This is not theory. This is a 50-item punch list with working patches. Let's get to work.

Chapter 2: Vulnerability Dependency Chain Analysis

Individual vulnerabilities are dangerous. Vulnerability chains are catastrophic. A MEDIUM-severity path traversal in ZIP extraction becomes a full code execution primitive when combined with an unsigned plugin download. A LOW-severity token override via environment variable becomes persistent unauthorized access when combined with a JWT that is decoded but never signature-verified.

This chapter dissects the seven dependency chains identified in Claude Code's vulnerability catalog. Each chain represents a group of findings that interact through shared code paths, shared data flows, or shared trust assumptions. Understanding these chains is prerequisite to the implementation roadmap in Chapter 3 -- you cannot sequence fixes correctly without knowing which vulnerabilities are load-bearing for others.

2.1 What Is a Dependency Chain?

A vulnerability dependency chain exists when exploiting one finding either enables or amplifies another. The relationship can be:

  • Sequential: Finding A must be exploited before Finding B becomes reachable (e.g., unsigned plugin download enables path traversal in extraction)
  • Amplifying: Finding A increases the blast radius of Finding B (e.g., plaintext credential storage makes token theft trivially easy once filesystem access is gained)
  • Compensating: Fixing Finding A partially mitigates Finding B even without a direct patch (e.g., process isolation for subagents limits damage from missing MCP sandboxing)

The seven chains span the entire vulnerability catalog. Some findings appear in multiple chains -- these are the highest-leverage fix targets. Others are chain-terminal findings that represent the final impact of an exploitation path.

2.2 Chain 1: Plugin Supply Chain

Severity: CRITICAL Findings: #1 (CVSS 9.1), #2 (CVSS 8.1), #4 (CVSS 7.5), #15 (CVSS 6.1), #25 (CVSS 5.3), #29 (CVSS 4.8) Affected Files: plugins/, utils/plugins/pluginLoader.ts, utils/plugins/marketplaceManager.ts, utils/plugins/zipCache.ts, utils/dxt/zip.ts, utils/plugins/pluginVersioning.ts Blast Radius: Full code execution on every developer machine that installs marketplace plugins

This is the highest-risk chain in the codebase. It flows from marketplace download through extraction to execution with no authenticity verification at any point.

The Attack Path

sequenceDiagram
    participant Attacker
    participant CDN as Marketplace CDN
    participant CLI as Claude Code CLI
    participant FS as Developer Filesystem

    Attacker->>CDN: Compromise marketplace entry or MITM download
    CDN->>CLI: Malicious plugin ZIP (valid hash, no signature)
    CLI->>CLI: SHA-256 hash check passes (computed over malicious payload)
    CLI->>FS: Extract ZIP
    Note over CLI,FS: #4: Symlinks followed without boundary check
    Note over CLI,FS: #15: No canonical path resolution
    CLI->>CLI: Register plugin
    Note over CLI: #29: Version uses 12-char git SHA (collision risk)
    CLI->>CLI: Plugin executes with full process privileges
    Note over CLI: Shell access, filesystem access, network access, credential access

The chain has five links:

  1. Root (Findings 1 + 2): No cryptographic signature verification. The marketplace JSON is fetched via axios.get() with no integrity check. Plugin ZIPs are downloaded without signature verification against a known author key. Hash checks confirm the download was not corrupted but do not verify authenticity.

  2. Extraction (Findings 4 + 15): Even if the ZIP contents were validated for authenticity, the extraction path has its own vulnerabilities. zipCache.ts:292-300 follows symlinks without validating that targets remain within the extraction root. The join() path construction does not canonicalize, allowing symlink-based escapes.

  3. Validation Gap (Finding 25): ZIP bomb detection occurs during extraction but not pre-download. There is no pre-flight check on the ZIP size from Content-Length headers. A multi-gigabyte ZIP bomb could consume disk and memory during extraction.

  4. Version Weakness (Finding 29): Plugin versions use 12-character git SHAs. While a 12-char hex prefix provides 48 bits of entropy (making random collisions improbable), targeted collision attacks against shortened hashes are well-documented. With sufficient compute, an attacker could produce a malicious commit with the same 12-character prefix as a legitimate plugin version.

Cascade Effect

Fixing Finding 1 (cryptographic plugin signing) provides the highest cascade reduction in the entire codebase. With signature verification in place:

  • Finding 2 is fully mitigated (signature covers the download)
  • Finding 4 is partially mitigated (a signed, authentic plugin is unlikely to contain malicious symlinks)
  • Finding 15 is partially mitigated (same reasoning)
  • Finding 25 is partially mitigated (signed plugins have known expected sizes)
  • Finding 29 is partially mitigated (signatures provide stronger version binding than hashes)

However, Findings 4 and 15 still require independent fixes because the path traversal defense should be robust against any ZIP input, not just malicious plugins. Defense in depth requires that extraction is safe regardless of whether the source is trusted. As we'll detail in Chapter 5, the three-layer defense for ZIP extraction (pre-extraction validation, canonical path resolution, post-write TOCTOU verification) should be implemented even after signing infrastructure is in place.

Implementation Dependency

Findings 4 and 15 can be fixed independently with direct patches to zipCache.ts. The fix is a realpath-based boundary check:

// Secure extraction with canonical path resolution
const canonicalTarget = await realpath(targetDir)
const targetPrefix = canonicalTarget + sep

for (const [relPath, data] of Object.entries(files)) {
  const fullPath = join(canonicalTarget, relPath)
  const resolvedPath = resolve(fullPath)

  // Reject any path that escapes the extraction root
  if (!resolvedPath.startsWith(targetPrefix) && resolvedPath !== canonicalTarget) {
    throw new Error(
      `Zip entry escapes target directory: ${relPath} resolves to ${resolvedPath}`
    )
  }

  // Post-write verification catches symlink TOCTOU
  await writeFile(fullPath, data)
  const realWrittenPath = await realpath(fullPath)
  if (!realWrittenPath.startsWith(targetPrefix)) {
    await unlink(fullPath).catch(() => {})
    throw new Error(
      `Zip extraction TOCTOU: ${relPath} wrote to ${realWrittenPath} outside target`
    )
  }
}

Findings 1 and 2 require architecture changes (ECDSA signing infrastructure, marketplace integration, key management) and are addressed in Chapters 4 and 5.

2.3 Chain 2: Credential Storage

Severity: HIGH Findings: #7 (CVSS 7.1), #8 (CVSS 7.1), #10 (CVSS 6.5), #20 (CVSS 5.5), #30 (CVSS 4.7), #37 (CVSS 3.7), #39 (CVSS 3.3) Affected Files: utils/secureStorage/index.ts, utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts, utils/secureStorage/macOsKeychainStorage.ts, utils/secureStorage/fallbackStorage.ts Blast Radius: OAuth tokens, API keys, and trusted device tokens exposed on all non-macOS platforms and macOS fallback scenarios

This chain targets the credential lifecycle from storage to retrieval, with every link weakening the protection of the most sensitive data in the system.

The Storage Decision Tree

The current credential storage architecture makes a single platform check:

flowchart TD
    A["getSecureStorage()"] --> B{"process.platform === 'darwin'?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["createFallbackStorage(keychain, plaintext)"]
    B -->|No| D["plainTextStorage<br/>#7: CWE-256 CVSS 7.1"]
    C --> E{"Keychain write succeeds?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["macOS Keychain<br/>(secure)"]
    E -->|No| G["plainTextStorage fallback<br/>#8: CWE-312 CVSS 7.1"]
    D --> H["~/.claude/.credentials.json<br/>chmod 0600<br/>Plaintext JSON"]
    G --> H
    H --> I{"writeFileSync then chmodSync"}
    I --> J["#30: TOCTOU race<br/>Permission window between write and chmod"]

Every non-macOS platform -- Linux desktops, WSL, Windows, Docker containers, CI/CD runners -- takes the plaintext path. On macOS, Docker containers and SSH sessions typically fail the keychain path and silently fall back to plaintext.

Chain Links

  1. Root (Findings 7 + 10): getSecureStorage() at index.ts:9 returns plainTextStorage for all non-macOS platforms. The TODO comment "add libsecret support for Linux" confirms this is a known gap. OAuth tokens and API keys are stored as JSON with only chmod 0600 protection.

  2. Fallback Amplifier (Finding 8): On macOS, when keychain fails (Docker, SSH, CI), fallbackStorage.ts silently activates plaintext storage. The createFallbackStorage wrapper logs a warning but proceeds. The fallback path at plainTextStorage.ts:57 writes credentials with writeFileSync then applies chmodSync(0o600) -- creating a TOCTOU window.

  3. TOCTOU Race (Finding 30): The write-then-chmod pattern at plainTextStorage.ts:57 creates a window where the file exists with default permissions (potentially 0o644) before chmodSync applies 0o600. Any process monitoring the directory can read credentials during this window.

  4. Keychain Injection (Finding 20): The macOS keychain read path at macOsKeychainStorage.ts:39 constructs shell commands with credential data. If a service name contains shell metacharacters, command injection is possible in the sync fallback path.

  5. Process Argument Leak (Finding 37): The keychain fallback path at macOsKeychainStorage.ts:118 passes credentials as command-line arguments, making them visible in ps output and /proc/*/cmdline.

  6. Migration Race (Finding 39): fallbackStorage.ts:37 implements credential migration from primary to fallback storage with a race condition -- concurrent migrations can corrupt the credential file.

Cascade Effect

Fixing Finding 7 (implementing libsecret for Linux and Windows Credential Manager for Windows) eliminates Findings 10 and 8 for their primary platforms. The plaintext path becomes a last-resort fallback rather than the default for 40%+ of installations.

Fixing Finding 30 (atomic credential writes with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, fsync, and rename) eliminates the TOCTOU window regardless of which storage backend is active:

// Atomic write: create temp file with correct permissions, then rename
const tmpPath = storagePath + '.tmp.' + process.pid
const fd = openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)
try {
  writeSync(fd, jsonStringify(updated), 0, 'utf8')
  fsyncSync(fd)
} finally {
  closeSync(fd)
}
renameSync(tmpPath, storagePath)

The credential storage chain has a strong dependency on the Auth Token Lifecycle chain (Chain 3). Secure credential storage is prerequisite to safe token rotation -- if the storage is plaintext, rotating tokens provides minimal additional security because both old and new tokens are equally exposed. This dependency drives the phase ordering in Chapter 3: credential storage (Phase 2) must precede token lifecycle hardening (Phase 3).

2.4 Chain 3: Auth Token Lifecycle

Severity: HIGH Findings: #5 (CVSS 7.5), #13 (CVSS 6.5), #16 (CVSS 5.9), #32 (CVSS 4.3), #34 (CVSS 4.3), #41 (CVSS 3.1) Affected Files: bridge/jwtUtils.ts, utils/auth.ts, bridge/trustedDevice.ts Blast Radius: JWT tokens decoded without signature verification, env var tokens that never refresh, token prefixes leaked in debug logs

This chain targets the complete lifecycle of authentication tokens from issuance through verification, refresh, and eventual expiration.

The Token Flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant Server as Auth Server
    participant CLI as Claude Code
    participant JWT as jwtUtils.ts
    participant Auth as auth.ts
    participant Trust as trustedDevice.ts
    participant Log as Debug Logs

    Server->>CLI: Issue JWT (signed server-side)
    CLI->>JWT: decodeJwtPayload()
    Note over JWT: #5: Base64 decode ONLY<br/>No signature verification
    JWT->>CLI: Payload with exp claim
    CLI->>CLI: scheduleTokenRefresh(exp)
    Note over CLI: #16: Unverified exp controls timer<br/>Far-future exp suppresses refresh

    alt Environment Variable Token
        Note over Auth: #13: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<br/>Never expires, never refreshes
        Auth->>Auth: Token used until process exit
    end

    alt Device Trust Token
        Trust->>Trust: Read from keychain
        Note over Trust: #34: CLAUDE_DEVICE_TOKEN<br/>env var overrides keychain
    end

    CLI->>Log: logForDebugging()
    Note over Log: #32: token.slice(0,15) logged<br/>#41: JWT prefix in debug output

Chain Links

  1. Root (Finding 5): decodeJwtPayload() at jwtUtils.ts:21 performs base64 decoding without signature verification. The exp claim from the unverified payload directly controls token refresh scheduling. An attacker who can modify the JWT in transit (via corporate proxy, compromised DNS, or MITM on the bridge connection) can forge arbitrary claims.

  2. Timer Manipulation (Finding 16): The schedule() function computes delayMs = expiry * 1000 - Date.now() - refreshBufferMs directly from the unverified exp claim. A far-future exp (year 2100) sets a delay of ~74 years, effectively suppressing token refresh forever. A near-past exp triggers constant refresh attempts (DoS). No bounds checking exists on the computed delay.

  3. Token Persistence (Finding 13): Tokens provided via ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable at auth.ts:1260 never expire and never refresh. Even if the server revokes the token, the CLI continues using it until the process exits. In CI/CD pipelines, this means leaked tokens remain valid indefinitely.

  4. Device Token Override (Finding 34): The CLAUDE_DEVICE_TOKEN environment variable at trustedDevice.ts:46 overrides the keychain-stored device trust token. Combined with Finding 13, an attacker who sets this env var gains persistent device-level trust without keychain access.

  5. Debug Log Leakage (Findings 32 + 41): Token prefixes appear in debug output at jwtUtils.ts:112 and jwtUtils.ts:110 via token.slice(0, 15). While 15 characters of a token prefix have limited direct value, they confirm token format, aid in targeted attacks, and may violate compliance requirements for credential logging.

Cascade Effect

The primary fix for this chain is the clampTokenRefreshDelay() defense at the schedule function. This bounds the refresh delay to a safe range regardless of the JWT payload:

const MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 // 24 hours
const MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS = 10_000 // 10 seconds

function clampTokenRefreshDelay(rawDelayMs: number): number {
  if (rawDelayMs <= 0) return 0
  if (rawDelayMs < MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS) return MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS
  if (rawDelayMs > MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS) return MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS
  return rawDelayMs
}

This single function mitigates Findings 5 and 16 simultaneously. The ideal fix (client-side JWKS-based signature verification) requires server-side changes to publish a JWKS endpoint, making it a longer-term solution explored in Chapter 10. The clamp is an immediate compensating control that limits damage even without signature verification.

Removing token.slice(0, 15) from debug log statements (Findings 32, 41) is a zero-risk, zero-dependency fix that can be applied in any phase.

2.5 Chain 4: Subagent Isolation

Severity: HIGH Findings: #3 (CVSS 7.8), #6 (CVSS 7.5), #14 (CVSS 6.2) Affected Files: tools/AgentTool/runAgent.ts, tools/AgentTool/forkSubagent.ts, services/mcp/ Blast Radius: Subagents and MCP server tools execute with full parent process privileges; recursive forking possible

This is the shortest chain but carries severe consequences. Three findings combine to create a scenario where a malicious plugin can achieve persistent, escalating access through the agent system.

The Exploitation Scenario

flowchart TD
    A["Malicious plugin defines agent"] --> B["runAgent() loads agent<br/>in parent process<br/>#3: CWE-269 CVSS 7.8"]
    B --> C["Agent inherits all tools<br/>Name-based filtering only<br/>Not process-level isolation"]
    C --> D["Agent accesses shared AppState<br/>Can read credentials, history"]
    D --> E["Agent calls AgentTool<br/>to fork children<br/>#14: CWE-674 CVSS 6.2"]
    E --> F{"isInForkChild() check"}
    F -->|"Only checks single-layer<br/>boilerplate tag"| G["Child agent spawned"]
    G --> H["Child inherits all tools<br/>Including AgentTool"]
    H --> I["Child forks grandchild<br/>Recursive until OOM"]

    J["MCP server tool approved"] --> K["Tool executes in CLI process<br/>#6: CWE-250 CVSS 7.5"]
    K --> C

Chain Links

  1. Root (Finding 3): runAgent.ts:248 runs subagents in the parent Bun process. At lines 332-338, the agent shares AppState. At lines 465-479, tool restriction is name-based filtering -- not process-level isolation. At lines 567-575, agent frontmatter hooks execute in the parent context. A malicious subagent has full access to credentials, filesystem, network, and the tool registry.

  2. MCP Amplifier (Finding 6): MCP server tools execute within the CLI process's security context with no sandboxing. The services/mcp/channelPermissions.ts implements permission prompts but not isolation. Once a user approves an MCP tool, it runs with complete CLI privileges. Combined with Finding 3, an MCP server can spawn agents that inherit the same unrestricted access.

  3. Recursive Forking (Finding 14): forkSubagent.ts:311 implements fork depth checking via isInForkChild(), which only detects a single-layer boilerplate tag. The function answers "am I in a fork child?" but not "how deep am I?" A child agent retains the AgentTool, enabling recursive forking. Each fork inherits the full tool set. The only limit is memory exhaustion.

Cascade Effect

This chain has a strong dependency on Chain 1 (Plugin Supply Chain). If plugin signing is implemented (Findings 1, 2), the probability of a malicious plugin being installed drops significantly. However, the subagent isolation fix is still necessary because:

  1. Legitimate plugins may be compromised through supply chain attacks
  2. MCP servers from the marketplace may contain vulnerabilities
  3. Defense in depth requires isolation regardless of source trust

The fix architecture involves three layers:

  • Process isolation (Finding 3): child_process.fork() with IPC channels for plugin-sourced agents
  • Fork depth enforcement (Finding 14): MAX_FORK_DEPTH=3 with cryptographic depth tracking via fork-depth tags
  • MCP sandboxing (Finding 6): seccomp-bpf profiles for Linux, sandbox-exec for macOS, capability-based restrictions per MCP server

The implementation order matters: fork depth enforcement (a direct patch, ~4-6 hours) should be deployed before process isolation (an architecture change, ~40+ hours) because it provides immediate protection against recursive fork bombs.

2.6 Chain 5: Data Exfiltration

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH Findings: #9 (CVSS 7.0), #24 (CVSS 5.3), #26 (CVSS 5.3), #33 (CVSS 4.3), #38 (CVSS 3.5), #43 (CVSS 2.7), #47 (CVSS 2.4), #49 (CVSS 1.8) Affected Files: history.ts, services/analytics/datadog.ts, services/analytics/firstPartyEventLogger.ts, services/analytics/metadata.ts, services/analytics/config.ts, utils/debug.ts Blast Radius: Conversation history, pasted secrets, telemetry metadata, debug artifacts

This is the largest chain by finding count, connecting conversation history storage to telemetry pipelines to debug logging. The attack is not a single exploitation but a persistent accumulation of sensitive data across multiple unprotected channels.

The Data Accumulation

flowchart LR

    B --> C["~/.claude/history.jsonl<br/>No encryption, no TTL"]

    D["Session metadata"] --> E["datadog.ts:14<br/>#24: Hardcoded client token<br/>CVSS 5.3"]
    E --> F["64+ event types<br/>sent to Datadog"]

    G["Tool arguments"] --> H["metadata.ts:291<br/>#47: Args in telemetry<br/>CVSS 2.4"]
    H --> F

    I["Analytics config"] --> J["firstPartyEventLogger.ts:95<br/>#38: GrowthBook remote config<br/>CVSS 3.5"]
    J --> F

    K["Debug logging"] --> L["debug.ts:221<br/>#43: Token prefixes, session IDs<br/>CVSS 2.7"]
    L --> M["Debug log files<br/>On disk"]

    F --> N["#33: No explicit consent UI<br/>#49: Opt-out incomplete<br/>CVSS 4.3 / 1.8"]

    style B fill:#db6d28,color:#fff
    style E fill:#d29922,color:#fff

Chain Links

  1. Root (Finding 9): All conversation history including pasted secrets persists in plaintext JSONL at ~/.claude/history.jsonl. The history.ts:115 path stores small pastes inline, large pastes in ~/.claude/paste-cache/{sha256}.txt. No secret detection, no redaction, no TTL, no purging.

  2. Hardcoded Telemetry Token (Findings 24 + 26): services/analytics/datadog.ts:13-14 contains a hardcoded Datadog client token. This token enables 64+ event types to be sent to a third-party analytics service. The token is visible in source code, making it extractable.

  3. Third-Party Data Sharing (Finding 33): Telemetry data is sent to Datadog at datadog.ts:160 without explicit user consent UI. While an opt-out mechanism exists, it is not prominently surfaced during onboarding.

  4. Remote Configuration (Finding 38): The analytics pipeline is partially controlled by GrowthBook remote configuration at firstPartyEventLogger.ts:95. A compromised GrowthBook endpoint could enable additional data collection without CLI-side code changes.

  5. Debug Log Leakage (Finding 43): Debug logs at utils/debug.ts:221 may contain token prefixes, session IDs, and URLs. These logs persist on disk without rotation or sanitization.

  6. Incomplete Opt-Out (Finding 49): Analytics opt-out at services/analytics/config.ts:19 does not cover all data flows, leaving some telemetry active even when the user has opted out.

Cascade Effect

The conversation history fix (Finding 9) has the highest impact: implementing automatic secret detection and redaction prevents the most sensitive data from ever reaching disk. This reduces the value of all downstream data channels.

The telemetry fixes (Findings 24, 26, 33) require both code changes (token rotation, data minimization) and process changes (explicit consent UI). These are addressed in Chapter 19.

2.7 Chain 6: Bridge Remote Session

Severity: MEDIUM Findings: #12 (CVSS 6.5), #17 (CVSS 5.9), #18 (CVSS 5.9), #21 (CVSS 5.5), #22 (CVSS 5.4), #23 (CVSS 5.3), #28 (CVSS 5.0), #31 (CVSS 4.4), #42 (CVSS 3.1), #44 (CVSS 2.5), #45 (CVSS 3.2) Affected Files: server/createDirectConnectSession.ts, remote/SessionsWebSocket.ts, upstreamproxy/relay.ts, upstreamproxy/upstreamproxy.ts, tools/WebFetchTool/utils.ts, services/api/client.ts Blast Radius: Enterprise users with remote/bridge sessions and upstream proxy configurations

This is the largest chain by affected file count, connecting remote session management through WebSocket communication to upstream proxy infrastructure. The attack scenario involves a compromised proxy intercepting and manipulating bridge sessions.

The Attack Scenario

The chain enables a multi-step attack:

  1. Attacker compromises the upstream proxy or performs DNS spoofing on the proxy endpoint
  2. CA bundle is downloaded without certificate pinning (#18), allowing a forged CA to be installed
  3. The proxy intercepts the bridge WebSocket connection (#21, no client-side origin validation)
  4. Proxy credentials are visible in WebSocket headers (#22) and persist in memory (#23, #31)
  5. The dangerouslySkipPermissions flag is forwarded to the remote server (#12)
  6. Custom headers are injectable via environment variables (#28)
  7. The compromised session operates with no permission guardrails

Key Fix Points

The highest-leverage fix in this chain is the localhost restriction for dangerouslySkipPermissions:

// server/createDirectConnectSession.ts -- SECURE
const parsedServerUrl = new URL(serverUrl)
const isLocalServer =
  parsedServerUrl.hostname === 'localhost' ||
  parsedServerUrl.hostname === '127.0.0.1' ||
  parsedServerUrl.hostname === '::1'

if (dangerouslySkipPermissions && !isLocalServer) {
  throw new DirectConnectError(
    'dangerouslySkipPermissions is only allowed for localhost connections. ' +
      `Refusing to send to remote server: ${parsedServerUrl.hostname}`
  )
}

This single check (Finding 12) prevents the most dangerous part of the chain -- sending permission bypass flags to remote servers. The remaining findings in this chain are defense-in-depth improvements that should be implemented but are not individually exploitable without the permission bypass.

The CA certificate pinning fix (Finding 18) at upstreamproxy/upstreamproxy.ts:254 validates downloaded certificates against known fingerprints, preventing proxy CA impersonation. The SSRF guard (Finding 17) at WebFetchTool/utils.ts:262 blocks DNS rebinding attacks where a permitted domain resolves to internal IP addresses.

2.8 Chain 7: Bash Security Bypass

Severity: MEDIUM Findings: #11 (CVSS 6.8), #19 (CVSS 5.9), #27 (CVSS 5.0), #35 (CVSS 4.0), #46 (CVSS 3.1) Affected Files: tools/BashTool/bashSecurity.ts, tools/BashTool/bashPermissions.ts, tools/BashTool/modeValidation.ts, tools/FileWriteTool/FileWriteTool.ts Blast Radius: All CLI users via the bash execution path

This chain targets the command validation pipeline -- the most security-critical path in the entire codebase. The existing defenses are substantial (100+ injection patterns, 40+ validators), but the architecture has a fundamental fragility: it depends on a single parser that may diverge from real shell behavior.

The Parser Differential Problem

flowchart TD
    A["LLM generates command"] --> B["tryParseShellCommand()<br/>shell-quote tokenization"]
    B --> C{"Parser output<br/>matches real shell?"}
    C -->|"Yes (99.9%)"| D["Security validators<br/>check tokens<br/>100+ patterns"]
    C -->|"No (0.1%)"| E["#11: Parser differential<br/>Validators operate on<br/>wrong tokens<br/>CWE-436 CVSS 6.8"]
    D --> F{"Validators pass?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["Command executes<br/>in real shell"]
    F -->|No| H["Command blocked"]
    E --> I["Command passes validators<br/>with different semantics<br/>than real shell"]
    I --> G
    G --> J["Real shell interprets<br/>command differently<br/>than validators expected"]

    K["#19: ReDoS in env var regex<br/>bashPermissions.ts:760<br/>CVSS 5.9"] --> L["Permission pipeline<br/>freezes"]
    M["#27: TOCTOU in FileWriteTool<br/>FileWriteTool.ts:267<br/>CVSS 5.0"] --> N["File contents change<br/>between check and write"]
    O["#35: acceptEdits auto-allows<br/>destructive commands<br/>CVSS 4.0"] --> P["rm, mv, chmod<br/>without prompt"]

Chain Links

  1. Root (Finding 11): bashSecurity.ts:27 calls tryParseShellCommand() which uses the custom shell-quote parser. On parse failure, line 29 returns an empty array. Six dedicated misparsing validators cover known divergences, but they are reactive -- they cannot anticipate unknown parser bugs. The 450+ lines of heredoc handling in isSafeHeredoc increase the parser attack surface.

  2. ReDoS (Finding 19): Complex regex patterns in bashPermissions.ts:760 for environment variable stripping are susceptible to catastrophic backtracking. A crafted input could freeze the permission pipeline, effectively creating a denial-of-service against the security validation itself.

  3. TOCTOU in File Write (Finding 27): FileWriteTool/FileWriteTool.ts:267 has a race condition between the read-state check (verifying what the file currently contains) and the write operation. Between these two operations, the file could be replaced by a symlink or modified by another process.

  4. Accept Edits Mode (Finding 35): modeValidation.ts:37 auto-allows filesystem commands (including destructive operations like rm, mv, chmod) in acceptEdits mode without prompting the user. This bypasses the permission system for an entire class of dangerous operations.

  5. Inherent Risk Acknowledgment (Finding 46): This INFO-level finding at bashSecurity.ts:1 acknowledges that regex-based security validation cannot achieve the same correctness guarantees as a proper AST-based parser. It is the informational companion to Finding 11.

Cascade Effect

This chain is unique in that no single fix eliminates the root vulnerability. The parser differential problem (Finding 11) is architectural -- it requires adding a secondary parser (tree-sitter-bash) for cross-validation and implementing fuzz testing to discover unknown divergences. This is the most complex fix in the entire remediation plan.

However, the compensating controls are effective:

  • Fixing Finding 19 (replacing ReDoS-susceptible regex with iterative parsing) ensures the permission pipeline cannot be frozen
  • Fixing Finding 27 (atomic file operations in FileWriteTool) closes the TOCTOU window
  • Fixing Finding 35 (splitting acceptEdits mode for destructive vs. non-destructive operations) restores user prompts for dangerous commands

2.9 Cross-Chain Dependencies

Three critical dependency relationships span across chains:

Chain 1 (Plugin Supply Chain) --> Chain 4 (Subagent Isolation)

A malicious plugin (Chain 1) that defines a subagent exploits the lack of process isolation (Chain 4). Fixing Chain 1 reduces the probability of malicious plugins; fixing Chain 4 limits the damage if one gets through. Both chains must be hardened.

Chain 2 (Credential Storage) --> Chain 3 (Auth Token Lifecycle)

Token rotation (Chain 3) is only as secure as the storage where rotated tokens are kept (Chain 2). Implementing token rotation on a plaintext storage backend means both old and new tokens are equally exposed. This drives the phase ordering: credential storage encryption must precede token lifecycle hardening.

Chain 5 (Data Exfiltration) --> Chain 2 (Credential Storage)

Plaintext conversation history (Chain 5, Finding 9) may contain credentials. Even if the credential storage is encrypted (Chain 2), secrets pasted during sessions remain exposed in history files. Both chains must be independently secured.

2.10 Prioritization Framework

Given the seven chains and their dependencies, the prioritization framework for Chapter 3's implementation roadmap follows this logic:

  1. Fix the highest blast radius first: Plugin Supply Chain (Chain 1) affects every user who installs plugins
  2. Fix prerequisites before dependents: Credential Storage (Chain 2) before Token Lifecycle (Chain 3)
  3. Fix enablers before amplifiers: Plugin signing (Chain 1) before subagent isolation (Chain 4)
  4. Fix high-urgency before low-urgency: Direct patches with known exploits before defense-in-depth improvements
  5. Batch by affected subsystem: Group fixes that touch the same files to minimize merge conflicts and regression risk

This prioritization produces the seven-phase roadmap detailed in Chapter 3, where each phase addresses one or more complete dependency chains while respecting the inter-chain dependencies documented in this chapter.

Chapter 3: Implementation Roadmap

You have the vulnerability map from Chapter 1. You have the dependency chains from Chapter 2. Now you need a plan that accounts for risk ordering, implementation dependencies, and resource constraints. This chapter defines the seven-phase remediation plan: 35 direct patches and 15 architecture solutions, sequenced to maximize risk reduction per engineering hour invested.

3.1 Roadmap Design Principles

Five principles drive the phase sequencing:

Principle 1: Highest blast radius first. The Plugin Supply Chain chain (Findings 1, 2, 4, 15) affects every CLI user who installs marketplace plugins. It is Phase 1 regardless of implementation complexity.

Principle 2: Prerequisites before dependents. Credential storage encryption (Phase 2) must precede token lifecycle hardening (Phase 3) because rotating tokens into a plaintext backend provides minimal security improvement.

Principle 3: Direct patches before architecture changes. Within each phase, deploy direct patches (code-level fixes that do not change interfaces or data flows) before architecture solutions (changes to system design, new infrastructure, cross-team coordination). Direct patches provide immediate risk reduction while architecture work proceeds.

Principle 4: Defense in depth at every phase. Each phase should leave the system in a strictly better security state, even if subsequent phases are delayed or deprioritized. No phase should introduce regression risk.

Principle 5: Testable milestones. Each phase has defined success metrics that can be verified without human judgment: specific tests that pass, specific attack scenarios that fail, specific compliance checkboxes that clear.

3.2 Resource Estimation

The 50 findings decompose into two categories with different resource profiles:

Category Count Total Hours Avg Hours/Finding Requires
Direct Patches 35 ~61 hours 1.7 hours Code change, unit tests, code review
Architecture Solutions 15 ~464 hours 31 hours Design doc, cross-team review, infrastructure, integration tests
Total 50 ~525 hours 10.5 hours

The disparity is stark: 70% of findings can be fixed with ~12% of the total effort. This is the 80/20 distribution that drives the direct-patches-first principle.

pie title Effort Distribution

    "Architecture Solutions (15 findings)" : 464

3.3 Phase 1: Plugin Supply Chain Hardening

Priority: CRITICAL Duration: 4-6 weeks Findings: #1 (CVSS 9.1), #2 (CVSS 8.1), #4 (CVSS 7.5), #15 (CVSS 6.1) Effort: ~160 hours (4h direct patches + 156h architecture) Dependency Chain: Plugin Supply Chain (Chapter 2, Section 2.2)

Why First

Unsigned plugins represent the highest blast radius vulnerability in the codebase. A compromised marketplace or CDN can deliver arbitrary code to every user who installs or updates plugins. No other vulnerability class affects as many users with as little attacker effort.

Phase 1A: Direct Patches (Week 1)

Deploy path traversal fixes before signing infrastructure is ready:

Finding Fix Hours Files Changed
#4 Canonical path resolution with realpath() + post-write TOCTOU check 4-6 zipCache.ts, zip.ts
#15 Same fix as #4 (shared extraction code path) 0 (included) Same files

The ZIP extraction fix is self-contained and can be deployed immediately:

// utils/plugins/zipCache.ts -- extractZipToDirectory()
import { realpath, unlink } from 'fs/promises'
import { resolve, sep } from 'path'

const canonicalTarget = await realpath(targetDir)
const targetPrefix = canonicalTarget + sep

for (const [relPath, data] of Object.entries(files)) {
  const fullPath = join(canonicalTarget, relPath)
  const resolvedPath = resolve(fullPath)

  // Pre-write: verify resolved path stays within extraction root
  if (!resolvedPath.startsWith(targetPrefix) && resolvedPath !== canonicalTarget) {
    throw new Error(
      `Zip entry escapes target directory: ${relPath} resolves to ${resolvedPath}`
    )
  }

  await getFsImplementation().mkdir(dirname(fullPath))
  await writeFile(fullPath, data)

  // Post-write: catch symlink TOCTOU where parent dir replaced between mkdir and write
  const realWrittenPath = await realpath(fullPath)
  if (!realWrittenPath.startsWith(targetPrefix)) {
    await unlink(fullPath).catch(() => {})
    throw new Error(
      `Zip extraction TOCTOU: ${relPath} wrote to ${realWrittenPath} outside target`
    )
  }
}

Verification: - Unit: ZIP entry with ../../etc/passwd rejected before write - Unit: ZIP entry resolving outside target via symlink rejected - Unit: Normal ZIP with nested directories extracts successfully - Unit: Post-write realpath check detects symlink TOCTOU

3.4 Phase 2: Credential Storage Encryption

Priority: HIGH Duration: 3-4 weeks Findings: #7 (CVSS 7.1), #8 (CVSS 7.1), #10 (CVSS 6.5), #30 (CVSS 4.7), #39 (CVSS 3.3) Effort: ~100 hours (12h direct patches + 88h architecture) Dependency Chain: Credential Storage (Chapter 2, Section 2.3) Prerequisite for: Phase 3 (Auth Token Lifecycle)

Why Second

Plaintext credential storage on Linux/non-macOS platforms is the most common real-world attack vector: backup exfiltration, container escape, shared filesystem access, CI/CD credential theft. This phase is prerequisite to Phase 3 because token rotation is only meaningful when the storage backend is encrypted.

Phase 2A: Direct Patches (Week 1)

Finding Fix Hours Files Changed
#30 Atomic credential write with O_CREAT\|O_EXCL + fsync + rename 2-4 plainTextStorage.ts
#39 Mutex/lock on credential migration path 2-3 fallbackStorage.ts

The atomic write fix eliminates the TOCTOU window between writeFileSync and chmodSync:

// utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts -- update()
import { openSync, writeSync, closeSync, fsyncSync, renameSync, unlinkSync } from 'fs'

async update(
  updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<void> {
  const storagePath = getStoragePath()
  const dir = dirname(storagePath)
  if (!existsSync(dir)) {
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })
  }
  const existing = await this.read()
  const updated = updater(existing ?? {})

  // Atomic write: file created with 0o600 from the start
  const tmpPath = storagePath + '.tmp.' + process.pid
  try {
    const fd = openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)
    try {
      writeSync(fd, jsonStringify(updated), 0, 'utf8')
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    renameSync(tmpPath, storagePath)
  } catch (err) {
    try { unlinkSync(tmpPath) } catch { /* ignore */ }
    throw err
  }
}

Verification: - Unit: update() creates file with 0o600 permissions atomically (no 0o644 window) - Unit: update() uses atomic rename (no half-written credential file) - Unit: update() cleans up temp file on write failure - Integration: stat() after update() confirms mode 0o600

3.5 Phase 3: Auth Token Lifecycle Hardening

Priority: HIGH Duration: 2-3 weeks Findings: #5 (CVSS 7.5), #13 (CVSS 6.5), #16 (CVSS 5.9), #32 (CVSS 4.3), #41 (CVSS 3.1) Effort: ~65 hours (18h direct patches + 47h architecture) Dependency Chain: Auth Token Lifecycle (Chapter 2, Section 2.4) Depends on: Phase 2 (Credential Storage)

Why Third

JWT signature verification and token refresh hardening depend on secure credential storage. Rotating a token into a plaintext file does not improve security. With Phase 2 complete, token lifecycle improvements provide meaningful additional protection.

Phase 3A: Direct Patches (Week 1)

Finding Fix Hours Files Changed

The clampTokenRefreshDelay() function is the highest-leverage patch in this phase:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts
const MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 // 24 hours
const MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS = 10_000 // 10 seconds

function clampTokenRefreshDelay(rawDelayMs: number): number {
  if (rawDelayMs <= 0) return 0
  if (rawDelayMs < MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS) return MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS
  if (rawDelayMs > MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS) return MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS
  return rawDelayMs
}

Combined with Number.isFinite() validation and reasonable range checks on the exp claim:

export function decodeJwtExpiry(token: string): number | null {
  const payload = decodeJwtPayload(token)
  if (
    payload !== null &&
    typeof payload === 'object' &&
    'exp' in payload &&
    typeof payload.exp === 'number' &&
    Number.isFinite(payload.exp)
  ) {
    const MIN_REASONABLE_EXP = 1577836800 // 2020-01-01
    const MAX_REASONABLE_EXP = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60
    if (payload.exp < MIN_REASONABLE_EXP || payload.exp > MAX_REASONABLE_EXP) {
      return null
    }
    return payload.exp
  }
  return null
}

Verification: - Unit: clampTokenRefreshDelay(0) returns 0 - Unit: clampTokenRefreshDelay(5000) returns MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS (10000) - Unit: clampTokenRefreshDelay(48 * 3600 * 1000) returns MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS - Unit: decodeJwtExpiry rejects NaN and Infinity exp claims - Unit: decodeJwtExpiry rejects exp before 2020 and more than 1 year in the future - Unit: Token prefix no longer appears in debug output

However, Phase 1 (plugin signing) significantly reduces the probability of malicious plugins entering the system, buying time for the isolation work. The fork depth fix is a direct patch that provides immediate protection against fork bombs.

Phase 4A: Direct Patch (Week 1)

Finding Fix Hours Files Changed
#14 MAX_FORK_DEPTH=3 with depth tracking via fork-depth tags 4-6 forkSubagent.ts

The fork depth enforcement replaces the single-layer boilerplate check:

const MAX_FORK_DEPTH = 3
const FORK_DEPTH_TAG = 'fork-depth'

export function getForkDepth(messages: MessageType[]): number {
  let maxDepth = 0
  for (const m of messages) {
    if (m.type !== 'user') continue
    const content = m.message.content
    if (!Array.isArray(content)) continue
    for (const block of content) {
      if (block.type !== 'text') continue
      const match = block.text.match(
        new RegExp(`<${FORK_DEPTH_TAG}>(\\d+)</${FORK_DEPTH_TAG}>`),
      )
      if (match) {
        const depth = parseInt(match[1], 10)
        if (depth > maxDepth) maxDepth = depth
      }
    }
  }
  return maxDepth
}

export function canFork(
  messages: MessageType[],
): { allowed: true } | { allowed: false; reason: string } {
  const depth = getForkDepth(messages)
  if (depth >= MAX_FORK_DEPTH) {
    return {
      allowed: false,
      reason: `Maximum fork depth (${MAX_FORK_DEPTH}) reached. Cannot create nested subagent at depth ${depth + 1}.`,
    }
  }
  return { allowed: true }
}

The secret detection and redaction pattern for conversation history:

// Patterns that indicate secrets in pasted content
const SECRET_PATTERNS = [
  /(?:sk|pk|api[_-]?key|token|secret|password|bearer)\s*[:=]\s*\S{20,}/gi,
  /(?:AKIA|ABIA|ACCA|ASIA)[A-Z0-9]{16}/g,  // AWS access key
  /ghp_[A-Za-z0-9_]{36}/g,                   // GitHub PAT
  /gho_[A-Za-z0-9_]{36}/g,                   // GitHub OAuth
  /sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}/g,                    // OpenAI/Anthropic keys
  /-----BEGIN (?:RSA |EC )?PRIVATE KEY-----/g,
]

function redactSecrets(text: string): string {
  let redacted = text
  for (const pattern of SECRET_PATTERNS) {
    redacted = redacted.replace(pattern, '[REDACTED]')
  }
  return redacted
}

3.13 Rollback Strategy

Every patch and architecture change must be independently rollbackable. The rollback strategy varies by fix type:

Direct patches: Feature-flagged behind environment variables. Rolling back means setting the flag:

const USE_SECURE_ZIP_EXTRACTION = process.env.CLAUDE_LEGACY_ZIP !== '1'

Architecture solutions: Blue-green deployment with fallback to previous storage backend:

// Credential storage migration with rollback
const storage = getSecureStorage()
try {
  await storage.write(credentials)
} catch (err) {
  // Fallback to previous storage on migration failure
  logForDebugging(`Secure storage write failed, falling back: ${err.message}`)
  await legacyStorage.write(credentials)
}

Cross-team changes (signing infrastructure, JWKS endpoints): Version negotiation where the client accepts both signed and unsigned plugins during a transition period, with unsigned acceptance sunset after a defined date.
