Performance Budget

The total overhead for all thirteen checkpoints:

Phase Added Latency Notes
HEAD request 50-100ms One-time per download, not per startup
Signature verification ~3.5ms SHA-256 + ECDSA-P256
Path traversal checks ~0.1ms per entry resolve() is string manipulation
Post-write realpath ~0.5ms per entry Filesystem call, cached by OS
Integrity manifest verify ~5ms per plugin SHA-256 of all files, once per install
Full SHA cache lookup ~0.1ms Longer string comparison
Total per plugin install ~60-110ms Dominated by HEAD request
Total per startup < 10ms Only integrity manifest if cached

The startup-time overhead (< 10ms for the version and integrity checks) is imperceptible. The install-time overhead (60-110ms) is a one-time cost that is dwarfed by the ZIP download time itself (typically 500ms-2s depending on archive size and network latency).

6.5 Compensating Controls

While the patches in this chapter are being implemented and deployed, the following compensating controls reduce risk:

For CWE-328 (short SHA collision):

  • Plugins are sourced from trusted marketplaces only. An attacker would need to compromise the marketplace or a publisher's account to inject a collision --- at which point they could simply replace the plugin directly without needing a collision.
  • Cache directories are keyed on the full SHA internally even though the version string displayed to the user is truncated. The cache is not directly addressable by external inputs.

For CWE-409 (ZIP bombs):

  • The existing extraction-time ratio check (50:1 maximum) catches most ZIP bombs during extraction. The pre-download check prevents downloading bombs that would waste bandwidth and memory even if caught during extraction.
  • MAX_FILE_SIZE and MAX_TOTAL_SIZE limits cap individual file and aggregate extraction sizes.
  • The validateZipFile() function enforces entry count limits, preventing entry-count bombs (archives with millions of tiny files designed to exhaust filesystem inodes).

6.6 Edge Cases and Corner Cases

Short SHA in Git Subdir Plugins

Monorepo plugins present a special case. Multiple plugins can share the same git commit SHA because they live in the same repository. The original code handled this with the short SHA alone, meaning two plugins at the same commit would have identical version identifiers. The patch adds a path hash:

const v = `${fullSha}-${pathHash}`
// Example: "a1b2c3...40chars...-3f2a7b81"

The path hash is only 8 hex characters (32 bits), which might seem insufficient. But the path hash is not the primary identifier --- it is a disambiguation suffix. Two plugins at the same commit with different paths will have different path hashes. Two plugins at different commits cannot collide regardless of path hash. The combination of 40-char SHA + 8-char path hash provides 192 bits of total identifier space.

Handling Pre-Patch Cache Entries

When a user upgrades their CLI from a pre-patch version, their plugin cache contains directories keyed by 12-character SHAs. The migration must be transparent:

  1. On first plugin use after upgrade, the CLI checks for the full SHA cache directory.
  2. If not found, it falls back to the 12-character prefix.
  3. If the 12-character directory is found, the plugin loads from it (no re-download).
  4. On next plugin update, the old directory is removed and a new full-SHA directory is created.

This ensures zero disruption for existing users while moving the cache to the stronger key format.

Content-Length Header Absent

Not all HTTP servers include a Content-Length header. Cloud storage services (GCS, S3) typically include it, but CDN edge servers and custom download handlers may omit it, especially for dynamically-generated responses or chunked transfer encoding.

When Content-Length is absent, validateArchiveDownloadSize returns { valid: true } --- the download proceeds. The buffer size check after download provides the second line of defense. And axios's maxContentLength option provides a third defense by aborting the download if the response body exceeds the limit, regardless of headers.

Race Condition in Concurrent Plugin Installs

Two concurrent loadPluginFromMarketplaceEntry() calls for the same plugin could race on the cache directory. The first call downloads and extracts. The second call checks the cache, finds it partially populated (extraction in progress), and either fails or loads an incomplete plugin.

The defense is the existing .gcs-sha sentinel file pattern: the sentinel is written only after extraction completes. A concurrent call that finds the cache directory but no sentinel re-downloads. The full-SHA version identifier makes this race harder to trigger because cache keys are longer and more specific, but the sentinel pattern remains the primary concurrency control.

6.9 Relationship to Part III and Beyond

Part II (Chapters 4, 5, and 6) closes the Plugin Supply Chain dependency chain. Part III begins with Credential Storage Encryption (Chapter 7), which addresses the second highest-priority dependency chain.

The connection between Part II and Part III is direct: a compromised plugin (prevented by the defenses in Part II) is one of the primary attack vectors for credential theft (defended in Part III). If an attacker bypasses plugin signing, escapes the extraction directory, and loads a malicious plugin, the first thing that plugin does is read ~/.claude/.credentials.json --- which, as Chapter 7 will reveal, is stored in plaintext on all non-macOS platforms.

The defense ordering matters. Plugin supply chain hardening (Part II) must be deployed before credential encryption (Part III) can be relied upon. An attacker who can load arbitrary code via a compromised plugin can bypass any client-side encryption --- they simply read the credentials after the legitimate code decrypts them. The defenses are complementary, not substitutable: Part II prevents the attacker from running code, Part III limits the damage if they succeed despite Part II.

This layered approach --- prevention before mitigation, authentication before authorization, integrity before confidentiality --- is the organizing principle for the entire remediation roadmap. The seven phases in the Implementation Roadmap (Chapter 3) are sequenced to maximize the security gain from each successive deployment, with each phase building on the protections established by the previous one.

Chapter 7: Cross-Platform Secure Storage

Claude Code runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows. On macOS, credentials flow into the system Keychain -- a hardware-backed, kernel-protected credential store that has been hardened over two decades of real-world attacks. On every other platform, credentials land in ~/.claude/.credentials.json as plaintext JSON, protected by nothing more than chmod 0o600. This chapter eliminates that gap.

The vulnerability is not subtle. Finding 7 (CWE-256, CVSS 7.1) and Finding 10 (CWE-922, CVSS 6.5) document it clearly: getSecureStorage() returns plainTextStorage for all non-macOS platforms, with a TODO comment that has been there since the initial implementation. Finding 8 (CWE-312, CVSS 7.1) extends the blast radius to macOS itself -- when the Keychain is unavailable (Docker containers, SSH sessions, CI pipelines), the fallback is that same plaintext file.

We will build a cross-platform storage abstraction that routes credentials to the strongest available backend on each platform: macOS Keychain, Linux libsecret (GNOME Keyring / KDE Wallet), Windows Credential Manager, and an encrypted file fallback for headless environments. The abstraction layer ensures that no calling code ever needs to know which backend is active.

7.1 The Vulnerability: Plaintext on Disk

The current getSecureStorage() dispatcher is seven lines that determine the security posture of every credential Claude Code stores:

// utils/secureStorage/index.ts:9
export function getSecureStorage(): SecureStorage {
  if (process.platform === "darwin") {
    return createFallbackStorage(macOsKeychainStorage, plainTextStorage)
  }
  // TODO: add libsecret support for Linux
  return plainTextStorage
}

The plainTextStorage implementation writes credentials as JSON via writeFileSync and sets chmod 0o600:

// utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts:57
writeFileSync_DEPRECATED(storagePath, jsonStringify(data), {
  encoding: 'utf8',
  flush: false,
})
chmodSync(storagePath, 0o600)

The data flow is direct: OAuth tokens obtained during authentication are serialized to JSON, written to ~/.claude/.credentials.json, and set to owner-readable permissions. On macOS, the Keychain is tried first and this path is the fallback. On Linux and Windows, this is the only path.

Why chmod 0o600 Is Not Enough

Unix file permissions prevent other users from reading the file. They do not prevent:

Attack Vector Bypasses chmod 0o600? Real-World Scenario
Root access Yes Container escape, privilege escalation, compromised admin
Same-user process Yes Malware, malicious npm postinstall script, trojan in PATH
Disk imaging / backup Yes Cloud VM snapshots, Time Machine, enterprise backup agents
Filesystem mount in container Yes Docker volume mounts, Kubernetes hostPath volumes
Memory dump of reading process Yes Core dumps, /proc/<pid>/mem on Linux
Cloud sync agents Yes Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud scanning ~/ subdirectories

In containerized environments -- where Claude Code increasingly runs for CI/CD -- the ~/.claude/ directory is often on a shared volume mount. File permissions on mounted volumes may not be enforced by the container runtime. A 0o600 file on a Docker bind mount is readable by any process with access to the host directory.

Impact Assessment

The credentials stored in .credentials.json include:

  • OAuth access tokens: Grant API access to the Claude service
  • OAuth refresh tokens: Can generate new access tokens indefinitely
  • Trusted device tokens: Bypass device enrollment checks
  • Session identifiers: Correlate to active authenticated sessions

An attacker who obtains the refresh token has persistent access to the Claude API under the victim's identity until the token is explicitly revoked server-side. The access token alone provides temporary access but the refresh token is the high-value target -- it is the equivalent of stealing a session cookie with no expiration.

7.2 Architecture: The Storage Abstraction Layer

The remediation replaces the two-path dispatcher (Keychain or plaintext) with a four-path dispatcher behind a uniform interface. Every platform gets a native credential store as the primary backend and an encrypted file as the fallback. Plaintext storage is eliminated entirely.

    style KCH fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style LSS fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style WCM fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style EF1 fill:#4a6a8a,color:#fff
    style EF2 fill:#4a6a8a,color:#fff
    style EF3 fill:#4a6a8a,color:#fff

The SecureStorage interface remains unchanged -- existing code that calls getSecureStorage().read() or getSecureStorage().write() requires zero modifications:

interface SecureStorage {
  read(): Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null>
  write(data: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void>
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>
  update(
    updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
  ): Promise<void>
}

The createFallbackStorage wrapper already handles the primary-to-fallback cascade: try the primary backend, log a warning if it fails, fall through to the fallback. The only change is that the fallback is now encryptedFileStorage instead of plainTextStorage.

7.3 Linux: libsecret Integration via D-Bus Secret Service

Linux desktop environments provide the D-Bus Secret Service API (specified by freedesktop.org) for secure credential storage. GNOME Keyring and KDE Wallet both implement this API. The secret-tool CLI provides a portable command-line interface.

Why secret-tool Over FFI

There are two approaches to integrating with libsecret: native FFI bindings via node-ffi-napi or subprocess calls to secret-tool. The tradeoff:

Approach Startup Cost Runtime Cost Dependency Weight Failure Modes
FFI (libsecret.so) High (native build) Low (direct call) Heavy (node-gyp, libsecret-dev) Build failures on Alpine, musl, ARM
CLI (secret-tool) None Medium (process spawn) Zero (uses system binary) Missing binary on headless systems

Claude Code already uses subprocess execution for macOS Keychain (security command). The secret-tool approach maintains consistency and avoids native build dependencies that break in container and CI environments. The credential operations (read, write, delete) happen at most a few times per session -- the ~50ms overhead of process spawning is irrelevant.

Implementation: linuxSecretStorage.ts

// utils/secureStorage/linuxSecretStorage.ts
import { execFileSync } from 'child_process'

const SCHEMA = 'org.claude.credentials'
const ATTRIBUTE_KEY = 'account'
const ATTRIBUTE_VALUE = 'claude-code'
const LABEL = 'Claude Code OAuth Credentials'

function isSecretToolAvailable(): boolean {
  try {
    execFileSync('which', ['secret-tool'], {
      stdio: 'pipe',
      timeout: 5000,
    })
    return true
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

export const linuxSecretStorage: SecureStorage = {
  async read(): Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null> {
    if (!isSecretToolAvailable()) return null
    try {
      const stdout = execFileSync(
        'secret-tool',
        ['lookup', ATTRIBUTE_KEY, ATTRIBUTE_VALUE],
        { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], timeout: 10000 },
      )
      if (!stdout.trim()) return null
      return JSON.parse(stdout) as Record<string, unknown>
    } catch {
      return null
    }
  },

  async write(data: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void> {
    if (!isSecretToolAvailable()) {
      throw new Error('secret-tool not available')
    }
    const json = JSON.stringify(data)
    execFileSync(
      'secret-tool',
      ['store', '--label', LABEL, ATTRIBUTE_KEY, ATTRIBUTE_VALUE],
      { input: json, stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], timeout: 10000 },
    )
  },

  async delete(): Promise<void> {
    if (!isSecretToolAvailable()) return
    try {
      execFileSync(
        'secret-tool',
        ['clear', ATTRIBUTE_KEY, ATTRIBUTE_VALUE],
        { stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], timeout: 10000 },
      )
    } catch {
      // Item may not exist -- not an error
    }
  },

  async update(
    updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
  ): Promise<void> {
    const existing = await this.read()
    const updated = updater(existing ?? {})
    await this.write(updated)
  },
}

How D-Bus Secret Service Protects Credentials

When secret-tool store is called, the credential data travels through a D-Bus session to the secret service daemon (gnome-keyring-daemon or kwalletd). The daemon encrypts the data using a master key derived from the user's login password. The encrypted data is stored in ~/.local/share/keyrings/ (GNOME) or ~/.local/share/kwalletd/ (KDE).

The security properties exceed chmod 0o600 significantly:

Property chmod 0o600 D-Bus Secret Service
Encryption at rest No AES-128-CBC (GNOME) or Blowfish (KDE)
Key derivation N/A PBKDF2 from login password
Automatic locking No Locks on screen lock / session timeout
Access control File owner only Per-application ACL (optional)
Backup safety Plaintext in backups Encrypted in backups

Headless Linux: When No Secret Service Exists

On headless servers, Docker containers, and CI runners, there is no D-Bus session and no secret service daemon. isSecretToolAvailable() returns false, and the createFallbackStorage wrapper routes to encryptedFileStorage. This is the expected behavior -- headless environments cannot provide interactive credential storage, so encrypted file storage is the appropriate fallback.

7.4 Windows: Credential Manager via wincred

Windows provides the Credential Manager (wincred) for storing credentials. It is backed by DPAPI (Data Protection API), which derives encryption keys from the user's login credentials and machine-specific secrets.

Implementation: windowsCredStorage.ts

The Windows implementation uses cmdkey.exe for credential operations. This avoids native module dependencies while accessing the same credential store:

// utils/secureStorage/windowsCredStorage.ts
import { execFileSync } from 'child_process'

const TARGET_PREFIX = 'ClaudeCode:'
const TARGET_NAME = `${TARGET_PREFIX}oauth`

export const windowsCredStorage: SecureStorage = {
  async read(): Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null> {
    try {
      // PowerShell provides programmatic access to Credential Manager
      const script = `
        $cred = Get-StoredCredential -Target '${TARGET_NAME}' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        if ($cred) {
          [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringAuto(
            [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($cred.Password)
          )
        }
      `
      const stdout = execFileSync(
        'powershell.exe',
        ['-NoProfile', '-NonInteractive', '-Command', script],
        { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], timeout: 15000 },
      )
      if (!stdout.trim()) return null
      return JSON.parse(stdout.trim()) as Record<string, unknown>
    } catch {
      return null
    }
  },

  async write(data: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void> {
    const json = JSON.stringify(data)
    // cmdkey stores credentials in Credential Manager
    execFileSync(
      'cmdkey.exe',
      ['/generic:' + TARGET_NAME, '/user:claude-code', '/pass:' + json],
      { stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], timeout: 10000 },
    )
  },

  async delete(): Promise<void> {
    try {
      execFileSync('cmdkey.exe', ['/delete:' + TARGET_NAME], {
        stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
        timeout: 10000,
      })
    } catch {
      // Credential may not exist
    }
  },

  async update(
    updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
  ): Promise<void> {
    const existing = await this.read()
    const updated = updater(existing ?? {})
    await this.write(updated)
  },
}

DPAPI Protection Properties

Windows Credential Manager credentials are encrypted with DPAPI, which provides:

  • User-scoped encryption: Only the user who stored the credential can decrypt it, even with local admin access (unless the admin resets the user's password)
  • Machine binding: Credentials cannot be decrypted on a different machine (the master key includes a machine-specific component)
  • Transparent to backups: Backed-up credentials remain encrypted; they can only be restored on the same machine under the same user account

The credential size limit for cmdkey is approximately 2,560 bytes. OAuth credential JSON typically fits within this limit, but the implementation should validate size before writing and fall through to encrypted file storage for oversized payloads.

7.5 Encrypted File Fallback: AES-256-GCM

When no platform credential store is available -- headless Linux, Docker containers, CI/CD runners, or any platform where the primary backend fails -- the encrypted file fallback provides defense in depth. It replaces the current plainTextStorage entirely.

Key Derivation

The encryption key is derived from machine-specific data that is available without user interaction:

// utils/secureStorage/encryptedFileStorage.ts
import { createHash, randomBytes, createCipheriv, createDecipheriv } from 'crypto'
import { readFileSync, existsSync } from 'fs'
import { homedir } from 'os'

const ALGORITHM = 'aes-256-gcm'
const KEY_LENGTH = 32 // 256 bits
const IV_LENGTH = 12  // 96 bits for GCM
const SALT_LENGTH = 32
const TAG_LENGTH = 16 // 128-bit auth tag

function getMachineIdentifier(): string {
  // Linux: /etc/machine-id (unique per installation, persists across reboots)
  // macOS: IOPlatformUUID via ioreg
  // Windows: MachineGuid from registry
  // Fallback: hostname + homedir hash
  const candidates = [
    '/etc/machine-id',
    '/var/lib/dbus/machine-id',
  ]
  for (const path of candidates) {
    try {
      const id = readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trim()
      if (id.length >= 16) return id
    } catch {
      continue
    }
  }
  // Fallback: hash of hostname + homedir + uid
  return createHash('sha256')
    .update(`${require('os').hostname()}:${homedir()}:${process.getuid?.() ?? 0}`)
    .digest('hex')
}

function deriveKey(salt: Buffer): Buffer {
  const machineId = getMachineIdentifier()
  const userContext = `claude-code:${process.getuid?.() ?? homedir()}`
  // HKDF-like derivation: HMAC-SHA256(salt, machineId || userContext)
  return createHash('sha256')
    .update(salt)
    .update(machineId)
    .update(userContext)
    .digest()
}

Encryption and Decryption

function encrypt(plaintext: string, key: Buffer): Buffer {
  const iv = randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)
  const cipher = createCipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv, { authTagLength: TAG_LENGTH })
  const encrypted = Buffer.concat([cipher.update(plaintext, 'utf8'), cipher.final()])
  const authTag = cipher.getAuthTag()
  // Format: [salt_len(1)][salt][iv][authTag][ciphertext]
  // Salt is stored alongside for key re-derivation on read
  return encrypted
}

function decrypt(bundle: Buffer, key: Buffer, iv: Buffer, authTag: Buffer): string {
  const decipher = createDecipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv, { authTagLength: TAG_LENGTH })
  decipher.setAuthTag(authTag)
  return decipher.update(bundle, undefined, 'utf8') + decipher.final('utf8')
}

File Format

The encrypted credential file (.credentials.enc) uses a binary format:

Byte layout of .credentials.enc:
┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────────────┐
│ Version  │  Salt    │  IV      │ Auth Tag │ Ciphertext       │
│ (1 byte) │ (32 B)  │ (12 B)  │ (16 B)  │ (variable)       │
│ 0x01     │          │          │          │                  │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────────────┘

The version byte enables future format changes without breaking existing encrypted files. The salt is stored with the ciphertext because it is needed to re-derive the key on read -- the salt is not secret (it randomizes the key derivation, but the secrecy comes from the machine identifier).

Complete Storage Implementation

export const encryptedFileStorage: SecureStorage = {
  async read(): Promise<Record<string, unknown> | null> {
    const encPath = getEncryptedStoragePath()
    if (!existsSync(encPath)) return null
    try {
      const raw = readFileSync(encPath)
      if (raw.length < 1 + SALT_LENGTH + IV_LENGTH + TAG_LENGTH + 1) return null

      const version = raw[0]
      if (version !== 0x01) {
        throw new Error(`Unknown credential file version: ${version}`)
      }
      let offset = 1
      const salt = raw.subarray(offset, offset + SALT_LENGTH); offset += SALT_LENGTH
      const iv = raw.subarray(offset, offset + IV_LENGTH); offset += IV_LENGTH
      const authTag = raw.subarray(offset, offset + TAG_LENGTH); offset += TAG_LENGTH
      const ciphertext = raw.subarray(offset)

      const key = deriveKey(salt)
      const plaintext = decrypt(ciphertext, key, iv, authTag)
      return JSON.parse(plaintext) as Record<string, unknown>
    } catch {
      return null
    }
  },

  async write(data: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<void> {
    const encPath = getEncryptedStoragePath()
    const dir = dirname(encPath)
    if (!existsSync(dir)) {
      mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })
    }

    const plaintext = JSON.stringify(data)
    const salt = randomBytes(SALT_LENGTH)
    const key = deriveKey(salt)
    const iv = randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)
    const cipher = createCipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv, { authTagLength: TAG_LENGTH })
    const encrypted = Buffer.concat([cipher.update(plaintext, 'utf8'), cipher.final()])
    const authTag = cipher.getAuthTag()

    const bundle = Buffer.concat([
      Buffer.from([0x01]),  // version
      salt, iv, authTag, encrypted,
    ])

    // Atomic write (see Chapter 8 for the full pattern)
    const tmpPath = encPath + '.tmp.' + process.pid
    const fd = openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)
    try {
      writeSync(fd, bundle)
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    renameSync(tmpPath, encPath)
  },

  // ... delete() and update() follow the same patterns
}

Security Properties of the Encrypted Fallback

Property plainTextStorage (BEFORE) encryptedFileStorage (AFTER)
At-rest encryption None AES-256-GCM
Authentication None GCM auth tag (tamper detection)
Key source N/A Machine-specific identifier + user context
Backup safety Plaintext in backups Encrypted in backups
Cross-machine portability File readable anywhere File decryptable only on same machine
Root access Full credential access Must know machine-id to derive key

Threat model limitation: An attacker with root access on the same machine can read /etc/machine-id and derive the key. The encrypted fallback is defense-in-depth, not a substitute for a proper credential store. It raises the bar from "read a JSON file" to "understand the key derivation scheme and extract machine-specific inputs." This stops backup exfiltration, casual disk access, and cloud sync leaks -- the most common real-world attack vectors.

7.6 The Updated Dispatcher

With all four backends implemented, the dispatcher becomes:

 // utils/secureStorage/index.ts
+import { linuxSecretStorage } from './linuxSecretStorage'
+import { windowsCredStorage } from './windowsCredStorage'
+import { encryptedFileStorage } from './encryptedFileStorage'

 export function getSecureStorage(): SecureStorage {
   if (process.platform === 'darwin') {
-    return createFallbackStorage(macOsKeychainStorage, plainTextStorage)
+    return createFallbackStorage(macOsKeychainStorage, encryptedFileStorage)
   }
-  // TODO: add libsecret support for Linux
-  return plainTextStorage
+  if (process.platform === 'linux') {
+    return createFallbackStorage(linuxSecretStorage, encryptedFileStorage)
+  }
+  if (process.platform === 'win32') {
+    return createFallbackStorage(windowsCredStorage, encryptedFileStorage)
+  }
+  // Unknown platform: encrypted file only
+  return encryptedFileStorage
 }

The diff is small because the architecture was already correct -- createFallbackStorage handled the cascade pattern. The missing piece was the platform-specific backends.

7.7 Container and CI/CD Considerations

Containerized environments present unique challenges for credential storage:

  1. No D-Bus session: Container images typically do not include gnome-keyring or any D-Bus secret service
  2. Ephemeral filesystems: Container filesystems may be destroyed between runs
  3. Shared volumes: Mounted directories may have relaxed permissions
  4. No interactive authentication: CI/CD pipelines cannot prompt for passwords

Container Detection

The storage layer should detect container environments and adjust behavior:

function isContainerEnvironment(): boolean {
  // Docker
  if (existsSync('/.dockerenv')) return true
  // Kubernetes
  if (process.env.KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST) return true
  // Generic cgroup detection
  try {
    const cgroup = readFileSync('/proc/1/cgroup', 'utf8')
    if (cgroup.includes('docker') || cgroup.includes('kubepods')) return true
  } catch {
    // Not on Linux or no access to /proc
  }
  return false
}

In container environments, the recommended credential injection method is environment variables with short-lived tokens:

if (isContainerEnvironment()) {
  logWarning(
    'Running in container environment. ' +
    'Recommend using CLAUDE_OAUTH_TOKEN env var with short-lived tokens. ' +
    'File-based credential storage in containers is inherently less secure.',
  )
}

Shared Volume Detection

When ~/.claude/ resides on a volume mount (the stat device differs from the home directory's device), the storage layer should warn:

function isOnSharedVolume(path: string): boolean {
  try {
    const pathStat = statSync(path)
    const homeStat = statSync(homedir())
    return pathStat.dev !== homeStat.dev
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

CI/CD Token Lifetime Management

In CI/CD pipelines, long-lived tokens stored in environment variables create risk -- if the CI runner is compromised, the token remains valid. The storage layer should support short-lived token requests:

interface TokenLifetimeConfig {
  /** Token lifetime in seconds. Default: 86400 (24h). CI recommended: 3600 (1h). */
  lifetimeSeconds: number
  /** Source identifier for audit trail */
  source: 'oauth_flow' | 'env_var' | 'ci_injection'
}

function getTokenLifetime(): number {
  const envLifetime = process.env.CLAUDE_TOKEN_LIFETIME
  if (envLifetime === 'short') return 3600      // 1 hour for CI/CD
  if (envLifetime === 'medium') return 28800     // 8 hours for dev sessions
  return 86400                                     // 24 hours default
}

The CLAUDE_TOKEN_LIFETIME=short environment variable signals that the token should expire quickly. This is documented as the recommended configuration for CI/CD environments in the Security Action Report's remediation guidance for Finding 10. Combined with container detection, the storage layer can automatically suggest short-lived tokens when it detects an ephemeral environment.

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)

WSL presents a unique case: it is a Linux environment but has access to Windows Credential Manager via cmd.exe /c cmdkey. The storage layer should detect WSL and offer the Windows backend as the primary, with the Linux encrypted fallback:

function isWSL(): boolean {
  try {
    const release = readFileSync('/proc/version', 'utf8')
    return release.toLowerCase().includes('microsoft')
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

// In the dispatcher:
if (process.platform === 'linux' && isWSL()) {
  return createFallbackStorage(windowsCredStorage, encryptedFileStorage)
}

This routes WSL users to the same DPAPI-backed credential store that native Windows users enjoy, avoiding the less-secure encrypted file fallback when a stronger option is available.

7.8 Migration: Plaintext to Encrypted

Existing installations have credentials in ~/.claude/.credentials.json. The migration must be seamless -- users should not need to re-authenticate.

Migration Strategy

graph TD
    START["getSecureStorage().read()"] --> CHECK{"Encrypted file<br/>exists?"}
    CHECK -->|Yes| READ_ENC["Read encrypted file"]
    CHECK -->|No| CHECK_PLAIN{"Plaintext file<br/>exists?"}

    CHECK_PLAIN -->|Yes| MIGRATE["Read plaintext<br/>Write to new backend<br/>Delete plaintext"]
    CHECK_PLAIN -->|No| RETURN_NULL["Return null<br/>(no stored credentials)"]

    MIGRATE --> VERIFY{"Migration<br/>successful?"}
    VERIFY -->|Yes| DELETE_PLAIN["Securely delete<br/>.credentials.json"]
    VERIFY -->|No| KEEP_PLAIN["Keep plaintext<br/>Log warning"]

    READ_ENC --> RETURN["Return credentials"]
    DELETE_PLAIN --> RETURN
    KEEP_PLAIN --> RETURN

Secure Deletion of Plaintext Credentials

After migrating credentials to the new backend, the plaintext file must be destroyed -- not just deleted. A simple unlink() leaves the data on disk until the filesystem overwrites those blocks.

function secureDeleteFile(filePath: string): void {
  try {
    const stat = statSync(filePath)
    // Overwrite with random data before deleting
    const fd = openSync(filePath, 'w')
    try {
      const randomData = randomBytes(stat.size)
      writeSync(fd, randomData)
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    unlinkSync(filePath)
  } catch {
    // Best effort -- if overwrite fails, still try to unlink
    try { unlinkSync(filePath) } catch { /* ignore */ }
  }
}

Caveat: On copy-on-write filesystems (ZFS, APFS, btrfs), overwriting a file does not destroy the original data blocks -- the filesystem allocates new blocks and marks old ones as free. On SSD media, TRIM may defer actual block erasure. Secure deletion is best-effort defense-in-depth, not a guarantee. The primary defense is preventing plaintext storage in the first place.

7.10 Residual Risk

The cross-platform secure storage eliminates the plaintext credential vulnerability on all platforms. However, residual risks remain:

Residual Risk Severity Mitigation
Root attacker on same machine can derive encryption key Medium Encrypted fallback is defense-in-depth; root is game-over in most threat models
Container environments have weaker isolation Medium Document env var token injection as preferred CI/CD path
Copy-on-write filesystems retain plaintext during migration Low Migration is one-time; TRIM eventually clears blocks
secret-tool CLI may not be installed on all Linux distros Low Encrypted file fallback activates automatically
Windows cmdkey credential size limit (~2.5KB) Low Fall through to encrypted file for oversized payloads

The dependency chain impact, as documented in the Security Action Report, is significant: Findings 7, 8, and 10 are all resolved by this implementation. The Credential Storage Chain (Findings 7, 8, 10, 20, 30, 37, 39) has its root cause -- plaintext storage on non-macOS platforms -- eliminated. As discussed in Chapter 8, the atomic write pattern addresses Finding 30. The chain effect means this single architectural change reduces risk across seven related findings.

Security Assessment: Cross-Platform Secure Storage

Property Before After
macOS with Keychain available Keychain (strong) Keychain (strong) -- unchanged
macOS without Keychain Plaintext JSON (weak) AES-256-GCM encrypted file (moderate)
Linux with GNOME/KDE Plaintext JSON (weak) D-Bus Secret Service (strong)
Linux headless Plaintext JSON (weak) AES-256-GCM encrypted file (moderate)
Windows Plaintext JSON (weak) Credential Manager / DPAPI (strong)
Container / CI Plaintext JSON (weak) AES-256-GCM + env var guidance (moderate)

CWEs resolved: CWE-256 (Plaintext Storage of a Password), CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information), CWE-922 (Insecure Storage of Sensitive Information)

OWASP mapping: A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures, A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

Estimated effort: 24-40 hours (architecture solution, as noted in the Security Action Report)

Chapter 8: Atomic Credential Operations

A security patch that eliminates plaintext storage (Chapter 7) can be undermined by a race condition in the write operation itself. Finding 30 (CWE-367, CVSS 4.7) documents exactly this: the plainTextStorage.update() function writes credentials with writeFileSync and then sets permissions with chmodSync. Between those two calls, the file exists on disk with whatever permissions the process's umask allows -- potentially world-readable.

This is a textbook Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability. The "check" is the intended permission (0o600), the "use" is the actual file creation (default umask), and the gap between them is a window where any process on the system can read freshly written OAuth tokens.

This chapter goes beyond fixing the TOCTOU race. We implement the atomic write pattern -- a crash-safe, race-free approach to credential file updates that eliminates three classes of vulnerability simultaneously: the permission window, partial writes from crashes, and data corruption from concurrent updates.

8.1 The Vulnerability: Write-Then-Chmod

The current credential write implementation in plainTextStorage.ts follows a two-step pattern:

// utils/secureStorage/plainTextStorage.ts:57-61
async update(
  updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<void> {
  const storagePath = getStoragePath()
  const dir = dirname(storagePath)
  if (!existsSync(dir)) {
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })
  }
  const existing = await this.read()
  const updated = updater(existing ?? {})
  writeFileSync_DEPRECATED(storagePath, jsonStringify(updated), {
    encoding: 'utf8',
    flush: false,
  })
  chmodSync(storagePath, 0o600)
}

The data flow creates a temporal gap:

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Claude Code
    participant FS as Filesystem
    participant Attacker as Malicious Process

    App->>FS: writeFileSync(.credentials.json, tokens)
    Note over FS: File created with umask permissions<br/>(e.g., 0o644 if umask is 0o022)

    rect rgb(200, 50, 50, 0.2)
        Note over FS,Attacker: VULNERABILITY WINDOW
        Attacker->>FS: open(.credentials.json, O_RDONLY)
        FS-->>Attacker: File contents (OAuth tokens)
    end

    App->>FS: chmodSync(.credentials.json, 0o600)
    Note over FS: Permissions now correct<br/>but attacker already read the file

Measuring the Window

The window between writeFileSync and chmodSync is typically microseconds -- but that metric is misleading. The question is not "how long is the window?" but "can an attacker reliably exploit it?"

On Linux, inotify provides filesystem event notification. A monitoring process watching ~/.claude/ receives an IN_CREATE or IN_CLOSE_WRITE event the moment the file is created. The attacker's response time to this event is limited only by the kernel scheduler -- typically under 100 microseconds on a modern system. The window is wide enough.

# Attacker's monitoring loop (conceptual)
inotifywait -m -e close_write ~/.claude/ | while read dir event file; do
  if [[ "$file" == ".credentials.json" ]]; then
    cat "$dir/$file"  # Read before chmod fires
  fi
done

On macOS, the equivalent is FSEvents or kqueue with NOTE_WRITE. The timing characteristics are similar.

Three Problems, Not One

The write-then-chmod pattern actually contains three distinct problems:

Problem CWE Consequence
Permission window CWE-367 (TOCTOU) Credential exposure between write and chmod
Non-atomic write CWE-367 (TOCTOU) Partial file on crash (corrupted JSON)
No flush guarantee CWE-404 (Improper Resource Shutdown) Data loss on power failure (flush: false)

The flush: false flag in the writeFileSync call is particularly concerning. Without flushing, the data may reside only in the OS page cache, not on physical storage. A system crash (kernel panic, power failure) could result in a zero-length or partially-written credential file, corrupting the authentication state.

8.2 The Atomic Write Pattern

The atomic write pattern solves all three problems with a single approach: write to a temporary file with correct permissions, flush to disk, then rename into place.

graph TD
    START["Credential Update"] --> CREATE["Create temp file<br/>openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)<br/>Permissions correct from birth"]
    CREATE --> WRITE["Write JSON to temp file<br/>writeSync(fd, data)"]
    WRITE --> FLUSH["Flush to disk<br/>fsyncSync(fd)"]
    FLUSH --> CLOSE["Close file descriptor<br/>closeSync(fd)"]
    CLOSE --> RENAME["Atomic rename<br/>renameSync(tmpPath, targetPath)"]
    RENAME --> DONE["Done: credential file updated<br/>atomically with correct permissions"]

    CREATE -.->|"On error"| CLEANUP["Delete temp file<br/>unlinkSync(tmpPath)"]
    WRITE -.->|"On error"| CLEANUP
    FLUSH -.->|"On error"| CLEANUP

    style CREATE fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style RENAME fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style CLEANUP fill:#8b4513,color:#fff

Why This Works: The Three Guarantees

Guarantee 1: No permission window. The openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600) call creates the file with the correct permissions from the moment it exists on disk. The mode parameter to open() is applied atomically during file creation -- there is no gap where the file exists with different permissions. The umask is irrelevant because the open() mode is ANDed with ~umask, but we set it explicitly.

Actually, that is not quite right. The mode parameter is indeed subject to the process's umask. If umask is 0o022, then open(path, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT, 0o600) creates the file with 0o600 & ~0o022 = 0o600 -- but only because 0o022 does not mask any bits in 0o600. If we wanted 0o660 and umask was 0o022, we would get 0o640. For the credential file case, 0o600 with any standard umask produces 0o600. However, to be defensive against unusual umask settings:

// Set umask to 0 temporarily for this operation
const oldUmask = process.umask(0o077)
try {
  const fd = openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)
  // ... write, flush, close, rename ...
} finally {
  process.umask(oldUmask)
}

This ensures the temp file gets exactly 0o600 regardless of the process's inherited umask.

Guarantee 2: No partial writes. The renameSync call is atomic on POSIX filesystems when the source and destination are on the same filesystem. At any point in time, targetPath either contains the complete old data or the complete new data -- never a partial write. If the process crashes between writeSync and renameSync, the temp file is orphaned but the target file retains its previous content.

Guarantee 3: Durability. The fsyncSync call forces the operating system to flush file data from the page cache to physical storage. After fsyncSync returns, the data is on disk even if the system loses power. Without fsync, data may reside only in volatile memory.

The Complete Implementation

The patched update() method from the Security Action Report:

async update(
  updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<void> {
  const storagePath = getStoragePath()
  const dir = dirname(storagePath)
  if (!existsSync(dir)) {
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })
  }
  const existing = await this.read()
  const updated = updater(existing ?? {})

  // Atomic write with correct permissions from creation.
  // Eliminates the TOCTOU window between writeFileSync and chmodSync
  // where the file exists with default (potentially 0o644) permissions.
  const tmpPath = storagePath + '.tmp.' + process.pid
  try {
    // Create file with restrictive permissions from the start
    const fd = openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600)
    try {
      writeSync(fd, jsonStringify(updated), 0, 'utf8')
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    // Atomic rename: permissions are already 0o600 on the new file
    renameSync(tmpPath, storagePath)
  } catch (err) {
    try { unlinkSync(tmpPath) } catch { /* ignore cleanup failure */ }
    throw err
  }
}

New imports required:

import { openSync, writeSync, closeSync, fsyncSync, renameSync, unlinkSync } from 'fs'

Lines removed: 4. Lines added: 13. Net increase: 9 lines. The security improvement is significant relative to the code change size -- this is a sign of a well-targeted patch.

8.4 Deep Dive: O_CREAT|O_EXCL for Exclusive Creation

The openSync(tmpPath, 'w', 0o600) call in the patch creates the file if it does not exist. But what if a temp file from a previous crashed invocation already exists? The 'w' flag truncates an existing file, which is correct for our use case. However, there is a subtlety: if an attacker pre-creates a file at the temp path (a symlink attack), the open() call follows the symlink and writes to the attacker's chosen location.

For maximum security, the temp file creation should use O_CREAT|O_EXCL:

import { constants } from 'fs'

// O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_WRONLY: create exclusively, fail if exists
const flags = constants.O_CREAT | constants.O_EXCL | constants.O_WRONLY
const fd = openSync(tmpPath, flags, 0o600)

O_EXCL guarantees that the open() call creates a new file. If a file (or symlink) already exists at that path, the call fails with EEXIST. This eliminates the symlink attack vector entirely.

The trade-off is that a crashed previous invocation leaves an orphaned temp file that blocks future writes. The solution: attempt O_CREAT|O_EXCL first; on EEXIST, delete the stale temp file and retry once:

function openExclusiveOrRetry(path: string, mode: number): number {
  const flags = constants.O_CREAT | constants.O_EXCL | constants.O_WRONLY
  try {
    return openSync(path, flags, mode)
  } catch (err: any) {
    if (err.code !== 'EEXIST') throw err
    // Stale temp file from crashed previous invocation -- remove and retry
    unlinkSync(path)
    return openSync(path, flags, mode)
  }
}

Temp File Naming Strategy

The current patch uses storagePath + '.tmp.' + process.pid as the temp file name. The PID provides uniqueness within a single machine's running processes. However, PIDs are recycled -- a PID from a crashed process may be reused by a new, unrelated process. For stronger uniqueness:

import { randomBytes } from 'crypto'

const nonce = randomBytes(8).toString('hex')
const tmpPath = `${storagePath}.tmp.${process.pid}.${nonce}`

The random nonce eliminates PID recycling as a concern and prevents an attacker from predicting the temp file name (which would be needed for a pre-creation attack if O_EXCL is not used).

8.5 The fsync Requirement

The fsyncSync(fd) call is the most expensive operation in the atomic write pattern -- it can take 1-10ms on SSD and 10-50ms on HDD. Why is it necessary?

Without fsync, the kernel may reorder operations. The rename could be persisted to disk before the file contents are persisted. If the system crashes after the rename is persisted but before the contents are written, the credential file contains garbage:

Timeline without fsync:
1. write(fd, data)       → data in page cache (not on disk)
2. rename(tmp, target)   → rename in journal (on disk)
3. [SYSTEM CRASH]
4. After reboot: target file exists but contains zero bytes

With fsync:

Timeline with fsync:
1. write(fd, data)       → data in page cache
2. fsync(fd)             → data forced to disk
3. rename(tmp, target)   → rename in journal (on disk)
4. [SYSTEM CRASH]
5. After reboot: target file contains complete data

fsync on the Directory

For complete durability, the directory entry for the renamed file should also be synced. On POSIX systems, rename() modifies the directory that contains the file. The directory entry update is also subject to reordering:

// After rename, fsync the parent directory to ensure
// the directory entry is persisted
const dirFd = openSync(dir, constants.O_RDONLY | constants.O_DIRECTORY)
try {
  fsyncSync(dirFd)
} finally {
  closeSync(dirFd)
}

This is the pattern used by databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL) for crash-safe file operations. For credential storage, where writes happen a few times per session and the data is small, the performance cost is negligible.

Platform-Specific fsync Behavior

Platform fsync Behavior Gotcha
Linux (ext4) Flushes file data and metadata Barrier writes may be disabled on some systems
Linux (btrfs) Copy-on-write; fsync creates a new extent Old data blocks retained until overwritten
macOS (APFS) Flushes to stable storage F_FULLFSYNC ioctl provides stronger guarantee than fsync
Windows (NTFS) FlushFileBuffers() equivalent May not flush disk write cache without FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH

On macOS, fsyncSync calls fsync(2), which APFS maps to a barrier flush. For applications requiring the strongest guarantee (financial transactions, database WAL), fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC) should be used instead. For credential storage, standard fsync is sufficient -- the credential file is written at most a few times per session, and the durability window is seconds, not milliseconds.

8.6 Concurrent Update Safety

What happens when two Claude Code processes update credentials simultaneously? The current implementation has a read-modify-write race independent of the permission TOCTOU:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P1 as Process 1
    participant P2 as Process 2
    participant FS as Filesystem

    P1->>FS: read() → {tokenA: "old"}
    P2->>FS: read() → {tokenA: "old"}
    P1->>P1: updater({tokenA: "old"}) → {tokenA: "new1"}
    P2->>P2: updater({tokenA: "old"}) → {tokenA: "new2"}
    P1->>FS: write({tokenA: "new1"})
    P2->>FS: write({tokenA: "new2"})
    Note over FS: Final state: {tokenA: "new2"}<br/>Process 1's update is lost

The atomic rename does not solve this -- it ensures each individual write is atomic, but the read-modify-write sequence across two processes can still lose updates. This is a lost-update problem (CWE-362: Concurrent Execution Using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization).

File Locking

POSIX advisory file locking can serialize access:

import { flockSync } from 'fs-ext' // or implement via fcntl

async update(
  updater: (data: Record<string, unknown>) => Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<void> {
  const storagePath = getStoragePath()
  const lockPath = storagePath + '.lock'
  const lockFd = openSync(lockPath, 'w', 0o600)
  try {
    // Acquire exclusive lock (blocks if another process holds it)
    flockSync(lockFd, 'ex')

    // Critical section: read, modify, write
    const existing = await this.read()
    const updated = updater(existing ?? {})
    await this.writeAtomic(storagePath, updated)
  } finally {
    // Release lock
    flockSync(lockFd, 'un')
    closeSync(lockFd)
  }
}

Node.js does not provide flock in the standard library. Options include:

  1. proper-lockfile npm package: Cross-platform file locking with stale lock detection
  2. fs-ext npm package: Provides flock() bindings
  3. Custom implementation using O_EXCL: Create a lock file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL; delete on release

For Claude Code's use case, where credential updates are infrequent (at most a few per session) and the critical section is short (read JSON, modify, write), the simplest approach is a retry loop with O_CREAT|O_EXCL:

const MAX_LOCK_RETRIES = 5
const LOCK_RETRY_DELAY_MS = 100

async function withCredentialLock<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const lockPath = getStoragePath() + '.lock'

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < MAX_LOCK_RETRIES; attempt++) {
    try {
      // Attempt to create lock file exclusively
      const lockFd = openSync(
        lockPath,
        constants.O_CREAT | constants.O_EXCL | constants.O_WRONLY,
        0o600,
      )
      closeSync(lockFd)

      try {
        return await fn()
      } finally {
        try { unlinkSync(lockPath) } catch { /* ignore */ }
      }
    } catch (err: any) {
      if (err.code !== 'EEXIST') throw err
      // Lock held by another process -- check staleness
      try {
        const lockStat = statSync(lockPath)
        const ageMs = Date.now() - lockStat.mtimeMs
        if (ageMs > 30000) {
          // Stale lock (>30s) -- process probably crashed
          unlinkSync(lockPath)
          continue
        }
      } catch { /* lock may have been released between check and stat */ }
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, LOCK_RETRY_DELAY_MS))
    }
  }
  throw new Error('Failed to acquire credential lock after retries')
}

8.7 Credential Migration Race Condition

Finding 39 in the audit report identifies a related TOCTOU in credential migration. When credentials are migrated from an old storage location to a new one (e.g., from plaintext to encrypted), the sequence is: read from old location, write to new location, delete old location. Two processes performing migration simultaneously can corrupt or lose credentials.

The atomic write pattern combined with file locking eliminates this race:

async function migrateCredentials(): Promise<void> {
  await withCredentialLock(async () => {
    const oldPath = getLegacyStoragePath() // ~/.claude/.credentials.json
    const newStorage = getSecureStorage()

    if (!existsSync(oldPath)) return // Already migrated

    // Read from old location
    const data = JSON.parse(readFileSync(oldPath, 'utf8'))

    // Write to new location (atomic write internally)
    await newStorage.write(data)

    // Verify write succeeded before deleting old file
    const readBack = await newStorage.read()
    if (!readBack) {
      throw new Error('Migration verification failed: could not read back credentials')
    }

    // Securely delete old plaintext file
    secureDeleteFile(oldPath)
  })
}

The verify-before-delete step is critical. Without it, a write failure silently destroys the only copy of the credentials. The lock ensures that only one process performs the migration, and the atomic write ensures the new file is either completely written or not at all.

8.8 Applying the Pattern to Other Sensitive Files

The atomic write pattern is not specific to credentials. Any file that contains sensitive data and must survive crashes should use it. In Claude Code's codebase, several other files benefit from the same treatment:

File Content Current Write Method Risk
.credentials.json OAuth tokens writeFileSync + chmodSync Finding 30 (TOCTOU)
settings.local.json User preferences writeFileSync Partial write on crash
history.jsonl Conversation history appendFileSync Discussed in Chapter 9
paste-cache/*.txt Pasted content writeFileSync May contain secrets

A shared utility function extracts the pattern:

// utils/atomicWrite.ts
import {
  openSync, writeSync, closeSync, fsyncSync,
  renameSync, unlinkSync, constants,
} from 'fs'
import { randomBytes } from 'crypto'

export function atomicWriteFileSync(
  targetPath: string,
  data: string | Buffer,
  options: { mode?: number; encoding?: BufferEncoding } = {},
): void {
  const { mode = 0o644, encoding = 'utf8' } = options
  const nonce = randomBytes(8).toString('hex')
  const tmpPath = `${targetPath}.tmp.${process.pid}.${nonce}`

  try {
    const fd = openSync(
      tmpPath,
      constants.O_CREAT | constants.O_EXCL | constants.O_WRONLY,
      mode,
    )
    try {
      if (typeof data === 'string') {
        writeSync(fd, data, 0, encoding)
      } else {
        writeSync(fd, data)
      }
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    renameSync(tmpPath, targetPath)
  } catch (err) {
    try { unlinkSync(tmpPath) } catch { /* ignore */ }
    throw err
  }
}

Usage in any storage implementation:

import { atomicWriteFileSync } from '../atomicWrite'

// Secure credential write
atomicWriteFileSync(storagePath, jsonStringify(updated), { mode: 0o600 })

// Settings write (less sensitive, standard permissions)
atomicWriteFileSync(settingsPath, jsonStringify(settings), { mode: 0o644 })

8.9 The O_TMPFILE Optimization (Linux)

Linux 3.11 introduced O_TMPFILE, which creates an anonymous file in a specified directory with no directory entry. The file is visible only through the file descriptor. This eliminates the need for temp file name generation and the cleanup-on-failure path:

// C equivalent (for understanding)
int fd = open("/path/to/dir", O_TMPFILE | O_WRONLY, 0600);
write(fd, data, len);
fsync(fd);
// Create directory entry atomically via /proc/self/fd
linkat(AT_FDCWD, "/proc/self/fd/" + fd, AT_FDCWD, "/path/to/file", AT_SYMLINK_FOLLOW);
close(fd);

In Node.js, O_TMPFILE is available via the constants object on supported Linux kernels:

import { constants } from 'fs'

// O_TMPFILE may not be defined on all platforms
const O_TMPFILE = constants.O_TMPFILE ?? 0o20000000

if (process.platform === 'linux' && O_TMPFILE) {
  // Use O_TMPFILE for anonymous temp file
  const fd = openSync(dir, O_TMPFILE | constants.O_WRONLY, 0o600)
  writeSync(fd, data)
  fsyncSync(fd)
  // Link into directory via procfs
  execFileSync('ln', ['-f', `/proc/self/fd/${fd}`, storagePath])
  closeSync(fd)
}

Advantages of O_TMPFILE: - No temp file visible on disk at any point (anonymous until linked) - No cleanup required on failure (file disappears when fd is closed) - No temp file name collision possible

Disadvantages: - Linux-only (not available on macOS or Windows) - Requires /proc to be mounted (not available in some container configurations) - The linkat from /proc/self/fd/ is not a standard rename -- it creates a new hard link

For a cross-platform codebase like Claude Code, the temp-file-and-rename pattern is the pragmatic choice. O_TMPFILE can be used as an optimization on Linux when available, falling back to the standard pattern otherwise.

Timing Attack Verification

To verify the permission window is eliminated, a test script monitors file creation events and checks permissions:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Monitor for file creation events in ~/.claude/
WATCH_DIR="$HOME/.claude"
FOUND_WEAK_PERMS=0

inotifywait -m -e create,close_write "$WATCH_DIR" 2>/dev/null | \
  while read -r dir event file; do
    if [[ "$file" == *".credentials"* ]]; then
      PERMS=$(stat -c '%a' "${dir}/${file}" 2>/dev/null || echo "gone")
      if [[ "$PERMS" != "600" && "$PERMS" != "gone" ]]; then
        echo "FAIL: ${file} created with permissions ${PERMS} (expected 600)"
        FOUND_WEAK_PERMS=1
      fi
    fi
  done &

MONITOR_PID=$!

# Trigger credential write
node -e "require('./utils/secureStorage').getSecureStorage().update(d => ({...d, test: Date.now()}))"

sleep 1
kill "$MONITOR_PID" 2>/dev/null || true

if [[ "$FOUND_WEAK_PERMS" -eq 1 ]]; then
  echo "VULNERABILITY: Permission window detected"
  exit 1
else
  echo "PASS: No permission window detected"
fi

Integration Tests

# Verify atomic write survives process kill
node -e "
  const { atomicWriteFileSync } = require('./utils/atomicWrite');
  // Write valid data
  atomicWriteFileSync('/tmp/test-creds', JSON.stringify({token: 'valid'}), {mode: 0o600});
  // Start a write that will be interrupted
  setTimeout(() => {
    atomicWriteFileSync('/tmp/test-creds', JSON.stringify({token: 'new'}), {mode: 0o600});
  }, 10);
" &
PID=$!
sleep 0.005  # Kill mid-write
kill -9 $PID 2>/dev/null || true

# Verify file is either old or new -- never partial
CONTENT=$(cat /tmp/test-creds)
if echo "$CONTENT" | python3 -c "import sys,json; json.load(sys.stdin)" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "PASS: File contains valid JSON after crash"
else
  echo "FAIL: File corrupted after crash"
fi

Standard Requirement How Atomic Write Addresses It

Residual Risk Severity Mitigation
NFS/CIFS: rename not atomic across network filesystems Low Credential storage should be on local filesystem; detect and warn for network mounts

The atomic write pattern, combined with the cross-platform storage abstraction from Chapter 7, eliminates the credential storage chain's write-path vulnerabilities. The read path (credential consumption after storage) is addressed by the token lifecycle hardening in Chapters 10-12.

Security Assessment: Atomic Credential Operations

Property Before After
Permission window during write Present (umask-dependent) Eliminated (create with 0o600)
Partial write on crash Possible (writeFileSync without flush) Impossible (fsync + atomic rename)
Concurrent update corruption Possible (no locking) Prevented (file-based locking)
Symlink attack on write path Possible (follows symlinks) Prevented (O_CREAT, O_EXCL)
