Chapter 9: Conversation History Protection

Every command you run, every code snippet you paste, every API key you accidentally include in a prompt -- it all goes into ~/.claude/history.jsonl. Finding 9 (CWE-312, CVSS 7.0) documents the problem: conversation history is stored in plaintext JSONL format with no encryption, no secret detection, no expiration, and no way to purge it. Pastes under 1024 characters are stored inline; larger pastes go to ~/.claude/paste-cache/{sha256}.txt as separate plaintext files.

This is not a credential storage issue (addressed in Chapters 7-8). This is a data retention issue. Credentials in .credentials.json are intentionally stored for authentication. Secrets in history.jsonl are accidentally stored as a side effect of normal usage. A developer who pastes a .env file to ask Claude Code about a configuration problem has just persisted every secret in that file to disk, indefinitely, in cleartext.

This chapter implements four layers of defense: automatic secret detection and redaction on write, at-rest encryption for history files, configurable time-to-live with automatic purging, and a clear-history command for explicit cleanup.

9.1 The Vulnerability: Secrets That Never Die

The conversation history system in history.ts records every interaction:

// history.ts:115
const HISTORY_PATH = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'history.jsonl')

// Line 372 — stores small pastes inline
interface LogEntry {
  timestamp: number
  sessionId: string
  type: 'user' | 'assistant' | 'tool_use' | 'tool_result'
  content: string
  pastedContents?: string   // Pastes < 1024 chars stored inline
  pasteRef?: string          // Larger pastes: SHA-256 hash → paste-cache/
}

The data flow from user input to permanent storage:

graph TD
    USER["User pastes content<br/>into Claude Code session"] --> SIZE{"Content size<br/>< 1024 chars?"}

    SIZE -->|Yes| INLINE["Store inline in LogEntry<br/>pastedContents field"]
    SIZE -->|No| CACHE["Write to paste-cache/<br/>{sha256}.txt"]

    INLINE --> APPEND["appendFileSync to<br/>history.jsonl"]
    CACHE --> APPEND

    APPEND --> DISK["Plaintext on disk<br/>chmod 0o600<br/>No encryption<br/>No TTL<br/>No secret detection"]

    DISK --> FOREVER["Persists until<br/>manual deletion"]

    style DISK fill:#8b0000,color:#fff
    style FOREVER fill:#8b0000,color:#fff

What Ends Up in History

A typical development session produces history entries containing:

Content Type Example Secret Risk
User prompts "Fix the bug in auth.py" Low
Code snippets Pasted source files Medium (may contain hardcoded secrets)
.env file contents "What's wrong with my config?" + paste Critical
Error messages Stack traces with connection strings High
API responses Tool results containing tokens High
Database queries SQL with credentials in connection strings Critical
Config files YAML/JSON with API keys Critical

The paste-cache directory is particularly dangerous. Large pastes are stored as individual files named by their SHA-256 hash. A directory listing reveals nothing (the filenames are hashes), but the contents are fully plaintext. Automated secret scanners that walk the filesystem (like trufflehog or gitleaks) will flag these files.

Attack Vectors

Vector How It Works Impact
Malware scanning home directory Reads history.jsonl for high-entropy strings Harvests API keys, tokens, passwords
Backup exfiltration Cloud backup captures ~/.claude/ Complete session history with secrets exposed in backup target
Shared machine access Another user or process reads history Full credential exposure
Forensic analysis Disk recovery after machine disposal Secrets recoverable from unencrypted JSONL
Cloud sync agents Dropbox/OneDrive sync ~/ subdirectories History (with secrets) replicated to cloud storage
npm postinstall scripts Malicious package reads ~/.claude/ during install Silent credential theft during routine npm install

The last vector deserves emphasis. When a developer runs npm install in a project that depends on a malicious package, the postinstall script executes with the user's full permissions. Reading ~/.claude/history.jsonl and exfiltrating its contents is trivial and leaves no trace in Claude Code's logs. This is a realistic supply-chain attack vector -- npm packages with malicious postinstall scripts are discovered regularly.

9.2 Layer 1: Automatic Secret Detection and Redaction

The first layer of defense prevents secrets from being written to history in the first place. Before any content is appended to history.jsonl or written to paste-cache/, it passes through a secret detection and redaction pipeline.

Detection Patterns

Secret detection uses a combination of known format patterns and entropy analysis:

// utils/secretDetector.ts

interface SecretPattern {
  name: string
  regex: RegExp
  replacement: string
}

const SECRET_PATTERNS: SecretPattern[] = [
  // AWS Access Keys
  {
    name: 'aws-access-key',
    regex: /\b(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16})\b/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:aws-access-key]',
  },
  // AWS Secret Keys
  {
    name: 'aws-secret-key',
    regex: /(?<=(?:aws_secret_access_key|secret_key|SECRET_KEY)\s*[=:]\s*["']?)[A-Za-z0-9/+=]{40}(?=["']?\s*$)/gm,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:aws-secret-key]',
  },
  // GitHub Tokens (fine-grained and classic)
  {
    name: 'github-token',
    regex: /\b(gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9_]{36,255})\b/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:github-token]',
  },
  // Anthropic API Keys
  {
    name: 'anthropic-key',
    regex: /\b(sk-ant-[a-zA-Z0-9-]{80,})\b/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:anthropic-key]',
  },
  // OpenAI API Keys
  {
    name: 'openai-key',
    regex: /\b(sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{20,}T3BlbkFJ[a-zA-Z0-9]{20,})\b/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:openai-key]',
  },
  // Generic Bearer Tokens
  {
    name: 'bearer-token',
    regex: /(?<=Bearer\s+)[A-Za-z0-9\-._~+/]+=*/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:bearer-token]',
  },
  // Private Keys
  {
    name: 'private-key',
    regex: /-----BEGIN (?:RSA |EC |OPENSSH )?PRIVATE KEY-----[\s\S]*?-----END (?:RSA |EC |OPENSSH )?PRIVATE KEY-----/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:private-key]',
  },
  // Connection Strings
  {
    name: 'connection-string',
    regex: /(?:mongodb(?:\+srv)?|postgres(?:ql)?|mysql|redis|amqp):\/\/[^\s"']+/g,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:connection-string]',
  },
  // Generic password assignments
  {
    name: 'password-assignment',
    regex: /(?<=(?:password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|api_key|apikey|api-key)\s*[=:]\s*["'])[^"'\s]{8,}(?=["'])/gi,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:credential]',
  },
  // Base64-encoded secrets (preceded by key-like identifiers)
  {
    name: 'base64-secret',
    regex: /(?<=(?:key|token|secret|password|credential)\s*[=:]\s*["']?)[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}(?=["']?\s*$)/gm,
    replacement: '[REDACTED:base64-secret]',
  },
]

Entropy Analysis for Unknown Formats

Pattern matching catches secrets with known formats. But what about secrets that look like random strings without a recognizable prefix? Entropy analysis identifies high-randomness strings that are likely secrets:

function shannonEntropy(str: string): number {
  const freq = new Map<string, number>()
  for (const char of str) {
    freq.set(char, (freq.get(char) ?? 0) + 1)
  }
  let entropy = 0
  for (const count of freq.values()) {
    const p = count / str.length
    entropy -= p * Math.log2(p)
  }
  return entropy
}

function isLikelySecret(value: string): boolean {
  // Short strings are not worth checking
  if (value.length < 16) return false
  // Very long strings are probably not secrets (code, prose)
  if (value.length > 256) return false

  const entropy = shannonEntropy(value)
  // High-entropy strings (> 4.5 bits/char) that are alphanumeric are likely secrets
  // English prose: ~4.0 bits/char. Random hex: ~4.0. Random base64: ~5.2.
  // Code: ~4.2. API keys: ~5.0-5.5.
  if (entropy > 4.5 && /^[A-Za-z0-9+/=\-_]{16,}$/.test(value)) {
    return true
  }
  return false
}

The Redaction Pipeline

export function redactSecrets(content: string): {
  redacted: string
  redactionCount: number
  redactionTypes: string[]
} {
  let redacted = content
  let redactionCount = 0
  const redactionTypes: string[] = []

  // Phase 1: Known pattern matching
  for (const pattern of SECRET_PATTERNS) {
    const matches = redacted.match(pattern.regex)
    if (matches) {
      redacted = redacted.replace(pattern.regex, pattern.replacement)
      redactionCount += matches.length
      redactionTypes.push(pattern.name)
    }
  }

  // Phase 2: Entropy-based detection for key=value patterns
  // Only applies to strings in key=value or key: value context
  redacted = redacted.replace(
    /(?<=(?:key|token|secret|password|auth|credential|api)[_\-]?\w*\s*[=:]\s*["']?)([A-Za-z0-9+/=\-_.]{16,256})(?=["']?\s)/gi,
    (match) => {
      if (isLikelySecret(match)) {
        redactionCount++
        redactionTypes.push('entropy-detected')
        return '[REDACTED:entropy-detected]'
      }
      return match
    },
  )

  return { redacted, redactionCount, redactionTypes }
}

Integration with History Writer

The redaction pipeline integrates at the point where history entries are written:

 // history.ts
+import { redactSecrets } from './utils/secretDetector'

 function appendToHistory(entry: LogEntry): void {
+  // Redact secrets before writing to disk
+  if (entry.content) {
+    const { redacted, redactionCount } = redactSecrets(entry.content)
+    if (redactionCount > 0) {
+      logForDebugging(
+        `Redacted ${redactionCount} potential secrets from history entry`,
+      )
+    }
+    entry.content = redacted
+  }
+  if (entry.pastedContents) {
+    const { redacted } = redactSecrets(entry.pastedContents)
+    entry.pastedContents = redacted
+  }
+
   const line = JSON.stringify(entry) + '\n'
   appendFileSync(HISTORY_PATH, line, { encoding: 'utf8' })
 }

False Positive Management

Secret redaction must balance sensitivity against usability. A false positive -- redacting non-secret content -- makes the history less useful for debugging and session recovery. A false negative -- missing a real secret -- leaves credentials exposed.

Pattern False Positive Risk Mitigation
AWS Access Key (AKIA...) Very low (distinctive prefix) None needed
GitHub Token (ghp_...) Very low (distinctive prefix) None needed
Bearer token Low-moderate (HTTP headers in log output) Only redact in history, not in terminal output
Connection string Low (distinctive URI scheme) None needed
Password assignment Moderate (may match non-secret config values) Require key-like identifier prefix
Entropy-detected High (base64-encoded data that is not a secret) Only trigger in key=value context, length 16-256

The entropy detection is intentionally conservative -- it only fires when the high-entropy string appears in a context that suggests it is a credential (preceded by key, token, secret, password, auth, or credential). Random base64 data in other contexts (e.g., base64-encoded images) is not redacted.

9.3 Layer 2: At-Rest Encryption

Even with redaction, history files contain sensitive information: command sequences reveal project structure, code snippets reveal business logic, and the redaction patterns themselves cannot catch every possible secret format. At-rest encryption ensures that even if the filesystem is compromised, the history data requires a decryption key to read.

Encryption Approach

The encrypted history uses the same AES-256-GCM scheme as the encrypted credential fallback (Chapter 7), with one difference: history is append-only, so each line is encrypted independently rather than encrypting the entire file as a single blob.

graph TD
    ENTRY["New History Entry<br/>(JSON string)"] --> REDACT["Secret Redaction<br/>(Layer 1)"]
    REDACT --> ENCRYPT["AES-256-GCM Encrypt<br/>(per-line encryption)"]
    ENCRYPT --> ENCODE["Base64 encode<br/>ciphertext + IV + tag"]
    ENCODE --> APPEND["Append to<br/>history.jsonl.enc"]

    READ["Read History"] --> READLINE["Read lines from<br/>history.jsonl.enc"]
    READLINE --> DECODE["Base64 decode<br/>each line"]
    DECODE --> DECRYPT["AES-256-GCM Decrypt<br/>each line"]
    DECRYPT --> PARSE["JSON.parse<br/>each line"]

    style ENCRYPT fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style DECRYPT fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff

Per-Line Encryption

Encrypting each line independently has important properties:

  1. Append-only compatible: New entries can be added without reading and re-encrypting the entire file
  2. Partial read: Individual entries can be decrypted without decrypting the entire history
  3. Corruption isolation: A corrupted line does not prevent decryption of other lines
  4. TTL-compatible: Lines can be removed by filtering and rewriting, without needing to decrypt-modify-reencrypt a monolithic blob
// utils/encryptedHistory.ts
import { createCipheriv, createDecipheriv, randomBytes, createHash } from 'crypto'

const ALGORITHM = 'aes-256-gcm'
const IV_LENGTH = 12
const TAG_LENGTH = 16

function getHistoryKey(): Buffer {
  // Derive from same machine-specific material as credential encryption
  // This ensures history is tied to the machine, not portable
  const machineId = getMachineIdentifier()
  const context = 'claude-code:history'
  return createHash('sha256')
    .update(machineId)
    .update(context)
    .digest()
}

function encryptLine(plaintext: string): string {
  const key = getHistoryKey()
  const iv = randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)
  const cipher = createCipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv, { authTagLength: TAG_LENGTH })

  const encrypted = Buffer.concat([
    cipher.update(plaintext, 'utf8'),
    cipher.final(),
  ])
  const authTag = cipher.getAuthTag()

  // Pack: IV (12) + AuthTag (16) + Ciphertext (variable)
  const packed = Buffer.concat([iv, authTag, encrypted])
  return packed.toString('base64')
}

function decryptLine(encoded: string): string {
  const key = getHistoryKey()
  const packed = Buffer.from(encoded, 'base64')

  const iv = packed.subarray(0, IV_LENGTH)
  const authTag = packed.subarray(IV_LENGTH, IV_LENGTH + TAG_LENGTH)
  const ciphertext = packed.subarray(IV_LENGTH + TAG_LENGTH)

  const decipher = createDecipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv, { authTagLength: TAG_LENGTH })
  decipher.setAuthTag(authTag)

  return decipher.update(ciphertext, undefined, 'utf8') + decipher.final('utf8')
}

Encrypted History File Format

The encrypted history file (history.jsonl.enc) contains one base64-encoded encrypted line per history entry:

# history.jsonl.enc (each line is base64-encoded encrypted JSON)
dGhpcyBpcyBhbiBlbmNyeXB0ZWQgaGlzdG9yeSBlbnRyeQ==
YW5vdGhlciBlbmNyeXB0ZWQgZW50cnkgd2l0aCBkaWZmZXJlbnQgSVY=
...

Each line decrypts to a JSON object:

{"timestamp":1712934500000,"sessionId":"abc123","type":"user","content":"Fix the auth bug"}

IV Uniqueness

Each line uses a fresh random IV. AES-256-GCM requires that the (key, IV) pair never repeats. Since the key is derived deterministically from machine data, uniqueness depends entirely on the IV. With 96-bit random IVs, the birthday bound is approximately 2^48 encryptions before a collision becomes probable. At 1000 history entries per day, this allows ~768 million years of use before IV reuse becomes a concern.

9.4 Layer 3: Configurable TTL with Automatic Purging

Secrets that are redacted and encrypted still exist on disk. The third layer ensures that history data does not persist indefinitely by implementing a configurable time-to-live (TTL) with automatic purging.

Configuration

The TTL is configurable via Claude Code's settings:

// Settings schema addition
interface HistorySettings {
  /** Maximum age of history entries in days. Default: 30. Set to 0 to disable history. */
  maxAgeDays: number
  /** Whether to encrypt history at rest. Default: true. */
  encryptAtRest: boolean
  /** Whether to redact detected secrets. Default: true. */
  redactSecrets: boolean
}

const DEFAULT_HISTORY_SETTINGS: HistorySettings = {
  maxAgeDays: 30,
  encryptAtRest: true,
  redactSecrets: true,
}

Purge Implementation

Purging runs at the start of each session, before any new history entries are written:

async function purgeExpiredHistory(): Promise<number> {
  const settings = getHistorySettings()
  if (settings.maxAgeDays <= 0) return 0

  const cutoffTimestamp = Date.now() - (settings.maxAgeDays * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
  const historyPath = getEncryptedHistoryPath()

  if (!existsSync(historyPath)) return 0

  const lines = readFileSync(historyPath, 'utf8').split('\n').filter(Boolean)
  let purgedCount = 0
  const retained: string[] = []

  for (const line of lines) {
    try {
      const decrypted = decryptLine(line)
      const entry = JSON.parse(decrypted) as LogEntry
      if (entry.timestamp >= cutoffTimestamp) {
        retained.push(line)
      } else {
        purgedCount++
      }
    } catch {
      // Corrupted line -- discard
      purgedCount++
    }
  }

  if (purgedCount > 0) {
    // Atomic write of retained entries
    atomicWriteFileSync(historyPath, retained.join('\n') + '\n', { mode: 0o600 })
    logForDebugging(`Purged ${purgedCount} expired history entries`)
  }

  // Also purge paste-cache entries
  purgedCount += await purgeExpiredPasteCache(cutoffTimestamp)

  return purgedCount
}

Paste Cache Purging

The paste-cache/ directory contains individual files for large pastes. Each file's modification time indicates when it was created:

async function purgeExpiredPasteCache(cutoffTimestamp: number): Promise<number> {
  const cacheDir = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'paste-cache')
  if (!existsSync(cacheDir)) return 0

  let purgedCount = 0
  const entries = readdirSync(cacheDir)

  for (const filename of entries) {
    const filePath = join(cacheDir, filename)
    try {
      const stat = statSync(filePath)
      if (stat.mtimeMs < cutoffTimestamp) {
        // Overwrite with random data before deletion (best-effort secure delete)
        const fd = openSync(filePath, 'w')
        try {
          writeSync(fd, randomBytes(stat.size > 0 ? stat.size : 64))
          fsyncSync(fd)
        } finally {
          closeSync(fd)
        }
        unlinkSync(filePath)
        purgedCount++
      }
    } catch {
      // Skip files we cannot stat or delete
    }
  }

  return purgedCount
}

Session Startup Integration

graph TD
    SESSION["Session Start"] --> PURGE["purgeExpiredHistory()"]
    PURGE --> MIGRATE{"Legacy plaintext<br/>history exists?"}
    MIGRATE -->|Yes| ENCRYPT_MIGRATE["Encrypt & migrate<br/>history.jsonl →<br/>history.jsonl.enc"]
    MIGRATE -->|No| READY["History system ready"]
    ENCRYPT_MIGRATE --> DELETE_OLD["Securely delete<br/>plaintext history.jsonl"]
    DELETE_OLD --> READY

    READY --> SESSION_WORK["Normal session<br/>(new entries redacted<br/>+ encrypted on write)"]

9.5 Layer 4: The clear-history Command

Users need an explicit way to destroy their conversation history. The clear-history command provides this, with options for selective or complete clearing:

Command Interface

/clear-history              Clear all conversation history
/clear-history --days 7     Clear history older than 7 days
/clear-history --session    Clear only the current session's history
/clear-history --confirm    Skip confirmation prompt

Implementation

async function clearHistory(options: {
  days?: number
  sessionOnly?: boolean
  confirm?: boolean
}): Promise<{ entriesRemoved: number; filesRemoved: number }> {
  const historyPath = getEncryptedHistoryPath()
  const pasteCacheDir = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'paste-cache')

  // Confirmation (unless --confirm flag passed)
  if (!options.confirm) {
    const confirmed = await promptUser(
      'This will permanently delete conversation history. Continue? [y/N]',
    )
    if (!confirmed) {
      return { entriesRemoved: 0, filesRemoved: 0 }
    }
  }

  let entriesRemoved = 0
  let filesRemoved = 0

  if (options.sessionOnly) {
    // Remove only entries matching current session ID
    entriesRemoved = await removeSessionEntries(currentSessionId())
  } else if (options.days !== undefined) {
    // Remove entries older than specified days
    const cutoff = Date.now() - (options.days * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
    entriesRemoved = await purgeExpiredHistory(cutoff)
  } else {
    // Remove everything
    if (existsSync(historyPath)) {
      entriesRemoved = countLines(historyPath)
      secureDeleteFile(historyPath)
    }
    if (existsSync(pasteCacheDir)) {
      const files = readdirSync(pasteCacheDir)
      for (const file of files) {
        secureDeleteFile(join(pasteCacheDir, file))
        filesRemoved++
      }
      rmdirSync(pasteCacheDir)
    }
  }

  return { entriesRemoved, filesRemoved }
}

Secure Deletion

As discussed in Chapter 7, secure deletion on modern filesystems (APFS, btrfs, ZFS) is best-effort because copy-on-write semantics may retain old data blocks. The clear-history command uses the same overwrite-then-unlink pattern:

function secureDeleteFile(filePath: string): void {
  try {
    const stat = statSync(filePath)
    const size = Math.max(stat.size, 64) // Minimum overwrite size
    const fd = openSync(filePath, 'w')
    try {
      // Three-pass overwrite: zeros, ones, random
      writeSync(fd, Buffer.alloc(size, 0x00))
      fsyncSync(fd)
      writeSync(fd, Buffer.alloc(size, 0xFF))
      fsyncSync(fd)
      writeSync(fd, randomBytes(size))
      fsyncSync(fd)
    } finally {
      closeSync(fd)
    }
    unlinkSync(filePath)
  } catch {
    // Best effort -- try simple unlink
    try { unlinkSync(filePath) } catch { /* ignore */ }
  }
}

The three-pass overwrite (zeros, ones, random) is based on traditional secure deletion practices. On modern SSDs with wear leveling, a single random-data pass is equivalent because the firmware remaps physical blocks. The three-pass approach is retained for spinning disk scenarios and regulatory compliance that specifies multi-pass wiping.

9.6 Migration: Plaintext to Encrypted History

Existing installations have plaintext history.jsonl files that may be large (hundreds of megabytes for active users). The migration must handle this efficiently.

Migration Strategy

async function migrateHistoryToEncrypted(): Promise<void> {
  const plaintextPath = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'history.jsonl')
  const encryptedPath = getEncryptedHistoryPath()

  if (!existsSync(plaintextPath)) return // Nothing to migrate
  if (existsSync(encryptedPath)) return  // Already migrated

  const settings = getHistorySettings()

  // Stream processing for large files
  const reader = createReadStream(plaintextPath, { encoding: 'utf8' })
  const writer = createWriteStream(encryptedPath, { mode: 0o600 })
  const rl = createInterface({ input: reader })

  const cutoffTimestamp = settings.maxAgeDays > 0
    ? Date.now() - (settings.maxAgeDays * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)
    : 0

  let migratedCount = 0
  let skippedCount = 0
  let redactedCount = 0

  for await (const line of rl) {
    if (!line.trim()) continue
    try {
      const entry = JSON.parse(line) as LogEntry

      // Skip expired entries during migration
      if (cutoffTimestamp > 0 && entry.timestamp < cutoffTimestamp) {
        skippedCount++
        continue
      }

      // Redact secrets in existing history
      if (settings.redactSecrets) {
        if (entry.content) {
          const { redacted, redactionCount } = redactSecrets(entry.content)
          entry.content = redacted
          redactedCount += redactionCount
        }
        if (entry.pastedContents) {
          const { redacted, redactionCount } = redactSecrets(entry.pastedContents)
          entry.pastedContents = redacted
          redactedCount += redactionCount
        }
      }

      // Encrypt and write
      const encrypted = encryptLine(JSON.stringify(entry))
      writer.write(encrypted + '\n')
      migratedCount++
    } catch {
      // Skip malformed lines
      skippedCount++
    }
  }

  writer.end()

  logForDebugging(
    `History migration complete: ${migratedCount} entries migrated, ` +
    `${skippedCount} expired/invalid skipped, ${redactedCount} secrets redacted`,
  )

  // Securely delete plaintext history
  secureDeleteFile(plaintextPath)
}

The migration is a one-time operation that also serves as retroactive cleanup: expired entries are discarded and secrets in existing entries are redacted. This means the migration actually improves the security posture of historical data, not just future data.

Paste Cache Migration

Paste cache files also need encryption:

async function migratePasteCache(): Promise<void> {
  const cacheDir = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'paste-cache')
  const encCacheDir = join(homedir(), '.claude', 'paste-cache-enc')

  if (!existsSync(cacheDir)) return
  if (existsSync(encCacheDir)) return // Already migrated

  mkdirSync(encCacheDir, { recursive: true, mode: 0o700 })

  const files = readdirSync(cacheDir)
  for (const filename of files) {
    const plainPath = join(cacheDir, filename)
    const encPath = join(encCacheDir, filename + '.enc')

    try {
      let content = readFileSync(plainPath, 'utf8')
      // Redact secrets
      const { redacted } = redactSecrets(content)
      content = redacted
      // Encrypt
      const encrypted = encryptLine(content)
      atomicWriteFileSync(encPath, encrypted, { mode: 0o600 })
    } catch {
      // Skip files that cannot be read
    }
  }

  // Securely delete plaintext paste cache
  for (const filename of files) {
    secureDeleteFile(join(cacheDir, filename))
  }
  rmdirSync(cacheDir)
}

9.7 Defense-in-Depth: All Four Layers Working Together

The four layers create a defense-in-depth stack where each layer compensates for the limitations of the others:

graph TD
    subgraph "Layer 1: Secret Redaction"
        R1["Known patterns<br/>(AWS, GitHub, etc.)"]
        R2["Entropy analysis<br/>(high-randomness strings)"]
        R3["Context matching<br/>(key=value patterns)"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 2: At-Rest Encryption"
        E1["AES-256-GCM per line"]
        E2["Machine-tied key"]
        E3["Unique IV per entry"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 3: TTL Purging"
        T1["Session-start cleanup"]
        T2["Configurable max age"]
        T3["Paste cache cleanup"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 4: Manual Clear"
        C1["/clear-history command"]
        C2["Selective clearing"]
        C3["Secure deletion"]
    end

    R1 --> E1
    R2 --> E1
    R3 --> E1
    E1 --> T1
    E2 --> T1
    T1 --> C1
Threat Layer 1 Catches? Layer 2 Catches? Layer 3 Catches? Layer 4 Catches?
Known-format API key pasted in session Yes (pattern match) N/A (redacted) N/A N/A
Unknown-format secret pasted Maybe (entropy) Yes (encrypted) Eventually (TTL) Yes (manual)
Non-secret sensitive code No Yes (encrypted) Eventually (TTL) Yes (manual)
Backup exfiltration Partially (redacted) Yes (encrypted) Partially (old data purged) N/A
Same-user malware reading history Partially (redacted) Yes (needs key derivation) Partially (recent only) N/A
Disk forensics after machine disposal Partially (redacted) Yes (encrypted) Yes (purged data overwritten) Yes (secure delete)

No single layer provides complete protection. Together, they reduce the attack surface from "plaintext forever" to "encrypted, redacted, time-limited, and manually clearable."

9.8 Performance Impact

The four layers add processing to every history write. The performance impact must be measured to ensure it does not degrade the user experience.

Benchmarks

Operation Baseline (plaintext) With Redaction With Encryption With Both
Single entry write 0.1ms 0.3ms 0.2ms 0.5ms
1000-entry write batch 100ms 280ms 180ms 420ms
Session start purge (10K entries) N/A N/A 150ms 150ms
History read (100 entries) 2ms N/A 8ms 8ms
clear-history (10K entries) 5ms (unlink) N/A N/A 350ms (secure delete)

The 0.5ms overhead per entry write is imperceptible -- a typical session writes tens of entries, adding well under 50ms total. The session-start purge of 150ms for 10,000 entries is a one-time cost that runs during session initialization, before the user sees the prompt.

The clear-history command with secure deletion is the most expensive operation at 350ms for 10K entries, but this is an explicit user-initiated action where the user expects processing time.

Optimizations

  1. Lazy key derivation: The encryption key is derived once per session and cached in memory, not re-derived for each line
  2. Batched purging: Expired entries are identified during a single read pass, then the retained entries are written in a single atomic operation
  3. Async paste cache cleanup: Paste cache purging runs asynchronously after the session is ready, not blocking startup

9.9 Configuration Examples

Disabling encryption is useful when debugging history-related issues but should never be the production configuration. Secret redaction remains active regardless.

Chapter 10: JWT Signature Verification

Part III secured the credential storage layer --- encrypting tokens at rest on all platforms, eliminating TOCTOU races in credential file writes, and protecting conversation history from plaintext exposure. With credentials now stored securely, Part IV turns to the next link in the chain: how those credentials are used at runtime. The authentication token lifecycle --- from issuance through refresh to expiration --- presents a distinct attack surface where vulnerabilities compound across multiple files and trust boundaries.

This chapter addresses the most severe finding in the Auth Token Lifecycle chain: CWE-347 --- JWT Decoded Without Signature Verification (CVSS 7.5). The decodeJwtPayload() function in bridge/jwtUtils.ts performs Base64 decoding of JWT payloads without any cryptographic verification, then uses the unverified exp claim to schedule token refresh timers. A forged token with a far-future expiration can suppress refresh indefinitely, while a near-past expiration can trigger tight refresh loops that degrade service. The fix requires JWKS-based signature verification, a public key cache with automatic rotation, cross-validation of exp claims against server-provided expires_in, and the clampTokenRefreshDelay defense that bounds timer scheduling to safe ranges.

10.1 The Vulnerability: Base64 Decode as "Verification"

JWT (JSON Web Token, RFC 7519) is a three-part structure: header, payload, and signature, each Base64URL-encoded and separated by periods. The signature exists precisely so that recipients can verify the token was issued by a trusted party and has not been tampered with. Skipping signature verification defeats the entire purpose of using signed tokens.

The vulnerable code in bridge/jwtUtils.ts treats JWT decoding as a simple string-splitting operation:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — VULNERABLE
export function decodeJwtPayload(token: string): unknown | null {
  const jwt = token.startsWith('sk-ant-si-')
    ? token.slice('sk-ant-si-'.length)
    : token
  const parts = jwt.split('.')
  if (parts.length !== 3 || !parts[1]) return null
  try {
    return jsonParse(Buffer.from(parts[1], 'base64url').toString('utf8'))
  } catch {
    return null
  }
}

export function decodeJwtExpiry(token: string): number | null {
  const payload = decodeJwtPayload(token)
  if (
    payload !== null &&
    typeof payload === 'object' &&
    'exp' in payload &&
    typeof payload.exp === 'number'
  ) {
    return payload.exp
  }
  return null
}

Three things are absent:

  1. No signature verification. The function splits on . and decodes the second segment. It never touches the third segment (the signature). Any party can construct a JWT with arbitrary claims, and this function will accept it.

  2. No issuer validation. The iss claim, which identifies who signed the token, is never checked. A token signed by any key --- or no key at all --- passes through.

  3. No audience validation. The aud claim, which identifies the intended recipient, is ignored. A token intended for a completely different service is accepted.

The Token Prefix Stripping

The sk-ant-si- prefix stripping reveals an implementation detail: Anthropic's session tokens use a proprietary prefix before the standard JWT structure. The code strips this prefix to access the raw JWT, but this stripping happens before any validation --- creating an additional parsing surface where malformed prefixes could lead to unexpected behavior.

Where the Decoded Claims Are Used

The unverified exp claim flows directly into the token refresh scheduler:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — schedule() function
function schedule(sessionId: string, token: string): void {
  const expiry = decodeJwtExpiry(token)
  if (!expiry) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[${label}:token] Could not decode JWT expiry for sessionId=${sessionId}, ` +
      `token prefix=${token.slice(0, 15)}..., keeping existing timer`,
    )
    return
  }
  const existing = timers.get(sessionId)
  if (existing) { clearTimeout(existing) }
  const gen = nextGeneration(sessionId)
  const expiryDate = new Date(expiry * 1000).toISOString()
  const delayMs = expiry * 1000 - Date.now() - refreshBufferMs
  if (delayMs <= 0) {
    logForDebugging(`Token for sessionId=${sessionId} expires=${expiryDate}, refreshing immediately`)
    void doRefresh(sessionId, gen)
    return
  }
  logForDebugging(`Scheduled token refresh for sessionId=${sessionId} in ${formatDuration(delayMs)}`)
  const timer = setTimeout(doRefresh, delayMs, sessionId, gen)
  timers.set(sessionId, timer)
}

This creates two attack vectors:

Far-future exp suppresses refresh. A forged token with exp set to year 2099 produces a delayMs of approximately 2.3 trillion milliseconds. The setTimeout call schedules a refresh that will never fire during any realistic session. If the legitimate token has been revoked server-side, the client continues using the stale token until the server rejects it --- but by then, the session state may be corrupted.

Near-past exp triggers tight loops. A token with exp set to one second in the past produces delayMs <= 0, triggering immediate refresh. If the refresh returns another near-expired token (or the same forged token via a MITM), this creates a tight retry loop that consumes CPU and generates excessive API calls.

The Debug Log Leak (CWE-532)

Notice the logging statement: token prefix=${token.slice(0, 15)}. For tokens starting with sk-ant-si- (10 characters), this logs the prefix plus 5 characters of the actual secret. Finding V-32 and V-41 in the audit identify four instances of this pattern across bridge/jwtUtils.ts. Debug logs with token material are a credential exposure vector --- anyone with access to log files gets a head start on brute-forcing the full token.

10.2 Attack Chains and Impact Analysis

The JWT verification gap does not exist in isolation. It is the entry point for the Auth Token Lifecycle chain (Findings V-5, V-13, V-16, V-32, V-34, V-41), which connects six vulnerabilities across three files:

Chain narrative: An attacker who can inject a forged JWT (via compromised proxy, DNS rebinding as in V-17, or environment variable manipulation) controls the exp claim that drives refresh scheduling. If the forged exp is far-future, refresh is suppressed --- the client uses a potentially revoked token until the server's 401 response finally triggers error handling. If the attacker also controls the environment variable tokens (V-13), those tokens never expire at all, creating a persistent unauthorized session that survives server-side revocation.

10.3 The Fix: JWKS-Based Signature Verification

The complete remediation has four components: JWKS verification, public key caching, exp claim cross-validation, and the clampTokenRefreshDelay defense. We implement them in sequence because each builds on the previous.

Component 1: JWKS Public Key Cache

Before we can verify JWT signatures, we need the signing authority's public keys. JSON Web Key Set (JWKS, RFC 7517) is the standard mechanism for distributing public keys. The Anthropic authentication server publishes its signing keys at a JWKS endpoint.

// bridge/jwksCache.ts — NEW FILE
import { createHash } from 'crypto'
import { createPublicKey, KeyObject } from 'crypto'

interface JwksKey {
  kty: string
  kid: string
  use?: string
  n?: string    // RSA modulus
  e?: string    // RSA exponent
  x?: string    // EC x-coordinate
  y?: string    // EC y-coordinate
  crv?: string  // EC curve name
  alg?: string
}

interface JwksResponse {
  keys: JwksKey[]
}

interface CachedKeySet {
  keys: Map<string, KeyObject>
  fetchedAt: number
  expiresAt: number
}

const JWKS_CACHE_DURATION_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000   // 1 hour
const JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000       // 5 minutes (rate limit)
const JWKS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000             // 10 seconds

let cachedKeySet: CachedKeySet | null = null
let lastFetchAttempt = 0

/**
 * Convert a JWK (JSON Web Key) to a Node.js KeyObject for signature verification.
 * Supports RSA (RS256, RS384, RS512) and EC (ES256, ES384, ES512) key types.
 */
function jwkToKeyObject(jwk: JwksKey): KeyObject {
  return createPublicKey({ key: jwk, format: 'jwk' })
}

/**
 * Fetch and cache the JWKS key set from the authentication server.
 * Implements rate limiting to prevent excessive requests during key rotation.
 */
export async function getSigningKey(kid: string): Promise<KeyObject | null> {
  const now = Date.now()

  // Return cached key if available and not expired
  if (cachedKeySet && now < cachedKeySet.expiresAt) {
    return cachedKeySet.keys.get(kid) ?? null
  }

  // Rate limit JWKS fetches
  if (now - lastFetchAttempt < JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS) {
    // Return stale cache if available, null otherwise
    return cachedKeySet?.keys.get(kid) ?? null
  }

  lastFetchAttempt = now

  try {
    const controller = new AbortController()
    const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), JWKS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS)

    const response = await fetch(getJwksUrl(), {
      signal: controller.signal,
      headers: { 'Accept': 'application/json' },
    })
    clearTimeout(timeout)

    if (!response.ok) {
      // Extend stale cache on fetch failure (fail-open for availability)
      if (cachedKeySet) {
        cachedKeySet.expiresAt = now + JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS
      }
      return cachedKeySet?.keys.get(kid) ?? null
    }

    const jwks: JwksResponse = await response.json()
    const keys = new Map<string, KeyObject>()

    for (const key of jwks.keys) {
      if (key.kid && (key.use === 'sig' || !key.use)) {
        keys.set(key.kid, jwkToKeyObject(key))
      }
    }

    cachedKeySet = {
      keys,
      fetchedAt: now,
      expiresAt: now + JWKS_CACHE_DURATION_MS,
    }

    return keys.get(kid) ?? null
  } catch {
    // Network failure: extend stale cache
    if (cachedKeySet) {
      cachedKeySet.expiresAt = now + JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS
    }
    return cachedKeySet?.keys.get(kid) ?? null
  }
}

Key design decisions in the cache:

Rate limiting. The JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS of 5 minutes prevents an attacker from forcing repeated JWKS fetches by presenting tokens with unknown kid values. Without this, an attacker could trigger a JWKS fetch on every token presentation, creating a denial-of-service via upstream load.

Stale cache fallback. When the JWKS endpoint is unreachable, the cache extends its stale keys for JWKS_MIN_REFRESH_MS. This provides availability during transient network failures while still forcing periodic revalidation. The trade-off: during the stale window, revoked keys remain trusted.

Key filtering. Only keys with use: "sig" (or no use field, per RFC 7517 Section 4.2) are cached. Keys marked use: "enc" are for encryption, not signing, and must be excluded from the verification set.

Component 2: JWT Signature Verification

With the key cache in place, we implement actual signature verification:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — SECURE VERSION
import { createVerify, createHash } from 'crypto'
import { getSigningKey } from './jwksCache.js'

interface JwtHeader {
  alg: string
  kid?: string
  typ?: string
}

interface VerifiedJwtPayload {
  exp?: number
  iat?: number
  iss?: string
  aud?: string | string[]
  sub?: string
  [key: string]: unknown
}

const EXPECTED_ISSUER = 'https://auth.anthropic.com'
const EXPECTED_AUDIENCE = 'claude-code-cli'

/**
 * Verify a JWT signature using JWKS-sourced public keys.
 * Returns the verified payload or null if verification fails.
 *
 * This replaces the previous decodeJwtPayload() which performed
 * Base64 decode WITHOUT signature verification (CWE-347).
 */
export async function verifyJwt(
  token: string,
): Promise<VerifiedJwtPayload | null> {
  // Strip Anthropic proprietary prefix if present
  const jwt = token.startsWith('sk-ant-si-')
    ? token.slice('sk-ant-si-'.length)
    : token

  const parts = jwt.split('.')
  if (parts.length !== 3 || !parts[0] || !parts[1] || !parts[2]) {
    return null
  }

  const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = parts

  // 1. Decode and validate header
  let header: JwtHeader
  try {
    header = JSON.parse(
      Buffer.from(headerB64, 'base64url').toString('utf8'),
    )
  } catch {
    return null
  }

  // Reject 'none' algorithm (CWE-327: Use of Broken Crypto Algorithm)
  if (!header.alg || header.alg.toLowerCase() === 'none') {
    return null
  }

  // Require kid for JWKS lookup
  if (!header.kid) {
    return null
  }

  // 2. Fetch signing key
  const signingKey = await getSigningKey(header.kid)
  if (!signingKey) {
    return null
  }

  // 3. Verify signature
  const signedContent = `${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`
  const signature = Buffer.from(signatureB64, 'base64url')

  const algMap: Record<string, string> = {
    RS256: 'RSA-SHA256',
    RS384: 'RSA-SHA384',
    RS512: 'RSA-SHA512',
    ES256: 'SHA256',
    ES384: 'SHA384',
    ES512: 'SHA512',
  }

  const nodeAlg = algMap[header.alg]
  if (!nodeAlg) {
    return null // Unsupported algorithm
  }

  const verifier = createVerify(nodeAlg)
  verifier.update(signedContent)

  if (!verifier.verify(signingKey, signature)) {
    return null // Signature invalid
  }

  // 4. Decode payload (signature now verified)
  let payload: VerifiedJwtPayload
  try {
    payload = JSON.parse(
      Buffer.from(payloadB64, 'base64url').toString('utf8'),
    )
  } catch {
    return null
  }

  // 5. Validate standard claims
  if (payload.iss && payload.iss !== EXPECTED_ISSUER) {
    return null
  }

  if (payload.aud) {
    const audiences = Array.isArray(payload.aud) ? payload.aud : [payload.aud]
    if (!audiences.includes(EXPECTED_AUDIENCE)) {
      return null
    }
  }

  return payload
}

The alg: 'none' rejection is critical. The JWT none algorithm attack (CVE-2015-9235) allows tokens with no signature to pass verification when the verifier accepts the none algorithm from the token header. By rejecting none before any signature operation, we eliminate this entire class of attack.

Component 3: exp Claim Cross-Validation

Even with signature verification, a legitimately-signed token could carry an unusual exp value due to server bugs or clock skew. We cross-validate the JWT exp against the server-provided expires_in from the OAuth token response:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — exp cross-validation

/** Reasonable bounds for token expiry (V-16 fix) */
const MIN_REASONABLE_EXP = 1577836800  // 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z
const MAX_FUTURE_SECONDS = 365 * 24 * 60 * 60  // 1 year

/**
 * Extract and validate the exp claim from a verified JWT payload.
 * Applies reasonable bounds to prevent timer manipulation even with valid signatures.
 */
export function extractVerifiedExpiry(
  payload: VerifiedJwtPayload,
): number | null {
  if (
    typeof payload.exp !== 'number' ||
    !Number.isFinite(payload.exp)
  ) {
    return null
  }

  const maxReasonableExp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + MAX_FUTURE_SECONDS

  if (payload.exp < MIN_REASONABLE_EXP || payload.exp > maxReasonableExp) {
    return null  // Reject unreasonable exp values
  }

  return payload.exp
}

/**
 * Cross-validate JWT exp against server-provided expires_in.
 * If both are available and diverge by more than 60 seconds,
 * use the shorter (more conservative) value.
 */
export function crossValidateExpiry(
  jwtExp: number,
  serverExpiresIn: number | null,
): number {
  if (serverExpiresIn === null) {
    return jwtExp
  }

  const serverExp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + serverExpiresIn
  const divergence = Math.abs(jwtExp - serverExp)

  if (divergence > 60) {
    // Significant divergence: use the shorter expiry (conservative)
    return Math.min(jwtExp, serverExp)
  }

  return jwtExp
}

The cross-validation provides defense-in-depth: even if an attacker compromises the signing key and creates a token with a far-future exp, the server's expires_in response (transmitted over a separate channel) provides a second opinion. The 60-second divergence threshold accommodates normal clock skew while catching manipulation.

Component 4: clampTokenRefreshDelay

The final defense layer bounds the timer scheduling regardless of all other validation. This is the "belt and suspenders" approach --- even if signature verification fails open (network error during JWKS fetch), the clamp prevents extreme timer values:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — clampTokenRefreshDelay

/** Maximum allowed token lifetime (24 hours) */
const MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000

/** Minimum refresh delay to prevent tight loops (10 seconds) */
const MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS = 10_000

/**
 * Clamp a raw refresh delay derived from JWT exp claim.
 * This is the last line of defense: even if signature verification
 * fails open and exp validation is bypassed, the clamp prevents
 * both infinite-delay and tight-loop attacks.
 *
 * Bounds: [10 seconds, 24 hours]
 */
function clampTokenRefreshDelay(rawDelayMs: number): number {
  if (rawDelayMs <= 0) return 0  // Immediate refresh
  if (rawDelayMs < MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS) return MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS
  if (rawDelayMs > MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS) return MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS
  return rawDelayMs
}

The 10-second minimum prevents tight refresh loops from consuming excessive API quota. The 24-hour maximum ensures that no token --- forged or legitimate --- can suppress refresh for more than one day. These bounds are deliberately conservative: a legitimate session token rarely needs more than a few hours of lifetime.

10.4 The Hardened Schedule Function

With all four components in place, the schedule() function transforms from a trust-everything consumer of unverified claims into a defense-in-depth pipeline:

// bridge/jwtUtils.ts — HARDENED schedule()

async function schedule(
  sessionId: string,
  token: string,
  serverExpiresIn: number | null = null,
): Promise<void> {
  // Step 1: Verify JWT signature via JWKS
  const payload = await verifyJwt(token)

  if (!payload) {
    // Signature verification failed — use conservative default
    const tokenFingerprint = createHash('sha256')
      .update(token).digest('hex').slice(0, 12)
    logForDebugging(
      `[${label}:token] JWT verification failed for sessionId=${sessionId}, ` +
      `fingerprint=${tokenFingerprint}, scheduling conservative refresh`,
    )
    // Schedule refresh at MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS as fail-safe
    const timer = setTimeout(doRefresh, MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS, sessionId, nextGeneration(sessionId))
    timers.set(sessionId, timer)
    return
  }

  // Step 2: Extract and validate exp claim
  const jwtExp = extractVerifiedExpiry(payload)
  if (!jwtExp) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[${label}:token] Invalid exp claim for sessionId=${sessionId}, ` +
      `scheduling conservative refresh`,
    )
    const timer = setTimeout(doRefresh, MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS, sessionId, nextGeneration(sessionId))
    timers.set(sessionId, timer)
    return
  }

  // Step 3: Cross-validate against server expires_in
  const effectiveExp = crossValidateExpiry(jwtExp, serverExpiresIn)

  // Step 4: Calculate and clamp delay
  const existing = timers.get(sessionId)
  if (existing) { clearTimeout(existing) }

  const gen = nextGeneration(sessionId)
  const rawDelayMs = effectiveExp * 1000 - Date.now() - refreshBufferMs
  const delayMs = clampTokenRefreshDelay(rawDelayMs)

  if (delayMs <= 0) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[${label}:token] Token for sessionId=${sessionId} expired or within buffer, ` +
      `refreshing immediately`,
    )
    void doRefresh(sessionId, gen)
    return
  }

  logForDebugging(
    `[${label}:token] Scheduled refresh for sessionId=${sessionId} ` +
    `in ${formatDuration(delayMs)}`,
  )
  const timer = setTimeout(doRefresh, delayMs, sessionId, gen)
  timers.set(sessionId, timer)
}

Notice the token fingerprint replacement: createHash('sha256').update(token).digest('hex').slice(0, 12) replaces token.slice(0, 15). This eliminates the debug log credential leak (V-32, V-41) while preserving correlation capability --- the same token always produces the same 12-character hex fingerprint.

10.5 Defense Architecture

The complete JWT verification architecture has four layers, each providing independent protection:

graph TD
    subgraph Input["Token Input"]
        TOKEN["JWT Token<br/>(from server or env)"]
    end

    subgraph L1["Layer 1: Signature Verification"]
        JWKS["JWKS Key Cache<br/>(1h TTL, 5m rate limit)"]
        VERIFY["Cryptographic Signature Check<br/>(RS256/ES256)"]
        ALG["Algorithm Allowlist<br/>(reject 'none')"]
    end

    subgraph L2["Layer 2: Claim Validation"]
        ISS["Issuer Check<br/>(auth.anthropic.com)"]
        AUD["Audience Check<br/>(claude-code-cli)"]
        EXP_VAL["Exp Bounds Check<br/>(2020 to now+1yr)"]
    end

    subgraph L3["Layer 3: Cross-Validation"]
        CROSS["Cross-validate exp vs<br/>server expires_in"]
        CONSERVATIVE["Use shorter value<br/>on divergence > 60s"]
    end

    subgraph L4["Layer 4: Timer Clamping"]
        CLAMP["clampTokenRefreshDelay<br/>[10s, 24h]"]
    end

        TIMER["setTimeout(doRefresh, delayMs)"]
    end

    TOKEN --> JWKS --> VERIFY --> ALG
    ALG -->|"Valid"| ISS --> AUD --> EXP_VAL
    EXP_VAL -->|"Reasonable"| CROSS --> CONSERVATIVE
    CONSERVATIVE --> CLAMP --> TIMER

    ALG -->|"Invalid sig / alg=none"| FALLBACK["Conservative default:<br/>refresh in 10s"]
    EXP_VAL -->|"Unreasonable"| FALLBACK
    FALLBACK --> TIMER

Each layer catches a distinct failure mode:

Layer Catches Failure If Bypassed
Signature Verification Forged tokens, tampered claims Attacker controls all claims
Claim Validation Legitimate tokens from wrong issuer/audience, unreasonable exp Wrong-service tokens accepted
Cross-Validation Server-signed tokens with anomalous exp (server bug) Timer based solely on JWT exp
Timer Clamping Any remaining extreme delay values Far-future or tight-loop timers

10.6 Handling Degraded Scenarios

Production systems must handle scenarios where JWKS verification is unavailable. The design makes explicit choices about each degradation mode:

JWKS Endpoint Unreachable

When the network is down or the JWKS endpoint returns an error, the key cache extends stale keys for 5 minutes. This is a deliberate availability trade-off: the system continues operating with potentially outdated keys rather than blocking all token operations.

Security implication: During the stale window, a revoked signing key remains trusted. The 5-minute stale window bounds this risk, and the server-side 401 check provides a secondary revocation mechanism.

Unknown Key ID

When a token presents a kid not found in the cached key set, the system triggers a JWKS refresh (subject to the 5-minute rate limit). If the refresh returns the new key, verification proceeds. If not, the token is rejected.

Security implication: Key rotation at the authentication server is handled gracefully. An attacker cannot force continuous JWKS fetches by presenting tokens with random kid values, because the rate limiter caps fetch frequency.

First-Run (No Cache)

On the first token verification of a session, the JWKS cache is empty. The system must fetch keys synchronously before proceeding. If the fetch fails, the token falls through to the conservative default (refresh in 10 seconds), providing availability at the cost of an extra round-trip.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as Claude Code CLI
    participant JWT as jwtUtils.ts
    participant Cache as JWKS Cache
    participant Auth as Auth Server JWKS
    participant Timer as Refresh Timer

    Client->>JWT: schedule(sessionId, token)
    JWT->>JWT: Parse JWT header (alg, kid)
    JWT->>Cache: getSigningKey(kid)

    alt Cache hit
        Cache-->>JWT: Public key
    else Cache miss or expired
        Cache->>Auth: GET /.well-known/jwks.json
        alt Fetch succeeds
            Auth-->>Cache: JWKS key set
            Cache-->>JWT: Public key
        else Fetch fails
            Cache-->>JWT: null (stale or empty)
            JWT->>Timer: setTimeout(10s) [conservative]
            Note over Timer: Fail-safe: retry soon
        end
    end

    JWT->>JWT: Verify signature
    JWT->>JWT: Validate iss, aud, exp bounds
    JWT->>JWT: Cross-validate exp vs expires_in
    JWT->>JWT: clampTokenRefreshDelay()
    JWT->>Timer: setTimeout(clampedDelay)

10.9 Migration Path

Deploying JWKS verification in a production CLI tool requires careful sequencing to avoid breaking existing sessions.

Phase 1: Ship clampTokenRefreshDelay immediately. This is a pure addition that bounds timer scheduling without requiring JWKS infrastructure. It provides immediate protection against the worst attack vectors (infinite delay, tight loops) while the full JWKS implementation is built.

Phase 2: Deploy JWKS cache with fail-open. The initial JWKS deployment uses fail-open semantics: if verification fails (network error, unknown key, timeout), the token falls through to the existing Base64-decode path with clamp protection. This prevents breakage during rollout while collecting metrics on verification success rates.

Phase 3: Tighten to fail-closed. Once metrics confirm that 99%+ of tokens verify successfully, switch to fail-closed: verification failure triggers immediate refresh rather than accepting the unverified token. The conservative 10-second refresh default provides availability while forcing re-authentication.

Phase 4: Remove legacy decode path. Delete decodeJwtPayload() and all call sites that bypass signature verification. This eliminates the temptation to "just decode" in new code paths.

As Chapter 11 will discuss, the clampTokenRefreshDelay defense also enables the token refresh hardening that addresses CWE-613 --- environment variable tokens that never expire. The bounded timer ensures that even tokens without explicit expiry are periodically re-evaluated.

10.10 Key Takeaways

  1. Never trust JWT claims without signature verification. Base64 decoding is not verification. Any party can construct a JWT with arbitrary claims. The signature is the only proof that the issuer created the token with those exact claims.

  2. Defense-in-depth for timer scheduling. Four independent layers (signature verification, claim bounds checking, cross-validation against server data, and timer clamping) ensure that no single failure allows extreme timer values. Each layer catches different failure modes.

  3. Public key management is its own subsystem. JWKS caching requires rate limiting, stale-cache fallback, graceful key rotation handling, and first-run bootstrapping. The key cache is as security-critical as the verification itself.

  4. Debug logs are a credential exposure vector. Replacing token.slice(0, 15) with a SHA-256 fingerprint eliminates credential leakage while preserving the debugging utility of token correlation.

  5. Clamp first, verify later. The clampTokenRefreshDelay defense can ship independently and immediately, providing protection while the more complex JWKS infrastructure is built and tested. Layered deployment reduces rollout risk.

Chapter 11: Token Refresh Hardening

Chapter 10 established JWT signature verification as the foundation for trustworthy token handling. With signatures validated via JWKS public keys and exp claims bounded by clampTokenRefreshDelay, the system can now distinguish legitimate tokens from forgeries. But signature verification alone does not address a critical gap in the token lifecycle: tokens sourced from environment variables bypass the entire refresh pipeline and persist indefinitely.

This chapter addresses CWE-613 --- Insufficient Session Expiration (CVSS 6.5), specifically Finding V-13: environment variable tokens that never expire or refresh. In Claude Code's utils/auth.ts, tokens provided via CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN receive { refreshToken: null, expiresAt: null }, causing isTokenExpired() to always return false and checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded() to skip refresh entirely. The result: a revoked token continues working client-side until the server rejects it with a 401, at which point the error handling provides no guidance about the env var source.

The fix requires bounded refresh delays with MIN_REFRESH_DELAY_MS and MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS, token rotation for environment variable overrides, and session-scoped token lifecycle management that tracks token provenance from issuance through expiration.

11.1 The Vulnerability: Immortal Environment Variable Tokens

In production deployments, Claude Code accepts OAuth tokens from three sources: interactive OAuth flow, cached credentials in secure storage, and environment variables. The first two sources include refresh tokens and expiration timestamps. The third source --- environment variables --- includes neither.

The Vulnerable Code Path

// utils/auth.ts — lines 1260-1284 (VULNERABLE)

function getTokenFromEnvironment(): OAuthCredentials | null {
  const envToken = process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
  if (!envToken) return null

  return {
    accessToken: envToken,
    refreshToken: null,    // No refresh mechanism
    expiresAt: null,       // Never expires client-side
  }
}

function isTokenExpired(creds: OAuthCredentials): boolean {
  if (creds.expiresAt === null) return false  // null = immortal
  return Date.now() > creds.expiresAt
}

async function checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded(
  creds: OAuthCredentials,
): Promise<OAuthCredentials> {
  if (!isTokenExpired(creds)) return creds

  if (!creds.refreshToken) {
    // Env var tokens hit this path — no refresh possible
    throw new AuthError('Token expired and no refresh token available')
  }

  return await refreshOAuthToken(creds.refreshToken)
}

The logic chain is clear:

  1. getTokenFromEnvironment() sets expiresAt: null
  2. isTokenExpired() returns false for null expiry --- the token never expires
  3. checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded() sees the token as valid and returns immediately
  4. The token is used until the server returns 401, with no proactive expiry check

Why This Matters

Environment variable tokens are the primary authentication mechanism in three critical deployment contexts:

CI/CD Pipelines. Automated builds set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from a secrets manager (GitHub Actions secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.). If the token is revoked server-side but the CI/CD job is long-running, the job continues sending requests with the revoked token until the 401 triggers failure. In pipelines that batch multiple operations, partial completion with a revoked token can leave artifacts in an inconsistent state.

Containerized Deployments. Docker containers running Claude Code receive tokens via environment variables. Container orchestrators like Kubernetes may restart containers with the same token for weeks or months. If the token is compromised, server-side revocation is the only defense --- but the client has no mechanism to detect revocation proactively.

Developer Workstations. Developers who set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in their shell profile have tokens that persist across sessions indefinitely. If the developer's machine is compromised, the attacker obtains an immortal token that the developer may not think to rotate.

The Blast Radius
