11.2 The Fix: Bounded Token Lifecycle

The remediation has four components: maximum token age for env var tokens, periodic token introspection, improved 401 error handling with source awareness, and session-scoped lifecycle management.

Component 1: Maximum Token Age

The simplest and highest-impact fix: assign an expiresAt to environment variable tokens instead of null. This forces periodic re-evaluation even when no refresh token is available.

// utils/auth.ts — SECURE VERSION

/** Maximum age for env var tokens before re-validation is required */
const ENV_TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000  // 24 hours

/** Minimum age — prevents overly aggressive re-validation */
const ENV_TOKEN_MIN_AGE_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000  // 1 hour

/** Introspection interval for env var tokens */
const TOKEN_INTROSPECTION_INTERVAL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000  // 30 minutes

interface TokenMetadata {
  source: 'oauth_flow' | 'secure_storage' | 'env_var'
  createdAt: number
  lastIntrospection: number | null
  introspectionFailures: number
}

function getTokenFromEnvironment(): (OAuthCredentials & { _meta: TokenMetadata }) | null {
  const envToken = process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
  if (!envToken) return null

  const now = Date.now()

  return {
    accessToken: envToken,
    refreshToken: null,
    expiresAt: now + ENV_TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS,  // Expires in 24h
    _meta: {
      source: 'env_var',
      createdAt: now,
      lastIntrospection: null,
      introspectionFailures: 0,
    },
  }
}

The 24-hour maximum age is a deliberate trade-off between security and usability:

  • Shorter (1 hour): More secure, but causes frequent interruptions in long CI/CD runs. Developers re-exporting tokens constantly is a usability burden that leads to workarounds (longer-lived tokens from the secrets manager, defeating the purpose).
  • 24 hours: Aligns with common CI/CD job durations. Most pipelines complete within hours, so a 24-hour window covers virtually all legitimate use cases while ensuring daily rotation.
  • Longer (7 days): Reduces friction but creates a week-long window where a revoked token remains active client-side.

Component 2: Token Introspection

For tokens that cannot be refreshed (no refreshToken), we add periodic introspection --- a lightweight server call that checks whether the token is still valid:

// utils/auth.ts — Token introspection

const MAX_INTROSPECTION_FAILURES = 3
const INTROSPECTION_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000

interface IntrospectionResponse {
  active: boolean
  exp?: number
  scope?: string
}

/**
 * Check whether a token is still valid via the introspection endpoint.
 * Returns true if the token is active, false if revoked or expired.
 * Returns null if the introspection check itself fails (network error, timeout).
 */
async function introspectToken(
  accessToken: string,
): Promise<boolean | null> {
  try {
    const controller = new AbortController()
    const timeout = setTimeout(
      () => controller.abort(),
      INTROSPECTION_TIMEOUT_MS,
    )

    const response = await fetch(getIntrospectionUrl(), {
      method: 'POST',
      signal: controller.signal,
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
        'Authorization': `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
      },
      body: new URLSearchParams({ token: accessToken }),
    })

    clearTimeout(timeout)

    if (!response.ok) return null

    const data: IntrospectionResponse = await response.json()
    return data.active
  } catch {
    return null  // Network failure — inconclusive
  }
}

/**
 * Perform periodic introspection for env var tokens.
 * Called from checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded() when the token
 * source is 'env_var' and introspection interval has elapsed.
 */
async function maybeIntrospect(
  creds: OAuthCredentials & { _meta: TokenMetadata },
): Promise<'valid' | 'revoked' | 'inconclusive'> {
  const now = Date.now()
  const timeSinceLastCheck = creds._meta.lastIntrospection
    ? now - creds._meta.lastIntrospection
    : Infinity

  if (timeSinceLastCheck < TOKEN_INTROSPECTION_INTERVAL_MS) {
    return 'valid'  // Too soon to check again
  }

  const result = await introspectToken(creds.accessToken)

  if (result === true) {
    creds._meta.lastIntrospection = now
    creds._meta.introspectionFailures = 0
    return 'valid'
  }

  if (result === false) {
    return 'revoked'
  }

  // Inconclusive — network failure
  creds._meta.introspectionFailures++
  if (creds._meta.introspectionFailures >= MAX_INTROSPECTION_FAILURES) {
    // Too many consecutive failures — treat as suspicious
    return 'revoked'
  }

  return 'inconclusive'
}

The introspection endpoint follows RFC 7662 (OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection). The MAX_INTROSPECTION_FAILURES threshold of 3 prevents a network partition from immediately invalidating a legitimate session while ensuring that persistent connectivity issues (which could indicate a MITM blocking revocation checks) eventually force re-authentication.

Component 3: Source-Aware Error Handling

When a 401 response arrives, the current error handling provides a generic "Token expired" message. With token source metadata, we can provide actionable guidance:

// utils/auth.ts — Source-aware 401 handling

async function handle401Response(
  creds: OAuthCredentials & { _meta?: TokenMetadata },
): Promise<never> {
  const source = creds._meta?.source ?? 'unknown'

  switch (source) {
    case 'env_var':
      throw new AuthError(
        'Your CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN has been revoked or expired. ' +
        'Please provide a new token via the environment variable.\n' +
        'Tip: For CI/CD, use short-lived tokens (1h max). ' +
        'See: https://docs.anthropic.com/claude-code/auth#ci-cd',
      )

    case 'secure_storage':
      throw new AuthError(
        'Your cached credentials have expired. ' +
        'Run `claude login` to re-authenticate.',
      )

    case 'oauth_flow':
      throw new AuthError(
        'Your session token has been revoked. ' +
        'This may indicate a security event. ' +
        'Run `claude login` to re-authenticate.',
      )

    default:
      throw new AuthError(
        'Authentication failed. Run `claude login` to re-authenticate.',
      )
  }
}

The error message for env_var tokens explicitly recommends short-lived tokens for CI/CD. This is a security nudge: developers who encounter this error learn the correct pattern (short-lived tokens) rather than simply re-exporting the same long-lived token.

Component 4: Session-Scoped Lifecycle Management

The final component integrates all of the above into a unified lifecycle manager that tracks tokens from creation through expiration:

// utils/tokenLifecycle.ts — NEW FILE

import { createHash } from 'crypto'

interface TokenLifecycleEntry {
  fingerprint: string
  source: 'oauth_flow' | 'secure_storage' | 'env_var'
  createdAt: number
  expiresAt: number
  lastUsed: number
  lastIntrospection: number | null
  refreshCount: number
  introspectionFailures: number
}

class TokenLifecycleManager {
  private tokens: Map<string, TokenLifecycleEntry> = new Map()

  /**
   * Register a token in the lifecycle manager.
   * The token is identified by its SHA-256 fingerprint (first 16 hex chars).
   */
  register(
    token: string,
    source: TokenLifecycleEntry['source'],
    expiresAt: number,
  ): string {
    const fingerprint = this.fingerprint(token)

    this.tokens.set(fingerprint, {
      fingerprint,
      source,
      createdAt: Date.now(),
      expiresAt,
      lastUsed: Date.now(),
      lastIntrospection: null,
      refreshCount: 0,
      introspectionFailures: 0,
    })

    return fingerprint
  }

  /**
   * Record that a token was used for an API call.
   */
  markUsed(fingerprint: string): void {
    const entry = this.tokens.get(fingerprint)
    if (entry) {
      entry.lastUsed = Date.now()
    }
  }

  /**
   * Record that a token was refreshed (new token replaces old).
   */
  recordRefresh(
    oldFingerprint: string,
    newToken: string,
    newExpiresAt: number,
  ): string {
    const oldEntry = this.tokens.get(oldFingerprint)
    const newFingerprint = this.fingerprint(newToken)

    this.tokens.set(newFingerprint, {
      fingerprint: newFingerprint,
      source: oldEntry?.source ?? 'oauth_flow',
      createdAt: Date.now(),
      expiresAt: newExpiresAt,
      lastUsed: Date.now(),
      lastIntrospection: null,
      refreshCount: (oldEntry?.refreshCount ?? 0) + 1,
      introspectionFailures: 0,
    })

    // Remove old token entry
    if (oldFingerprint !== newFingerprint) {
      this.tokens.delete(oldFingerprint)
    }

    return newFingerprint
  }

  /**
   * Check if a token needs proactive renewal.
   * Returns the reason for renewal or null if the token is still good.
   */
  needsRenewal(fingerprint: string): string | null {
    const entry = this.tokens.get(fingerprint)
    if (!entry) return 'unknown token'

    const now = Date.now()

    // Hard expiry
    if (now >= entry.expiresAt) {
      return `expired ${Math.round((now - entry.expiresAt) / 1000)}s ago`
    }

    // Approaching expiry (within 10% of lifetime)
    const lifetime = entry.expiresAt - entry.createdAt
    const remaining = entry.expiresAt - now
    if (remaining < lifetime * 0.1) {
      return `${Math.round(remaining / 1000)}s remaining (within 10% threshold)`
    }

    // Too many introspection failures
    if (entry.introspectionFailures >= MAX_INTROSPECTION_FAILURES) {
      return `${entry.introspectionFailures} consecutive introspection failures`
    }

    return null  // Token is healthy
  }

  /**
   * Get lifecycle statistics for debugging.
   * Uses fingerprints — never exposes raw tokens.
   */
  getStats(): Record<string, unknown>[] {
    return Array.from(this.tokens.values()).map(entry => ({
      fingerprint: entry.fingerprint,
      source: entry.source,
      ageMinutes: Math.round((Date.now() - entry.createdAt) / 60_000),
      remainingMinutes: Math.round(
        Math.max(0, entry.expiresAt - Date.now()) / 60_000,
      ),
      refreshCount: entry.refreshCount,
      introspectionFailures: entry.introspectionFailures,
    }))
  }

  private fingerprint(token: string): string {
    return createHash('sha256').update(token).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)
  }
}

export const tokenLifecycle = new TokenLifecycleManager()

11.3 The Hardened Refresh Pipeline

With all four components integrated, the token refresh pipeline becomes provenance-aware and proactively expires all tokens regardless of source:

// utils/auth.ts — HARDENED checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded()

async function checkAndRefreshOAuthTokenIfNeeded(
  creds: OAuthCredentials & { _meta?: TokenMetadata },
): Promise<OAuthCredentials> {
  const source = creds._meta?.source ?? 'unknown'

  // Step 1: Check hard expiry (now applies to env var tokens too)
  if (isTokenExpired(creds)) {
    if (creds.refreshToken) {
      // Standard OAuth refresh
      return await refreshOAuthToken(creds.refreshToken)
    }

    if (source === 'env_var') {
      // Re-read from environment (may have been rotated)
      const fresh = getTokenFromEnvironment()
      if (fresh && fresh.accessToken !== creds.accessToken) {
        return fresh  // Token was rotated in the environment
      }
    }

    // No refresh mechanism and token expired
    await handle401Response(creds)
  }

  // Step 2: Periodic introspection for env var tokens
  if (source === 'env_var' && creds._meta) {
    const status = await maybeIntrospect(creds as OAuthCredentials & { _meta: TokenMetadata })

    if (status === 'revoked') {
      await handle401Response(creds)
    }
    // 'inconclusive' — continue with caution (failure counter incremented)
    // 'valid' — proceed normally
  }

  // Step 3: Proactive renewal check via lifecycle manager
  const fingerprint = tokenLifecycle.register(
    creds.accessToken,
    source as TokenLifecycleEntry['source'],
    creds.expiresAt ?? Date.now() + ENV_TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS,
  )

  const renewalReason = tokenLifecycle.needsRenewal(fingerprint)
  if (renewalReason && creds.refreshToken) {
    logForDebugging(`Proactive token renewal: ${renewalReason}`)
    return await refreshOAuthToken(creds.refreshToken)
  }

  return creds
}

Token Re-Read on Expiry

Notice the env var re-read in Step 1: when an env var token expires, the system re-reads process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. If the value has changed (e.g., a sidecar process rotated it, or the user re-exported a new token), the fresh token is used. This enables a rotation pattern for CI/CD:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Secrets as Secrets Manager
    participant Sidecar as Token Sidecar
    participant Env as Environment
    participant CLI as Claude Code CLI
    participant Server as Auth Server

    Secrets->>Sidecar: Issue short-lived token (1h)
    Sidecar->>Env: Export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
    CLI->>Server: API call with token A
    Server-->>CLI: 200 OK

    Note over Sidecar: Token approaches expiry
    Secrets->>Sidecar: Issue new token
    Sidecar->>Env: Re-export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN

    Note over CLI: expiresAt reached (24h max)
    CLI->>CLI: isTokenExpired() = true
    CLI->>Env: Re-read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
    CLI->>CLI: Detect new token (different value)
    CLI->>Server: API call with token B
    Server-->>CLI: 200 OK

This pattern works with AWS Secrets Manager's automatic rotation, HashiCorp Vault's dynamic secrets, and Kubernetes external secrets operators. The CLI does not need to know the rotation mechanism --- it simply re-reads the environment variable when the current token expires.

11.4 Bounded Refresh Delays

Chapter 10 introduced clampTokenRefreshDelay with bounds of [10 seconds, 24 hours]. This section expands on how those bounds interact with the token lifecycle for each source type:

Token Source MIN_REFRESH_DELAY MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME Rationale
OAuth flow (interactive) 10s 24h Server controls expiry via expires_in; clamp is safety net
Secure storage (cached) 10s 24h Same as OAuth flow; refresh token available
Environment variable 10s 24h No refresh token; forces re-read of env var at expiry
Bridge session JWT 10s 24h Cross-validated with clampTokenRefreshDelay (Chapter 10)

The 10-second minimum applies uniformly because the attack vector (tight refresh loop from near-past exp) is source-independent. The 24-hour maximum is also uniform: regardless of what the server claims, the client will not wait more than 24 hours before attempting to refresh or re-validate.

Why Not Per-Source Maximums?

An alternative design uses shorter maximums for env var tokens (e.g., 1 hour) and longer maximums for OAuth tokens (e.g., 7 days). We rejected this because:

  1. Complexity breeds bugs. Per-source timeout logic creates more code paths to test and more opportunities for misconfiguration. A single MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME_MS is easier to audit.

  2. The server already controls OAuth token lifetime. For OAuth tokens with refresh capability, the server's expires_in drives refresh scheduling. The 24-hour maximum is a safety net, not the normal operating point. Most OAuth tokens refresh within 1-4 hours.

  3. Env var tokens need the same ceiling. The 24-hour ceiling for env var tokens aligns with common secrets rotation policies. Making it shorter penalizes legitimate long-running CI jobs; making it longer undermines the security goal.

11.5 Token Rotation for Environment Variable Overrides

Beyond the env var re-read on expiry, we implement explicit token rotation guidance and detection:

// utils/auth.ts — Token rotation detection

interface RotationState {
  currentFingerprint: string
  previousFingerprints: string[]
  rotationCount: number
  lastRotation: number
}

const rotationState: Map<string, RotationState> = new Map()

/**
 * Detect and record token rotation in environment variables.
 * Called when a fresh env var token differs from the current one.
 */
function recordTokenRotation(
  envName: string,
  oldToken: string,
  newToken: string,
): void {
  const oldFp = createHash('sha256').update(oldToken).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)
  const newFp = createHash('sha256').update(newToken).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)

  const state = rotationState.get(envName) ?? {
    currentFingerprint: oldFp,
    previousFingerprints: [],
    rotationCount: 0,
    lastRotation: 0,
  }

  state.previousFingerprints.push(state.currentFingerprint)
  // Keep last 10 fingerprints for audit trail
  if (state.previousFingerprints.length > 10) {
    state.previousFingerprints.shift()
  }

  state.currentFingerprint = newFp
  state.rotationCount++
  state.lastRotation = Date.now()

  rotationState.set(envName, state)

  logForDebugging(
    `[auth] Token rotation detected for ${envName}: ` +
    `fingerprint ${oldFp} -> ${newFp} ` +
    `(rotation #${state.rotationCount})`,
  )
}

Detecting Stale Tokens

The rotation tracker also enables detection of tokens that have not been rotated when they should have been:

/**
 * Check if an env var token appears stale (has been in use
 * for longer than the recommended maximum without rotation).
 */
function isTokenStale(envName: string): boolean {
  const state = rotationState.get(envName)
  if (!state) return false

  const timeSinceRotation = Date.now() - state.lastRotation
  const STALE_THRESHOLD_MS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000  // 7 days

  return timeSinceRotation > STALE_THRESHOLD_MS
}

When a token is detected as stale, the system emits a warning (not an error) in the debug log. This creates an audit trail for security reviews without blocking legitimate usage.

CI/CD Token Lifecycle Best Practices

The token rotation mechanism enables several deployment patterns that security teams should recommend to their organizations:

GitHub Actions with OIDC. The preferred pattern for GitHub-hosted runners. Instead of storing a long-lived CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in GitHub Secrets, configure GitHub Actions OIDC to exchange a short-lived OIDC token for a Claude Code access token on each workflow run. The access token expires with the workflow, and no long-lived secrets are stored.

# .github/workflows/review.yml — Recommended CI/CD pattern
jobs:
  ai-review:
    permissions:
      id-token: write  # Required for OIDC token
    steps:
      - name: Get Claude Code token
        uses: anthropic/claude-code-oidc@v1
        with:
          audience: claude-code-cli
      # Token automatically set in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
      # Expires when the job completes (typically 1-4 hours)

Kubernetes with External Secrets Operator. For Kubernetes deployments, the External Secrets Operator can rotate the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN secret on a schedule. The CLI's env var re-read on expiry picks up the rotated token automatically.

Self-Hosted Runners with Vault. For self-hosted CI runners, HashiCorp Vault's dynamic secrets engine issues a unique token per job with a configurable TTL (typically 1 hour). The Claude Code CLI uses the token until it expires, then re-reads the environment variable for the next Vault-issued token.

The common thread across all patterns: the token lifetime should match the task lifetime. A CI job that takes 30 minutes needs a 1-hour token, not a 30-day token. The 24-hour maximum in ENV_TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS provides a safety net, but the correct pattern is to issue tokens with the shortest practical lifetime from the source.

Introspection Security Considerations

The token introspection endpoint itself becomes a potential target. An attacker who can call the introspection endpoint can probe whether arbitrary tokens are valid. RFC 7662 Section 4 addresses this by requiring the introspection endpoint to authenticate the caller --- the introspection request must include a valid token or client credential.

Our implementation sends the token-under-test as both the Bearer credential and the introspection target. This means a revoked token cannot be used to introspect itself (the Bearer authentication fails first). However, it also means we cannot introspect tokens that have already been rejected by the server's authentication layer --- which is the correct behavior, since a token rejected by the server is definitively invalid.

The MAX_INTROSPECTION_FAILURES threshold of 3 deserves security analysis. A man-in-the-middle who can selectively block introspection responses (while allowing API calls to succeed) could prevent the client from detecting server-side revocation. The 3-failure threshold means the MITM must sustain the block for 90 minutes (3 * 30-minute intervals) before the client treats the token as revoked. During this window, the revoked token continues to be used for API calls. This is an acceptable trade-off: the alternative --- treating a single introspection failure as revocation --- would cause false-positive lockouts during transient network issues.

11.6 Session-Scoped Lifecycle Architecture

The complete token lifecycle architecture tracks every token from creation through expiration, with provenance metadata enabling source-specific behavior:

11.7 The isTokenExpired Fix

The most impactful single-line change in this chapter:

// BEFORE (VULNERABLE)
function isTokenExpired(creds: OAuthCredentials): boolean {
  if (creds.expiresAt === null) return false  // null = never expires
  return Date.now() > creds.expiresAt
}

// AFTER (SECURE)
function isTokenExpired(creds: OAuthCredentials): boolean {
  if (creds.expiresAt === null) {
    // Tokens without explicit expiry are treated as expired.
    // This forces re-validation for env var tokens and surfaces
    // bugs in credential creation that fail to set expiresAt.
    return true
  }
  return Date.now() > creds.expiresAt
}

Changing the default from "null means immortal" to "null means expired" is a fundamental shift in the security posture. Under the new semantics:

  • Correctly-created tokens always have expiresAt set, so this change does not affect them.
  • Env var tokens now have expiresAt = now + 24h (from Component 1), so they never reach the null check.
  • Buggy token creation that forgets to set expiresAt now fails safe (token treated as expired) rather than failing dangerous (token treated as immortal).

This is the principle of fail-closed design: when a security-relevant value is missing, assume the restrictive interpretation.

11.8 Verification and Testing

Unit Tests

describe('isTokenExpired', () => {
  it('returns true for null expiresAt (fail-closed)', () => {
    expect(isTokenExpired({ expiresAt: null } as OAuthCredentials))
      .toBe(true)
  })

  it('returns true for expired timestamp', () => {
    expect(isTokenExpired({ expiresAt: Date.now() - 1000 } as OAuthCredentials))
      .toBe(true)
  })

  it('returns false for future timestamp', () => {
    expect(isTokenExpired({ expiresAt: Date.now() + 3600_000 } as OAuthCredentials))
      .toBe(false)
  })
})

describe('getTokenFromEnvironment', () => {
  it('sets expiresAt to now + 24h', () => {
    process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN = 'test-token'
    const creds = getTokenFromEnvironment()
    expect(creds?.expiresAt).toBeGreaterThan(Date.now())
    expect(creds?.expiresAt).toBeLessThanOrEqual(
      Date.now() + ENV_TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS + 100,
    )
    delete process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
  })

  it('includes source metadata', () => {
    process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN = 'test-token'
    const creds = getTokenFromEnvironment()
    expect(creds?._meta.source).toBe('env_var')
    delete process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
  })
})

describe('maybeIntrospect', () => {
  it('skips introspection within interval', async () => {
    const creds = makeEnvVarCreds({
      lastIntrospection: Date.now() - 1000,  // 1 second ago
    })
    expect(await maybeIntrospect(creds)).toBe('valid')
  })

  it('returns revoked when server says inactive', async () => {
    mockIntrospection({ active: false })
    const creds = makeEnvVarCreds({ lastIntrospection: null })
    expect(await maybeIntrospect(creds)).toBe('revoked')
  })

  it('returns revoked after 3 consecutive failures', async () => {
    const creds = makeEnvVarCreds({
      lastIntrospection: null,
      introspectionFailures: 2,
    })
    mockIntrospection(null)  // Network failure
    expect(await maybeIntrospect(creds)).toBe('revoked')
  })
})

Integration Tests

    process.env.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN = 'token-v1'
    const creds1 = getTokenFromEnvironment()!

11.10 Deployment Sequence

The changes in this chapter should be deployed in a specific order that minimizes disruption:

Phase 1: Deploy isTokenExpired null-means-expired change. This is the highest-impact single change. Combined with the expiresAt assignment in getTokenFromEnvironment(), it eliminates immortal tokens. Deploy these two changes together.

Phase 2: Deploy token introspection. The introspection endpoint requires server-side support. Coordinate with the authentication team to ensure the /v1/token/validate endpoint is available before enabling client-side introspection. Start with a 60-minute introspection interval and tighten to 30 minutes after confirming acceptable load.

Phase 3: Deploy source-aware error handling. This is purely a UX improvement that helps developers fix authentication issues faster. It can deploy independently of the other phases.

Phase 4: Deploy lifecycle manager. The full TokenLifecycleManager provides the audit trail and proactive renewal features. This is the most complex component and benefits from the stability of Phases 1-3 before deployment.

Chapter 12 will extend this token lifecycle work to the OAuth and device trust layers, addressing the predictable OAuth callback port (CWE-352), the environment variable override for trusted device tokens (CWE-473), and PKCE validation strengthening.

11.11 Key Takeaways

  1. Null means dangerous, not immortal. When a security-relevant timestamp is missing, the fail-closed interpretation (treat as expired) prevents an entire class of "immortal token" vulnerabilities. Design defaults to be restrictive.

  2. Environment variable tokens need the same lifecycle as interactive tokens. The deployment context (CI/CD, containers, developer workstations) does not reduce the security requirements. Env var tokens must expire, rotate, and be introspectable.

  3. Token provenance enables targeted remediation. Tracking where a token came from (OAuth flow, secure storage, env var) allows the system to provide actionable error messages, choose the right renewal mechanism, and build an audit trail.

  4. Introspection is the bridge between client and server revocation. Without introspection, a client has no way to know that a token has been revoked server-side. Periodic introspection closes this gap with configurable aggressiveness.

  5. Rotation detection via env var re-read is a zero-cost feature. Re-reading the environment variable when the current token expires enables external rotation without requiring any integration beyond the secrets manager writing to the environment. The CLI adapts to whatever rotation mechanism the deployment uses.

Chapter 12: OAuth & Device Trust Hardening

Chapters 10 and 11 secured the JWT verification pipeline and the token refresh lifecycle. Tokens are now cryptographically verified via JWKS, bounded by clampTokenRefreshDelay, and tracked through a session-scoped lifecycle manager that eliminates immortal environment variable tokens. This chapter addresses two remaining authentication vulnerabilities that sit at the boundary between the client and the identity provider: the OAuth authorization code flow and the device trust mechanism.

Finding V-36: OAuth Callback Listener on Predictable Localhost Port (CWE-352, CVSS 4.3). The OAuth callback server binds to a fixed port on localhost, making it possible for other local processes to predict when and where the callback will arrive. While the existing PKCE state parameter prevents cross-site request forgery on the OAuth flow itself, the predictable port creates an unnecessary attack surface for local privilege escalation.

Finding V-34: Trusted Device Token Overridable via Environment Variable (CWE-473, CVSS 4.3). The readStoredToken() function in bridge/trustedDevice.ts gives unconditional precedence to CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN from the environment. This means any process that can set environment variables for the Claude Code process can override the trusted device identity --- bypassing keychain storage entirely.

Finding V-50: PKCE Implementation Verification (Positive Finding). The audit confirmed that the PKCE implementation in services/oauth/crypto.ts uses correct cryptographic primitives: 256-bit random verifiers, SHA-256 S256 challenges, and 256-bit state parameters. This section documents the existing strength and identifies hardening opportunities.

12.1 The OAuth Authorization Code Flow

Before addressing specific vulnerabilities, we need to understand the complete OAuth flow as implemented in Claude Code. The flow follows RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0) with the PKCE extension (RFC 7636):

sequenceDiagram
    participant User as User
    participant CLI as Claude Code CLI
    participant Crypto as oauth/crypto.ts
    participant Listener as auth-code-listener.ts
    participant Browser as Default Browser
    participant AuthServer as OAuth Provider

    User->>CLI: claude login
    CLI->>Crypto: generateCodeVerifier()
    Note over Crypto: randomBytes(32) -> base64url
    Crypto-->>CLI: code_verifier (256-bit)

    CLI->>Crypto: generateCodeChallenge(verifier)
    Note over Crypto: SHA-256(verifier) -> base64url
    Crypto-->>CLI: code_challenge (S256)

    CLI->>Crypto: generateState()
    Note over Crypto: randomBytes(32) -> base64url
    Crypto-->>CLI: state (256-bit)

    CLI->>Listener: Start HTTP server on localhost:PORT
    Note over Listener: PORT is currently FIXED

    CLI->>Browser: Open authorization URL
    Note over Browser: code_challenge + state in URL

    Browser->>AuthServer: User authenticates
    AuthServer->>Browser: Redirect to localhost:PORT/callback
    Browser->>Listener: GET /callback?code=XXX&state=YYY

    Listener->>Listener: Validate state matches
    alt State mismatch
        Listener-->>CLI: CSRF detected
    else State valid
        Listener->>AuthServer: POST /token (code + code_verifier)
        AuthServer-->>Listener: access_token + refresh_token
        Listener->>CLI: Credentials received
        CLI->>CLI: Store in secure storage
    end

The flow has three security-critical moments:

  1. Code challenge generation --- must be cryptographically strong to prevent authorization code interception
  2. Callback reception --- must verify state and only accept the expected callback
  3. Token exchange --- must use the original code_verifier to prove possession

PKCE: What the Audit Confirmed

Finding V-50 is a positive finding --- the PKCE implementation is correct:

// services/oauth/crypto.ts — VERIFIED CORRECT
export function generateCodeVerifier(): string {
  return base64URLEncode(randomBytes(32))  // 256-bit entropy
}

export function generateCodeChallenge(verifier: string): string {
  const hash = createHash('sha256')
  hash.update(verifier)
  return base64URLEncode(hash.digest())  // SHA-256 S256 method
}

export function generateState(): string {
  return base64URLEncode(randomBytes(32))  // 256-bit CSRF protection
}

This implementation is compliant with RFC 7636 Section 4.1: the verifier has at least 256 bits of entropy, the challenge uses S256 (not the weaker plain method), and the state parameter provides adequate CSRF protection. These primitives are correctly used --- but the flow around them has weaknesses.

12.2 The Predictable Port Vulnerability (CWE-352)

The Problem

The OAuth callback listener in services/oauth/auth-code-listener.ts binds to a deterministic port on localhost. While the exact port number is configurable, it defaults to a fixed value that is consistent across installations.

// services/oauth/auth-code-listener.ts — VULNERABLE
private handleRedirect(req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse): void {
  const parsedUrl = new URL(
    req.url || '',
    `http://${req.headers.host || 'localhost'}`,
  )
  // ... process callback
}

The vulnerability is subtle: any other process running on the same machine that knows the port can:

  1. Race to bind the port first. If a malicious local process binds the callback port before Claude Code starts its listener, it receives the OAuth callback with the authorization code. The PKCE code_verifier prevents the attacker from exchanging the code (they do not have the verifier), but the authorization code exposure is still an information leak.

  2. Predict callback timing. A local process monitoring port activity can detect exactly when the OAuth flow is in progress, which is useful for timing-based attacks on the token exchange.

  3. Host header injection. The handleRedirect code constructs a URL using req.headers.host, which is client-controlled. While this specific usage does not create an exploitable vulnerability (the URL is parsed locally), it establishes a pattern where attacker-controlled headers influence URL construction.

Why PKCE Mitigates but Does Not Eliminate the Risk

The PKCE extension provides the primary defense: even if an attacker captures the authorization code from the callback, they cannot exchange it for tokens without the code_verifier, which never leaves the Claude Code process memory. This reduces the practical severity from HIGH to LOW.

However, PKCE does not protect against:

  • Authorization code replay against the legitimate client. If the attacker can also inject the captured code back into the legitimate callback (e.g., by racing), the legitimate client exchanges the code successfully, but the attacker now knows which authorization was granted.
  • Local denial of service. By occupying the callback port, the attacker prevents the OAuth flow from completing, forcing the user to retry or use alternative authentication methods.

The Fix: Ephemeral Port Selection

The remediation replaces the fixed port with an OS-assigned ephemeral port:

// services/oauth/auth-code-listener.ts — SECURE VERSION
import { createServer, IncomingMessage, ServerResponse, Server } from 'http'

interface CallbackListenerOptions {
  timeoutMs?: number
  allowedHost?: string
}

const DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000  // 2 minutes
const ALLOWED_HOSTS = new Set(['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '[::1]'])

export class AuthCodeListener {
  private server: Server | null = null
  private assignedPort: number | null = null

  /**
   * Start the OAuth callback listener on an OS-assigned ephemeral port.
   * Returns the port number for inclusion in the authorization URL.
   */
  async start(options: CallbackListenerOptions = {}): Promise<number> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      this.server = createServer((req, res) => {
        this.handleRedirect(req, res)
      })

      // Bind to port 0: OS assigns an available ephemeral port
      this.server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
        const addr = this.server!.address()
        if (typeof addr === 'object' && addr !== null) {
          this.assignedPort = addr.port
          resolve(this.assignedPort)
        } else {
          reject(new Error('Failed to determine assigned port'))
        }
      })

      this.server.on('error', reject)

      // Timeout: close listener if no callback received
      const timeout = options.timeoutMs ?? DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS
      setTimeout(() => {
        if (this.server?.listening) {
          this.stop()
          reject(new Error(`OAuth callback timeout after ${timeout}ms`))
        }
      }, timeout)
    })
  }

  /**
   * Handle the OAuth redirect callback.
   * Validates Host header against allowlist before processing.
   */
  private handleRedirect(
    req: IncomingMessage,
    res: ServerResponse,
  ): void {
    // Validate Host header
    const host = req.headers.host
    if (host) {
      const hostname = host.split(':')[0]
      if (!ALLOWED_HOSTS.has(hostname ?? '')) {
        res.writeHead(400, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' })
        res.end('Invalid host header')
        return
      }
    }

    // Construct URL using known-good base (never from request headers)
    const parsedUrl = new URL(
      req.url || '',
      `http://127.0.0.1:${this.assignedPort}`,
    )

    // ... process callback with state validation
  }

  /**
   * Stop the listener and release the port.
   */
  stop(): void {
    if (this.server) {
      this.server.close()
      this.server = null
      this.assignedPort = null
    }
  }
}

Key changes:

  1. Port 0 binding. Passing 0 to server.listen() causes the OS to assign a random available ephemeral port (typically in the 49152-65535 range). This eliminates port prediction --- each OAuth flow uses a different port.

  2. Host header validation. Instead of trusting the Host header for URL construction, we validate it against an allowlist (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]). Requests with unexpected Host headers receive a 400 response.

  3. Known-good URL base. The URL is constructed using the known bound address (127.0.0.1:${this.assignedPort}) rather than the client-provided Host header. This eliminates the Host header injection vector entirely.

  4. Explicit timeout. A 2-minute timeout closes the listener if no callback arrives, preventing port squatting on the ephemeral port.

OAuth Redirect URI Registration

Ephemeral ports introduce a challenge: OAuth providers typically require pre-registered redirect URIs. Two patterns solve this:

Pattern 1: Loopback URI exception. RFC 8252 Section 7.3 specifies that OAuth providers SHOULD allow any port in loopback redirect URIs (http://127.0.0.1:*/callback). Most major providers implement this exception. The redirect URI registration uses http://127.0.0.1 without specifying a port, and the provider matches any port.

Pattern 2: Dynamic registration. If the provider does not support the loopback exception, the CLI can use OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) to register a new redirect URI for each flow. This adds a round-trip but ensures compatibility.

12.3 The Device Trust Override Vulnerability (CWE-473)

The Problem

The trusted device mechanism in bridge/trustedDevice.ts establishes persistent identity for the CLI installation. When a device is "trusted," subsequent operations skip certain verification steps. The vulnerability is in the token retrieval:

// bridge/trustedDevice.ts — VULNERABLE
const readStoredToken = memoize((): string | undefined => {
  // Env var takes precedence for testing/canary.
  const envToken = process.env.CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN
  if (envToken) {
    return envToken
  }
  return getSecureStorage().read()?.trustedDeviceToken
})

The comment says "for testing/canary," but the env var is available in all environments, not gated behind a feature flag. This means:

  1. Any process that can set environment variables for the Claude Code process can impersonate the device identity. On shared systems (CI runners, containers with shared env), one process can set CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN to impersonate another device's identity.

  2. The env var token bypasses keychain security. The macOS Keychain requires user authentication (password, Touch ID) to release stored secrets. The env var bypass means an attacker who cannot access the Keychain (because they do not have the user's password) can still override the device trust token.

  3. No expiry or validation. The env var token is memoized unconditionally --- it is read once and cached for the process lifetime. Even if the env var is later unset, the memoized value persists.

The Attack: Local Privilege Escalation via Device Identity

The Fix: Gated Override with Validation

The remediation gates the env var override behind a feature flag and adds validation for the override when permitted:

// bridge/trustedDevice.ts — SECURE VERSION
import { logForDebugging } from '../utils/debug.js'
import { getSecureStorage } from '../utils/secureStorage/index.js'
import { isFeatureEnabled } from '../services/featureGates.js'

interface DeviceTokenSource {
  token: string
  source: 'keychain' | 'env_var'
  validatedAt: number
}

/**
 * Read the trusted device token with source tracking and validation.
 *
 * Env var override is ONLY available when:
 * 1. The 'env_device_token_override' feature gate is enabled (server-controlled)
 * 2. The env var token passes JWT format validation (if JWT-formatted)
 * 3. The env var token is not expired (if JWT-formatted)
 *
 * This prevents local processes from silently overriding device identity.
 */
function readStoredTokenSecure(): DeviceTokenSource | undefined {
  const envToken = process.env.CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN

  if (envToken) {
    // Gate check: only allow env override when explicitly enabled
    if (!isFeatureEnabled('env_device_token_override')) {
      logForDebugging(
        '[trusted-device] CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN env var present but ' +
        'env_device_token_override feature gate is disabled. ' +
        'Using keychain token instead.',
        { level: 'warn' },
      )
      // Fall through to keychain
    } else {
      // Validate JWT-format tokens
      const validationResult = validateDeviceToken(envToken)
      if (!validationResult.valid) {
        logForDebugging(
          `[trusted-device] CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN env var ` +
          `failed validation: ${validationResult.reason}. ` +
          `Using keychain token instead.`,
          { level: 'warn' },
        )
        // Fall through to keychain
      } else {
        logForDebugging(
          '[trusted-device] Using device token from env var ' +
          '(env_device_token_override gate enabled)',
          { level: 'warn' },
        )
        return {
          token: envToken,
          source: 'env_var',
          validatedAt: Date.now(),
        }
      }
    }
  }

  // Default path: read from secure storage
  const stored = getSecureStorage().read()?.trustedDeviceToken
  if (!stored) return undefined

  return {
    token: stored,
    source: 'keychain',
    validatedAt: Date.now(),
  }
}

/**
 * Validate a device token from the environment variable.
 * - JWT tokens: check format, decode payload, verify not expired
 * - Opaque tokens: accept if non-empty string
 */
function validateDeviceToken(
  token: string,
): { valid: true } | { valid: false; reason: string } {
  if (!token || token.trim().length === 0) {
    return { valid: false, reason: 'empty token' }
  }

  // JWT-format validation
  if (token.startsWith('eyJ')) {
    try {
      const parts = token.split('.')
      if (parts.length !== 3) {
        return { valid: false, reason: 'malformed JWT (expected 3 parts)' }
      }

      const payload = JSON.parse(
        Buffer.from(parts[1]!, 'base64url').toString('utf8'),
      ) as { exp?: number }

      if (payload.exp && payload.exp * 1000 < Date.now()) {
        return { valid: false, reason: 'JWT expired' }
      }
    } catch {
      return { valid: false, reason: 'JWT decode failed' }
    }
  }

  return { valid: true }
}

Key changes:

  1. Feature gate. The env_device_token_override gate is server-controlled (via GrowthBook or equivalent). In production, this gate is disabled. Enterprise deployments that need env var override for their specific use case can request gate enablement.

  2. Expiry validation. JWT-formatted device tokens from the env var are checked for expiry. Expired tokens fall through to the keychain, preventing stale env vars from overriding fresh keychain tokens.

  3. Source tracking. The DeviceTokenSource type records whether the token came from the keychain or the env var, enabling audit trail and source-aware error handling (following the pattern from Chapter 11).

  4. Warning logs. Every env var usage or rejection is logged at warn level, creating a clear audit trail. Security teams can monitor for unexpected env var override attempts.

Removing Memoization

The original code used memoize() to cache the token read, meaning the env var was only read once per process. The secure version reads fresh on each call, enabling:

  • Detection of mid-process environment changes
  • Immediate effect of feature gate changes
  • Fresh expiry checks on JWT-formatted tokens

The performance cost is negligible: reading an env var is a single hash table lookup in the process, and the keychain read is already cached by the secure storage layer.

12.4 PKCE S256 Strengthening

While Finding V-50 confirmed that the PKCE implementation is cryptographically correct, there are hardening opportunities that strengthen the overall OAuth flow.

Verifier Length Validation

RFC 7636 Section 4.1 requires code verifiers to be between 43 and 128 characters. The current implementation generates a 43-character verifier (32 bytes base64url-encoded), which meets the minimum. Adding explicit length validation prevents accidental shortening:

// services/oauth/crypto.ts — HARDENED

const CODE_VERIFIER_MIN_LENGTH = 43
const CODE_VERIFIER_MAX_LENGTH = 128

export function generateCodeVerifier(): string {
  const verifier = base64URLEncode(randomBytes(32))

  // Defense-in-depth: verify the output meets RFC 7636 requirements
  if (
    verifier.length < CODE_VERIFIER_MIN_LENGTH ||
    verifier.length > CODE_VERIFIER_MAX_LENGTH
  ) {
    throw new Error(
      `Generated code verifier length ${verifier.length} outside ` +
      `RFC 7636 range [${CODE_VERIFIER_MIN_LENGTH}, ${CODE_VERIFIER_MAX_LENGTH}]`,
    )
  }

  return verifier
}

/**
 * Validate that the code challenge method is S256, not plain.
 * The 'plain' method transmits the verifier as the challenge,
 * which defeats PKCE's security if the authorization request
 * is intercepted.
 */
export function assertS256Method(method: string): void {
  if (method !== 'S256') {
    throw new Error(
      `PKCE challenge method must be S256, got: ${method}. ` +
      'The "plain" method is insecure and not permitted.',
    )
  }
}

State Parameter Binding

The state parameter prevents CSRF by binding the authorization request to the callback. The current implementation generates a random state and validates it on callback. We strengthen this by binding the state to the session:

// services/oauth/crypto.ts — State binding

/**
 * Generate a state parameter that is bound to the session context.
 * This prevents state reuse across different sessions or machines.
 *
 * State = base64url(random(32) || SHA-256(sessionContext))
 * The random component ensures uniqueness.
 * The session component prevents cross-session replay.
 */
export function generateBoundState(sessionContext: {
  machineId: string
  processId: number
  timestamp: number
}): string {
  const random = randomBytes(32)
  const contextHash = createHash('sha256')
    .update(JSON.stringify(sessionContext))
    .digest()

  // Combine: 32 bytes random + 32 bytes context hash
  const combined = Buffer.concat([random, contextHash])
  return base64URLEncode(combined)
}

/**
 * Validate a state parameter against the expected session context.
 */
export function validateBoundState(
  receivedState: string,
  expectedState: string,
): boolean {
  // Constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks
  if (receivedState.length !== expectedState.length) return false

  const a = Buffer.from(receivedState)
  const b = Buffer.from(expectedState)

  return timingSafeEqual(a, b)
}

The timingSafeEqual comparison is critical: without it, a timing side-channel could allow an attacker to discover the expected state value byte-by-byte by measuring response times.

describe('AuthCodeListener', () => {

12.10 Key Takeaways

  1. Ephemeral ports eliminate an entire class of local attacks. Using port 0 with OS-assigned ephemeral ports makes port prediction infeasible. Combined with PKCE, the OAuth callback is protected against both remote CSRF and local port racing.

  2. Environment variable overrides for security-critical values must be gated. The "testing convenience" of CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN env var becomes a privilege escalation vector in production. Feature gates make the override available when explicitly needed (enterprise testing) and disabled by default.

  3. Host headers are attacker-controlled. Never use req.headers.host to construct security-sensitive URLs. Use the known-good server address (from server.address()) instead.

  4. PKCE is correct but incomplete. Cryptographically sound PKCE protects the authorization code exchange, but does not protect against port-level attacks, timing side-channels in state comparison, or device identity override. Defense-in-depth across multiple layers is required.

  5. Constant-time comparison prevents subtle information leaks. Using timingSafeEqual for state parameter validation eliminates timing side-channels that could allow byte-by-byte state discovery. This is a small code change with significant security impact.

  6. Audit logging is a feature, not overhead. Every env var override attempt, rejected Host header, and feature gate decision is logged. These logs are the security team's first indicator of attack attempts.

Chapter 13: Process-Level Agent Isolation

Part IV secured the authentication token lifecycle: JWT signatures are verified via JWKS (Chapter 10), token refresh is bounded and source-aware (Chapter 11), and the OAuth/device trust flows are hardened against local attacks (Chapter 12). With authentication solid, Part V turns to the most architecturally significant vulnerability in Claude Code: subagents execute in the same process as the parent agent, sharing memory, file descriptors, and tool access without isolation boundaries.

This chapter addresses Finding V-3: Subagent Execution Without Process-Level Isolation (CWE-269, CVSS 7.8). In the current architecture, when Claude Code spawns a subagent --- whether from a user-defined agent file, a plugin-supplied agent, or a recursive fork --- the subagent runs as a function call within the parent Node.js process. It shares the parent's AppState store, has access to all tools (filtered only by name-based string matching), and can fork additional children recursively. A single malicious plugin agent has full access to credentials, filesystem, network, and shell execution through the parent's process context.

The fix requires process isolation via child_process.fork() with IPC channels, capability-based tool filtering enforced at process boundaries, and memory isolation between parent and child agents.

13.1 The Vulnerability: Shared Process, Shared Everything

Current Architecture

The subagent system in tools/AgentTool/runAgent.ts spawns agents as in-process function calls. When the LLM's tool response includes an AgentTool call, the handler creates a new conversation loop within the same Node.js process:

// tools/AgentTool/runAgent.ts — lines 332-338 (VULNERABLE)
// Subagent shares parent's AppState store
const subagentState = parentState.clone()  // Shallow clone — shared refs
subagentState.tools = filterToolsByName(parentState.tools, agentConfig.tools)

// Lines 465-479 — Tool restriction is name-based filtering only
function filterToolsByName(
  allTools: ToolRegistry,
  allowedNames: string[],
): ToolRegistry {
  if (allowedNames.includes('*')) return allTools  // Wildcard = all tools
  return allTools.filter(t => allowedNames.includes(t.name))
}

// Lines 567-575 — Agent frontmatter hooks execute in parent context
for (const hook of agentConfig.hooks ?? []) {
  await executeHook(hook, parentContext)  // Parent context, not isolated
}

And in tools/AgentTool/forkSubagent.ts:

// forkSubagent.ts:311 — Fork children retain Agent tool for recursive forking
const childTools = parentTools.filter(t =>
  agentConfig.tools.includes(t.name) || agentConfig.tools.includes('*'),
)
// The AgentTool itself is in childTools — child can fork grandchildren

What Is Shared

The in-process execution model means every subagent has access to:

The Name-Based Filtering Illusion

The tool restriction appears to limit subagent capabilities:

// Agent frontmatter
tools: ['Read', 'Grep', 'Glob']

But this restriction is advisory, not enforced:

  1. Same process memory. The filtered ToolRegistry is a JavaScript array in the same heap. The subagent's LLM conversation is limited to the filtered tools, but the parent's tool implementations are still in memory. A sufficiently sophisticated prompt injection in the subagent's context could, through chain-of-thought manipulation, cause the parent to execute unfiltered tools on the subagent's behalf.

  2. Wildcard access. Many plugin-defined agents specify tools: ['*'], which bypasses filtering entirely. The audit found this pattern in real marketplace plugins.

  3. Agent tool recursion. The AgentTool itself is available to subagents, enabling recursive forking. Each child inherits the parent's tool set (or a superset if wildcard is specified), creating an exponential expansion of capability.

  4. Hooks in parent context. Agent frontmatter can define hooks that execute in the parent's context, not the subagent's context. A malicious hook specification could execute arbitrary code with full parent privileges.

The Recursive Forking Amplification (CWE-674)

Finding V-14 compounds the isolation problem. The current fork depth guard is a single-layer check based on message content:

// forkSubagent.ts — VULNERABLE depth guard
export function isInForkChild(messages: MessageType[]): boolean {
  return messages.some(m => {
    if (m.type !== 'user') return false
    const content = m.message.content
    if (!Array.isArray(content)) return false
    return content.some(
      block =>
        block.type === 'text' &&
        block.text.includes(`<${FORK_BOILERPLATE_TAG}>`),
    )
  })
}

This check only detects whether we are in a fork child, not how deep the fork tree is. A depth-2 fork child passes the same check as a depth-1 child. Without hard depth tracking, the following attack chain is possible:

Parent Agent
├── Subagent A (depth 1) — from malicious plugin
│   ├── Subagent B (depth 2) — recursive fork
│   │   ├── Subagent C (depth 3) — recursive fork
│   │   │   └── ... (continues until OOM)
│   │   └── Subagent D (depth 3)
│   └── Subagent E (depth 2)
└── Subagent F (depth 1) — legitimate

Each subagent consumes memory for its conversation context, LLM state, and tool results. With no depth limit, exponential growth quickly exhausts system resources.

CVSS Scoring Breakdown

Vector Component Value Rationale
Attack Vector Local Requires malicious plugin installation
Attack Complexity Low Plugin defines agent with tools: ['*']
Privileges Required None Plugin installation only requires user approval once
User Interaction Required User must install the malicious plugin
Scope Changed Subagent escapes intended isolation to affect parent
Confidentiality High Full access to credentials, env vars, file system
Integrity High Can modify files, execute commands, send network requests
Availability High Recursive forking causes OOM/resource exhaustion
CVSS Score 7.8 HIGH

13.2 The Fix: Process-Level Isolation Architecture

The remediation replaces in-process subagent execution with child_process.fork() for plugin-sourced agents, creating a true process boundary between parent and child.

Design Principles

  1. Plugin agents run in child processes. Any agent defined by a plugin (marketplace or local) executes in a forked child process with IPC message passing.

  2. Built-in agents run in-process. Agents defined in .claude/agents/ by the user are trusted (same trust level as the user's own code) and run in-process for performance.

  3. Capability enforcement at process boundary. Tool calls from child processes pass through a ToolProxy in the parent that validates each call against the agent's declared capabilities.

  4. AppState isolation. Child processes receive a serialized read-only snapshot of AppState. Mutations require explicit IPC roundtrips to the parent.

  5. Resource limits. Each child process has CPU, memory, and file descriptor limits enforced by the OS.

Architecture Overview

graph TD

        ORCHESTRATOR --> PROXY
        PROXY --> TOOLS
        PROXY --> STATE

Component 1: Process Forking with IPC

// tools/AgentTool/isolatedAgent.ts — NEW FILE
import { fork, ChildProcess } from 'child_process'
import { createHash, randomBytes } from 'crypto'
import { EventEmitter } from 'events'

interface AgentCapabilities {
  filesystem: 'none' | 'read' | 'readwrite'
  network: 'none' | 'allowed'
  shell: 'none' | 'restricted' | 'allowed'
  maxMemoryMB: number
  maxCpuSeconds: number
  maxFileDescriptors: number
  allowedTools: string[]
  deniedPaths: string[]
}

interface IpcToolRequest {
  type: 'tool_request'
  requestId: string
  toolName: string
  toolInput: Record<string, unknown>
  agentId: string
}

interface IpcToolResponse {
  type: 'tool_response'
  requestId: string
  success: boolean
  result?: unknown
  error?: string
}

interface IpcStateRequest {
  type: 'state_request'
  requestId: string
  path: string  // dot-separated path into AppState
}

const MAX_FORK_DEPTH = 3
const MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS = 10
const CHILD_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000
const CHILD_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000  // 5 minutes

/**
 * Spawn an isolated agent in a child process with capability-based restrictions.
 * Communication is via structured IPC messages only — no shared memory.
 */
export class IsolatedAgentRunner extends EventEmitter {
  private child: ChildProcess | null = null
  private capabilities: AgentCapabilities
  private agentId: string
  private forkDepth: number
  private pendingRequests: Map<string, {
    resolve: (value: IpcToolResponse) => void
    timeout: NodeJS.Timeout
  }> = new Map()

  constructor(
    agentConfig: AgentConfig,
    parentForkDepth: number,
  ) {
    super()
    this.agentId = createHash('sha256')
      .update(randomBytes(16))
      .digest('hex')
      .slice(0, 16)
    this.forkDepth = parentForkDepth + 1
    this.capabilities = this.deriveCapabilities(agentConfig)
  }

  /**
   * Derive capability set from agent configuration.
   * Plugin agents get restricted capabilities by default.
   * User-defined agents get broader access (but still process-isolated if from plugin).
   */
  private deriveCapabilities(config: AgentConfig): AgentCapabilities {
    const tools = config.tools ?? []
    const hasWildcard = tools.includes('*')

    return {
      filesystem: this.deriveFilesystemAccess(tools, hasWildcard),
      network: tools.some(t => ['WebFetch', 'WebSearch'].includes(t))
        ? 'allowed' : 'none',
      shell: this.deriveShellAccess(tools, hasWildcard),
      maxMemoryMB: config.maxMemoryMB ?? 512,
      maxCpuSeconds: config.maxCpuSeconds ?? 300,
      maxFileDescriptors: 256,
      allowedTools: hasWildcard ? [] : tools,  // Empty = check denied
      deniedPaths: [
        '~/.claude/.credentials.json',
        '~/.claude/settings.local.json',
        '**/.env',
        '**/*.pem',
        '**/*.key',
      ],
    }
  }

  private deriveFilesystemAccess(
    tools: string[],
    hasWildcard: boolean,
  ): 'none' | 'read' | 'readwrite' {
    if (hasWildcard) return 'readwrite'
    const writeTools = ['Write', 'Edit', 'NotebookEdit']
    const readTools = ['Read', 'Glob', 'Grep']
    if (tools.some(t => writeTools.includes(t))) return 'readwrite'
    if (tools.some(t => readTools.includes(t))) return 'read'
    return 'none'
  }

  private deriveShellAccess(
    tools: string[],
    hasWildcard: boolean,
  ): 'none' | 'restricted' | 'allowed' {
    if (!hasWildcard && !tools.includes('Bash')) return 'none'
    // Even with Bash access, plugin agents get restricted shell
    return 'restricted'
  }

  /**
   * Start the isolated agent process.
   */
  async start(
    directive: string,
    stateSnapshot: SerializedAppState,
  ): Promise<void> {
    if (this.forkDepth > MAX_FORK_DEPTH) {
      throw new Error(
        `Maximum fork depth (${MAX_FORK_DEPTH}) reached. ` +
        `Cannot create nested subagent at depth ${this.forkDepth}.`,
      )
    }

    // Fork child process with restricted environment
    this.child = fork(
      require.resolve('./agentChildProcess.js'),
      [],
      {
        stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe', 'ipc'],
        env: this.buildRestrictedEnv(),
        execArgv: [
          `--max-old-space-size=${this.capabilities.maxMemoryMB}`,
        ],
      },
    )

    // Set up IPC message handling
    this.child.on('message', (msg: IpcToolRequest | IpcStateRequest) => {
      this.handleChildMessage(msg)
    })

    this.child.on('exit', (code, signal) => {
      this.emit('exit', { code, signal, agentId: this.agentId })
      this.cleanup()
    })

    // Send initialization message
    this.child.send({
      type: 'init',
      agentId: this.agentId,
      directive,
      capabilities: this.capabilities,
      stateSnapshot,
      forkDepth: this.forkDepth,
    })

    // Startup timeout
    await this.waitForReady(CHILD_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS)
  }

  /**
   * Build a restricted environment for the child process.
   * Strips sensitive variables and adds isolation markers.
   */
  private buildRestrictedEnv(): NodeJS.ProcessEnv {
    const restricted: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = {}

    // Allowlist of safe environment variables
    const allowedEnvVars = [
      'PATH', 'HOME', 'USER', 'SHELL', 'TERM', 'LANG',
      'NODE_ENV', 'TZ', 'TMPDIR',
    ]

    for (const key of allowedEnvVars) {
      if (process.env[key]) {
        restricted[key] = process.env[key]
      }
    }

    // Add isolation markers
    restricted.CLAUDE_AGENT_ISOLATED = '1'
    restricted.CLAUDE_AGENT_ID = this.agentId
    restricted.CLAUDE_FORK_DEPTH = String(this.forkDepth)

    // Explicitly exclude sensitive variables
    // CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, etc. are NOT copied

    return restricted
  }
}

Key design decisions:

Environment variable stripping. The child process receives only an allowlist of safe environment variables. All CLAUDE_*, ANTHROPIC_*, and AWS_* variables are excluded. This prevents the child from reading credentials or API keys from the environment --- a significant isolation improvement over the in-process model where process.env was fully shared.

Memory limits via --max-old-space-size. Node.js V8 heap size is capped per child process. The default 512MB is sufficient for most agent tasks while preventing a single child from consuming all available memory.

IPC-only communication. The child process has no direct access to parent memory. All tool calls must be serialized as IPC messages, pass through the ToolProxy, and return as IPC responses. This creates a mechanical enforcement boundary --- the child physically cannot access parent memory because it runs in a separate OS process with a separate address space.

Component 2: Capability-Based Tool Proxy

The ToolProxy sits in the parent process and mediates every tool call from child agents:

// tools/AgentTool/toolProxy.ts — NEW FILE

interface ProxyDecision {
  allowed: boolean
  reason?: string
}

/**
 * ToolProxy enforces capability-based restrictions on tool calls
 * from isolated agent processes. Every tool request from a child
 * process passes through this proxy before reaching the actual
 * tool implementation.
 *
 * This replaces the name-based filtering (which was advisory)
 * with process-boundary enforcement (which is mechanical).
 */
export class ToolProxy {
  private capabilities: AgentCapabilities
  private callCount: number = 0
  private readonly MAX_CALLS_PER_AGENT = 1000

  constructor(capabilities: AgentCapabilities) {
    this.capabilities = capabilities
  }

  /**
   * Evaluate whether a tool call is permitted under the agent's
   * capability set. Returns a decision with reason.
   */
  evaluate(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    this.callCount++

    // Rate limiting
    if (this.callCount > this.MAX_CALLS_PER_AGENT) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Agent exceeded maximum tool calls (${this.MAX_CALLS_PER_AGENT})`,
      }
    }

    // Tool allowlist check
    if (
      this.capabilities.allowedTools.length > 0 &&
      !this.capabilities.allowedTools.includes(request.toolName)
    ) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Tool '${request.toolName}' not in agent's allowed tools`,
      }
    }

    // Capability-specific checks
    switch (request.toolName) {
      case 'Read':
      case 'Glob':
      case 'Grep':
        return this.evaluateFilesystemRead(request)

      case 'Write':
      case 'Edit':
      case 'NotebookEdit':
        return this.evaluateFilesystemWrite(request)

      case 'Bash':
        return this.evaluateShellExec(request)

      case 'WebFetch':
      case 'WebSearch':
        return this.evaluateNetwork(request)

      case 'AgentTool':
        return this.evaluateNestedAgent(request)

      default:
        return { allowed: true }
    }
  }

  private evaluateFilesystemRead(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    if (this.capabilities.filesystem === 'none') {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: 'Agent does not have filesystem read permission',
      }
    }

    // Check denied paths
    const path = String(request.toolInput.file_path ?? request.toolInput.path ?? '')
    for (const denied of this.capabilities.deniedPaths) {
      if (matchesGlob(path, denied)) {
        return {
          allowed: false,
          reason: `Path '${path}' matches denied pattern '${denied}'`,
        }
      }
    }

    return { allowed: true }
  }

  private evaluateFilesystemWrite(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    if (this.capabilities.filesystem !== 'readwrite') {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: 'Agent does not have filesystem write permission',
      }
    }

    const path = String(request.toolInput.file_path ?? '')
    for (const denied of this.capabilities.deniedPaths) {
      if (matchesGlob(path, denied)) {
        return {
          allowed: false,
          reason: `Write to '${path}' blocked by denied pattern '${denied}'`,
        }
      }
    }

    return { allowed: true }
  }

  private evaluateShellExec(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    if (this.capabilities.shell === 'none') {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: 'Agent does not have shell execution permission',
      }
    }

    const command = String(request.toolInput.command ?? '')

    if (this.capabilities.shell === 'restricted') {
      // Restricted shell: block destructive commands
      const blocked = [
        /rm\s+-rf/,
        /chmod\s+777/,
        /curl.*\|\s*sh/,
        /wget.*\|\s*sh/,
        />\s*\/dev\/sd/,
        /mkfs/,
        /dd\s+if=/,
      ]

      for (const pattern of blocked) {
        if (pattern.test(command)) {
          return {
            allowed: false,
            reason: `Command matches restricted pattern in isolated agent context`,
          }
        }
      }
    }

    return { allowed: true }
  }

  private evaluateNetwork(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    if (this.capabilities.network === 'none') {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: 'Agent does not have network access permission',
      }
    }

    return { allowed: true }
  }

  private evaluateNestedAgent(request: IpcToolRequest): ProxyDecision {
    // Nested agent calls are always routed through the parent's
    // IsolatedAgentRunner, which enforces MAX_FORK_DEPTH.
    // We permit the request here but it will be depth-checked
    // by the parent before forking.
    return { allowed: true }
  }
}

The proxy provides mechanical enforcement rather than advisory filtering:

Property Name-Based Filtering (Before) ToolProxy (After)
Enforcement point Same process (advisory) Process boundary (mechanical)
Bypass method Prompt injection, memory access Must compromise parent process
Path restrictions None Glob-based denied paths
Rate limiting None MAX_CALLS_PER_AGENT
Shell restrictions None Pattern-based command blocking
Network restrictions None Capability flag check
Credential access Full (shared process.env) None (stripped environment)

Component 3: Fork Depth Enforcement

The recursive forking vulnerability (V-14) requires hard depth tracking that cannot be spoofed by message manipulation:

// tools/AgentTool/forkDepth.ts — NEW FILE

/** Maximum allowed fork depth. Prevents exponential process/memory growth. */
export const MAX_FORK_DEPTH = 3

/** Maximum concurrent agent processes across all depths. */
export const MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS = 10

/**
 * Global registry of active agent processes.
 * Tracks depth, resource usage, and parent-child relationships.
 */
class AgentRegistry {
  private agents: Map<string, {
    agentId: string
    depth: number
    parentId: string | null
    pid: number
    startedAt: number
    capabilities: AgentCapabilities
  }> = new Map()

  register(
    agentId: string,
    depth: number,
    parentId: string | null,
    pid: number,
    capabilities: AgentCapabilities,
  ): { allowed: true } | { allowed: false; reason: string } {
    // Check depth limit
    if (depth > MAX_FORK_DEPTH) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Fork depth ${depth} exceeds maximum ${MAX_FORK_DEPTH}`,
      }
    }

    // Check concurrent limit
    if (this.agents.size >= MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Maximum concurrent agents (${MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS}) reached`,
      }
    }

    // Check for circular fork chains
    if (parentId && this.hasAncestor(parentId, agentId)) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: 'Circular fork chain detected',
      }
    }

    this.agents.set(agentId, {
      agentId,
      depth,
      parentId,
      pid,
      startedAt: Date.now(),
      capabilities,
    })

    return { allowed: true }
  }

  unregister(agentId: string): void {
    this.agents.delete(agentId)
  }

  /**
   * Check if `candidateAncestor` is an ancestor of `agentId`.
   * Prevents circular fork chains where A forks B forks A.
   */
  private hasAncestor(agentId: string, candidateAncestor: string): boolean {
    let current = agentId
    const visited = new Set<string>()

    while (current) {
      if (visited.has(current)) return false  // Cycle guard
      visited.add(current)

      if (current === candidateAncestor) return true
      current = this.agents.get(current)?.parentId ?? ''
    }

    return false
  }

  /**
   * Get a tree visualization of active agents for debugging.
   */
  getTree(): string {
    const roots = Array.from(this.agents.values())
      .filter(a => a.parentId === null)

    const lines: string[] = []
    for (const root of roots) {
      this.printTree(root.agentId, 0, lines)
    }
    return lines.join('\n')
  }

  private printTree(agentId: string, indent: number, lines: string[]): void {
    const agent = this.agents.get(agentId)
    if (!agent) return

    const prefix = '  '.repeat(indent) + (indent > 0 ? '|- ' : '')
    const age = Math.round((Date.now() - agent.startedAt) / 1000)
    lines.push(
      `${prefix}[${agent.agentId.slice(0, 8)}] depth=${agent.depth} ` +
      `pid=${agent.pid} age=${age}s`,
    )

    for (const child of this.agents.values()) {
      if (child.parentId === agentId) {
        this.printTree(child.agentId, indent + 1, lines)
      }
    }
  }
}

export const agentRegistry = new AgentRegistry()

The depth is tracked in the parent process's AgentRegistry, not in the child's message context. This means a malicious child process cannot manipulate its perceived depth by editing its conversation messages --- the depth is recorded by the parent when the child is forked and cannot be changed by the child.

Component 4: Memory Isolation

With child_process.fork(), memory isolation is provided by the operating system:

graph TD
    subgraph OS["Operating System"]
        subgraph VMParent["Virtual Memory: Parent Process"]
            HEAP_P["V8 Heap<br/>(AppState, credentials,<br/>tool implementations)"]
            STACK_P["Call Stack"]
            ENV_P["process.env<br/>(all secrets)"]
        end

        subgraph VMChild["Virtual Memory: Child Process"]
            HEAP_C["V8 Heap<br/>(agent conversation,<br/>tool results only)"]
            STACK_C["Call Stack"]
            ENV_C["process.env<br/>(allowlisted vars only)"]
        end

        IPC["IPC Channel<br/>(serialized messages only)"]
    end

    VMParent <-->|"Messages"| IPC <-->|"Messages"| VMChild

    VMParent x--x|"NO direct access"| VMChild

    style VMParent fill:#44cc44,color:#000
    style VMChild fill:#4488cc,color:#fff
    style IPC fill:#cc8844,color:#fff

The isolation is mechanical:

  1. Separate address spaces. The child process has its own virtual memory. There is no way to read parent heap memory from the child process (without kernel exploits, which are out of scope).

  2. Serialized IPC only. Messages passed via child.send() are serialized to JSON (or structured clone) and deserialized in the other process. No object references, closures, or buffer pointers cross the boundary.

  3. Stripped environment. The child's process.env contains only the allowlisted variables. CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and all other sensitive variables are absent.

  4. Separate file descriptor table. The child cannot access the parent's open file handles, network sockets, or database connections. The stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe', 'ipc'] configuration gives the child its own stdin/stdout/stderr plus the IPC channel.

Component 5: OS-Level Resource Limits

Beyond Node.js --max-old-space-size, we apply OS-level limits to contain resource consumption:

// tools/AgentTool/resourceLimits.ts — NEW FILE

import { execSync } from 'child_process'

interface ResourceLimits {
  maxMemoryMB: number
  maxCpuSeconds: number
  maxFileDescriptors: number
  maxProcesses: number
}

/**
 * Apply OS-level resource limits to a child process.
 * Uses platform-specific mechanisms:
 * - Linux: cgroups v2 or ulimit
 * - macOS: launchctl limits or ulimit
 */
export function applyResourceLimits(
  pid: number,
  limits: ResourceLimits,
): void {
  if (process.platform === 'linux') {
    applyLinuxLimits(pid, limits)
  } else if (process.platform === 'darwin') {
    applyDarwinLimits(pid, limits)
  }
  // Windows: not yet supported (child_process inherits parent limits)
}

function applyLinuxLimits(pid: number, limits: ResourceLimits): void {
  try {
    // Create a cgroup for this agent process
    const cgroupPath = `/sys/fs/cgroup/claude-agents/${pid}`

    // Memory limit
    execSync(`mkdir -p ${cgroupPath}`)
    execSync(`echo ${limits.maxMemoryMB * 1024 * 1024} > ${cgroupPath}/memory.max`)

    // CPU limit (in microseconds per 100ms period)
    const cpuQuota = Math.min(limits.maxCpuSeconds * 10000, 100000)
    execSync(`echo ${cpuQuota} 100000 > ${cgroupPath}/cpu.max`)

    // Process count limit
    execSync(`echo ${limits.maxProcesses} > ${cgroupPath}/pids.max`)

    // Add the child process to the cgroup
    execSync(`echo ${pid} > ${cgroupPath}/cgroup.procs`)
  } catch {
    // cgroups may not be available (container, unprivileged)
    // Fall back to ulimit-based limits via child process
  }
}

function applyDarwinLimits(pid: number, limits: ResourceLimits): void {
  // macOS doesn't have cgroups. Use sandbox-exec for process restriction.
  // Note: sandbox-exec is deprecated but still functional in current macOS.
  // For production, consider using the Endpoint Security framework.
  try {
    // File descriptor limit can be set via the child's startup
    // Memory is limited via --max-old-space-size in V8
    // CPU limiting on macOS requires custom monitoring (no cgroups equivalent)
  } catch {
    // Best-effort on macOS
  }
}

13.3 IPC Protocol Design

The IPC channel between parent and child uses a structured message protocol:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Parent as Parent Process
    participant Proxy as ToolProxy
    participant Child as Child Process (Agent)
    participant LLM as LLM API

    Parent->>Child: init { agentId, directive, capabilities, stateSnapshot }
    Child-->>Parent: ready { agentId }

    loop Agent Conversation
        Child->>LLM: Query with tool definitions
        LLM-->>Child: Tool call response

        Child->>Parent: tool_request { requestId, toolName, toolInput }
        Parent->>Proxy: evaluate(request)

        alt Allowed
            Proxy-->>Parent: { allowed: true }
            Parent->>Parent: Execute tool
            Parent-->>Child: tool_response { requestId, success: true, result }
        else Denied
            Proxy-->>Parent: { allowed: false, reason }
            Parent-->>Child: tool_response { requestId, success: false, error }
        end

        Child->>Child: Feed result to LLM conversation
    end

    Child-->>Parent: complete { agentId, result }
    Parent->>Parent: Cleanup child process

Message Types

// tools/AgentTool/ipcProtocol.ts — NEW FILE

/** Messages from parent to child */
type ParentToChildMessage =
  | { type: 'init'; agentId: string; directive: string;
      capabilities: AgentCapabilities; stateSnapshot: SerializedAppState;
      forkDepth: number }
  | { type: 'tool_response'; requestId: string; success: boolean;
      result?: unknown; error?: string }
  | { type: 'abort'; reason: string }

/** Messages from child to parent */
type ChildToParentMessage =
  | { type: 'ready'; agentId: string }
  | { type: 'tool_request'; requestId: string; toolName: string;
      toolInput: Record<string, unknown>; agentId: string }
  | { type: 'state_request'; requestId: string; path: string }
  | { type: 'complete'; agentId: string; result: string }
  | { type: 'error'; agentId: string; message: string }
  | { type: 'log'; level: 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn'; message: string }

The protocol is deliberately simple: the child sends requests, the parent evaluates and responds. There is no mechanism for the child to execute code in the parent's context, access parent memory, or modify parent state. The IPC channel is the only interface.

13.4 Trust Tiers for Agent Sources

Not all agents need the same level of isolation. The system defines three trust tiers based on agent source:

Trust Tier Source Isolation Level Example
Tier 1: Trusted User's .claude/agents/ In-process User-written agents
Tier 2: Verified Marketplace (signed + reviewed) Process-isolated, broad capabilities Popular community agents
Tier 3: Community Marketplace (signed, not reviewed) Process-isolated, restricted capabilities New/unreviewed agents 
// tools/AgentTool/trustTier.ts — NEW FILE

type TrustTier = 'trusted' | 'verified' | 'community'

function determineAgentTrustTier(agentConfig: AgentConfig): TrustTier {
  // User-defined agents in .claude/agents/ are trusted
  if (agentConfig.source === 'local' &&
      agentConfig.path?.includes('.claude/agents/')) {
    return 'trusted'
  }

  // Marketplace agents with verified badge
  if (agentConfig.source === 'marketplace' &&
      agentConfig.verified === true) {
    return 'verified'
  }

  // Everything else is community tier
  return 'community'
}

function shouldIsolate(tier: TrustTier): boolean {
  return tier !== 'trusted'
}

function getDefaultCapabilities(tier: TrustTier): Partial<AgentCapabilities> {
  switch (tier) {
    case 'trusted':
      return {} // No restrictions (in-process)

    case 'verified':
      return {
        filesystem: 'readwrite',
        network: 'allowed',
        shell: 'restricted',
        maxMemoryMB: 1024,
        maxCpuSeconds: 600,
      }

    case 'community':
      return {
        filesystem: 'read',
        network: 'none',
        shell: 'none',
        maxMemoryMB: 512,
        maxCpuSeconds: 300,
      }
  }
}
