Migration Strategy

The sandbox cannot be deployed as a hard requirement overnight -- existing MCP servers do not have capability declarations. The migration follows three phases:

  1. Phase 1 (Week 1-4): Deploy monitoring-only sandbox. Log all operations that would be blocked. Publish capability schema specification.
  2. Phase 2 (Week 5-12): Require capability declarations for new marketplace submissions. Existing servers run with a permissive default capability set derived from monitoring data.
  3. Phase 3 (Week 13+): Enable enforcement for all servers. Servers without declarations receive a minimal default capability set (read-only workspace, no network, no process spawning).

As discussed in Chapter 14, the resource budget system governs agents within the Claude Code process tree. This chapter extends that governance to the MCP server boundary. Together, they ensure that no component in the system -- whether an internal subagent or an external MCP server -- can exceed its declared privileges.

Chapter 16: Remote Permission Controls

Part V has so far addressed isolation within the local machine: process-level agent separation (Chapter 13), fork depth and resource governance (Chapter 14), and MCP server sandboxing (Chapter 15). This chapter crosses the network boundary. When Claude Code operates in remote mode -- connecting to a server over HTTP/WebSocket to execute tools on a remote machine -- the permission model faces a fundamentally different threat: the permission bypass flag can be transmitted across the network.

Finding 12 from the security audit -- CWE-862: Missing Authorization (CVSS 6.5) -- identifies the core vulnerability: createDirectConnectSession() accepts a dangerouslySkipPermissions parameter and sends it to the remote server as dangerously_skip_permissions: true in the POST body. The function is at server/createDirectConnectSession.ts:54. A compromised or malicious server URL could be used to create sessions with no permission checks on the remote side.

This chapter implements the controls that prevent permission bypass flags from escaping the local trust boundary, enforces server-side authorization validation, and builds the warning system that ensures users understand the risk of remote permission escalation.

16.1 The Remote Permission Problem

How Remote Sessions Work

Claude Code supports a remote execution mode where the CLI connects to a server that hosts the agent runtime. This enables use cases like:

  • Cloud development environments: The agent runs on a remote server with access to cloud resources
  • Team collaboration: Multiple users connect to a shared agent session
  • CI/CD integration: Build pipelines invoke the agent on build servers
  • Container execution: The agent runs inside a Docker container or Kubernetes pod

The connection flow:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as CLI (local)
    participant Server as Remote Server
    participant Agent as Agent Runtime

    Client->>Server: POST /sessions<br/>{cwd, dangerously_skip_permissions: true}
    Server->>Agent: Create session with no permission checks
    Agent->>Agent: All tool calls auto-approved
    Agent->>Server: Tool results
    Server->>Client: Session output

    Note over Agent: Every Bash, Write, Edit<br/>executes WITHOUT user approval

The Vulnerable Code

The audit identified the exact code path:

// server/createDirectConnectSession.ts:54
const response = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/sessions`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`,
  },
  body: jsonStringify({
    cwd,
    ...(dangerouslySkipPermissions && {
      dangerously_skip_permissions: true,
    }),
  }),
})

When dangerouslySkipPermissions is true, the request body includes dangerously_skip_permissions: true. The remote server receives this flag and creates a session where all tool calls bypass the permission system. The flag name -- prefixed with "dangerously" -- signals risk, but it provides no technical enforcement.

Why This Is a Security Boundary Violation

The permission system in Claude Code is the primary defense against tool abuse. It gates every destructive operation: file writes, bash execution, MCP tool calls. When dangerouslySkipPermissions is active, none of these gates exist. The assumption is that the user explicitly chose to bypass permissions and accepts the risk.

Locally, this assumption holds: the user controls the CLI, the flag is passed via command-line argument, and the permissions apply to the user's own machine. Remotely, the assumption breaks:

Concern Local Context Remote Context
Who set the flag? The user, via CLI argument Could be the user, or could be an automation script, a deployment template, or an environment variable
What does it affect? The user's own filesystem A remote server that may host shared resources, production data, or other users' environments
Can it be intercepted? No -- stays in process memory Yes -- transmitted as JSON over HTTPS to a URL that may be misconfigured
Who verifies it? The local permission system The remote server, which may have a different (or absent) authorization model

The fundamental problem: a security-critical flag designed for local trust contexts is being transmitted across a network boundary without additional authorization checks.

Attack Scenarios

Scenario 1: Malicious Server URL

An attacker crafts a server URL that mimics a legitimate Claude Code server. The victim's CI pipeline is configured with CLAUDE_SERVER_URL=https://attacker.example.com and dangerouslySkipPermissions=true. When the pipeline runs, it sends a permissionless session request to the attacker's server. The attacker now has an agent session on the victim's build machine with no permission restrictions.

Scenario 2: URL Injection via Environment Variable

# Legitimate CI configuration
export CLAUDE_SERVER_URL="https://claude-server.internal:8080"
export CLAUDE_SKIP_PERMISSIONS="true"

# Attacker modifies .env or CI variables
export CLAUDE_SERVER_URL="https://attacker.example.com"
# The existing SKIP_PERMISSIONS flag now goes to the attacker

Scenario 3: Shared Server Permission Escalation

In a team environment, one user creates a remote session with dangerously_skip_permissions: true for debugging. Another user connects to the same server and discovers that all sessions are running without permission checks, because the server applied the flag globally rather than per-session.

16.2 Localhost-Only Restriction

The first and most important defense: dangerouslySkipPermissions should only be accepted by servers running on localhost.

Rationale

The original purpose of dangerouslySkipPermissions is local development convenience: the user wants the agent to execute without interactive prompts. This use case does not require network transmission. If the server is on the same machine (localhost), the flag can be communicated through local IPC mechanisms that do not cross a network boundary.

Implementation

import { URL } from 'node:url'
import { isLoopbackAddress } from './networkUtils'

interface CreateSessionOptions {
  serverUrl: string
  cwd: string
  dangerouslySkipPermissions: boolean
  token: string
}

async function createDirectConnectSession(
  options: CreateSessionOptions
): Promise<SessionResponse> {
  const { serverUrl, cwd, dangerouslySkipPermissions, token } = options

  // DEFENSE 1: Localhost-only restriction for permission bypass
  if (dangerouslySkipPermissions) {
    const url = new URL(serverUrl)
    const isLocalhost = await isLoopbackAddress(url.hostname)

    if (!isLocalhost) {
      throw new SecurityError(
        'dangerouslySkipPermissions cannot be used with remote servers. ' +
        'This flag is restricted to localhost connections. ' +
        `Server URL "${serverUrl}" resolves to a non-loopback address.`
      )
    }
  }

  // DEFENSE 2: Never include the raw flag in the request body
  const body: SessionRequest = {
    cwd,
    permissions_mode: dangerouslySkipPermissions
      ? 'skip_local'   // Server knows it was requested locally
      : 'standard',    // Normal permission mode
  }

  const response = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/sessions`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  })

  return response.json()
}

Loopback Address Verification

The loopback check must be resistant to DNS tricks:

import { resolve as dnsResolve } from 'node:dns/promises'
import { isIP, isIPv4, isIPv6 } from 'node:net'

async function isLoopbackAddress(hostname: string): Promise<boolean> {
  // Direct IP check
  if (isIP(hostname)) {
    return isLoopbackIP(hostname)
  }

  // Hostname resolution -- check ALL resolved IPs
  try {
    const addresses = await dnsResolve(hostname)
    // ALL resolved addresses must be loopback
    return addresses.length > 0 &&
      addresses.every(addr => isLoopbackIP(addr))
  } catch {
    return false  // DNS failure = not localhost
  }
}

function isLoopbackIP(ip: string): boolean {
  if (isIPv4(ip)) {
    return ip.startsWith('127.')  // 127.0.0.0/8
  }
  if (isIPv6(ip)) {
    return ip === '::1' || ip === '0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1'
  }
  return false
}

The critical detail: ALL resolved addresses must be loopback. A hostname that resolves to both 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.5 is not treated as localhost. This prevents DNS rebinding attacks where evil.example.com initially resolves to 127.0.0.1 (passing the check) and later resolves to an attacker's IP.

16.3 Server-Side Authorization Validation

Even when the permission bypass flag is restricted to localhost, the server must independently validate that the requesting client is authorized to create permissionless sessions.

The Server-Side Check

// Server: POST /sessions handler
async function handleCreateSession(
  req: Request,
  authContext: AuthContext
): Promise<Response> {
  const body = await req.json() as SessionRequest

  // Server-side permission bypass authorization
  if (body.permissions_mode === 'skip_local') {
    // Check 1: Request must come from loopback
    const clientIp = getClientIp(req)
    if (!isLoopbackIP(clientIp)) {
      return new Response(
        JSON.stringify({
          error: 'Permission bypass only allowed from localhost',
          code: 'PERMISSION_BYPASS_REMOTE',
        }),
        { status: 403 }
      )
    }

    // Check 2: User must have admin/owner role
    if (!authContext.roles.includes('admin') &&
        !authContext.roles.includes('owner')) {
      return new Response(
        JSON.stringify({
          error: 'Permission bypass requires admin or owner role',
          code: 'PERMISSION_BYPASS_UNAUTHORIZED',
        }),
        { status: 403 }
      )
    }

    // Check 3: Session must be flagged and time-limited
    const session = createSession({
      cwd: body.cwd,
      permissionMode: 'skip',
      skipExpiresAt: Date.now() + 3600_000,  // 1 hour max
      skipRequestedBy: authContext.userId,
      auditLog: true,  // Force audit logging
    })

    // Log the permission bypass for compliance
    logAuditEvent({
      event: 'permission_bypass_session_created',
      userId: authContext.userId,
      sessionId: session.id,
      expiresAt: session.skipExpiresAt,
      sourceIp: clientIp,
    })

    return new Response(JSON.stringify(session), { status: 201 })
  }

  // Standard session creation
  const session = createSession({
    cwd: body.cwd,
    permissionMode: 'standard',
  })

  return new Response(JSON.stringify(session), { status: 201 })
}

Three-Layer Authorization

graph TD
    REQ["Session request with<br/>permissions_mode: skip_local"] --> L1["Layer 1: Source Check<br/>Is request from loopback?"]
    L1 -->|No| DENY1["403: Remote bypass denied"]
    L1 -->|Yes| L2["Layer 2: Role Check<br/>Does user have admin role?"]
    L2 -->|No| DENY2["403: Insufficient privileges"]
    L2 -->|Yes| L3["Layer 3: Time Limit<br/>Set 1-hour expiry on bypass"]
    L3 --> ALLOW["201: Session created<br/>with time-limited bypass"]
    L3 --> AUDIT["Audit log entry"]

    style DENY1 fill:#fce4ec
    style DENY2 fill:#fce4ec
    style ALLOW fill:#e8f5e9
    style AUDIT fill:#e1f5fe
Layer What It Checks Defense Against
Source check Request from loopback IP Remote servers cannot create bypass sessions
Role check User has admin/owner role Non-admin users cannot bypass permissions
Time limit Session bypass expires in 1 hour Forgotten bypass sessions auto-expire

16.4 Warning Prompts with Risk Context

When a user attempts to use dangerouslySkipPermissions, the CLI should display a warning that provides specific risk context. The current behavior -- silently sending the flag -- does not inform the user of the consequences.

The Risk-Aware Warning

async function confirmPermissionBypass(
  serverUrl: string,
  isRemote: boolean
): Promise<boolean> {
  if (!process.stdout.isTTY) {
    // Non-interactive: check for explicit env var confirmation
    return process.env.CLAUDE_CONFIRM_SKIP_PERMISSIONS === 'yes_i_understand'
  }

  const url = new URL(serverUrl)

  console.log('\n' + '='.repeat(60))
  console.log('  WARNING: Permission Bypass Requested')
  console.log('='.repeat(60))
  console.log()
  console.log('  You are about to create a session that SKIPS ALL')
  console.log('  permission checks. This means:')
  console.log()
  console.log('  - Bash commands execute WITHOUT confirmation')
  console.log('  - Files are written WITHOUT read-before-write checks')
  console.log('  - MCP tools run WITHOUT approval prompts')
  console.log('  - Destructive operations are NOT blocked')
  console.log()
  console.log(`  Target server: ${url.hostname}:${url.port}`)
  console.log(`  Connection:    ${isRemote ? 'REMOTE' : 'localhost'}`)
  console.log()

  if (isRemote) {
    console.log('  ADDITIONAL RISK: This is a remote server.')
    console.log('  The permission bypass flag will be sent over the network.')
    console.log('  You are granting unrestricted access to a remote machine.')
    console.log()
  }

  const answer = await readline.question(
    '  Type "I understand the risks" to proceed: '
  )

  return answer.trim() === 'I understand the risks'
}

Non-Interactive Confirmation

In CI/CD environments where there is no TTY, the confirmation relies on an environment variable with an explicit acknowledgment value:

# CI pipeline configuration
export CLAUDE_CONFIRM_SKIP_PERMISSIONS="yes_i_understand"
export CLAUDE_SERVER_URL="http://localhost:8080"

claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --server $CLAUDE_SERVER_URL

The value yes_i_understand is intentionally verbose -- it cannot be set accidentally. A boolean flag like CONFIRM=true could be set by any number of automation tools without the operator understanding its significance.

16.5 Removing the Raw Flag from Network Transmission

The current implementation sends dangerously_skip_permissions: true as a raw boolean in the JSON body. This is problematic because:

  1. Replay attacks: If a request is intercepted (even over HTTPS, via log files or proxy inspection), the flag can be replayed against any server.
  2. Flag confusion: The server receives a boolean with no context about who authorized it, when it was authorized, or for how long it should be valid.
  3. Audit gap: There is no traceable record of the authorization decision.

Replacing the Boolean with a Signed Token

Instead of transmitting a raw boolean, the client generates a time-limited, signed authorization token:

interface PermissionBypassToken {
  action: 'skip_permissions'
  requestedBy: string     // User ID or machine identity
  requestedAt: number     // ISO timestamp
  expiresAt: number       // Maximum lifetime: 1 hour
  serverUrl: string       // Bound to specific server
  nonce: string           // Replay prevention
  signature: string       // HMAC-SHA256 of above fields
}

function createPermissionBypassToken(
  userId: string,
  serverUrl: string,
  lifetimeMs: number = 3600_000
): PermissionBypassToken {
  const requestedAt = Date.now()
  const expiresAt = requestedAt + lifetimeMs
  const nonce = randomBytes(16).toString('hex')

  const payload = JSON.stringify({
    action: 'skip_permissions',
    requestedBy: userId,
    requestedAt,
    expiresAt,
    serverUrl,
    nonce,
  })

  // Sign with the user's local session key
  const signature = createHmac('sha256', getSessionKey())
    .update(payload)
    .digest('hex')

  return {
    action: 'skip_permissions',
    requestedBy: userId,
    requestedAt,
    expiresAt,
    serverUrl,
    nonce,
    signature,
  }
}

Using the Token in Session Creation

async function createDirectConnectSession(
  options: CreateSessionOptions
): Promise<SessionResponse> {
  const { serverUrl, cwd, dangerouslySkipPermissions, token } = options

  const body: Record<string, unknown> = { cwd }

  if (dangerouslySkipPermissions) {
    // Validate localhost restriction
    await validateLocalhostOnly(serverUrl)

    // Generate time-limited, server-bound token
    const bypassToken = createPermissionBypassToken(
      getUserId(),
      serverUrl,
      3600_000  // 1 hour maximum
    )

    body.permission_bypass_token = bypassToken
  }

  const response = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/sessions`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  })

  return response.json()
}

Server-Side Token Validation

function validateBypassToken(
  token: PermissionBypassToken,
  expectedServerUrl: string
): { valid: boolean; reason?: string } {
  // Check expiry
  if (Date.now() > token.expiresAt) {
    return { valid: false, reason: 'Token expired' }
  }

  // Check server binding
  if (token.serverUrl !== expectedServerUrl) {
    return {
      valid: false,
      reason: `Token bound to ${token.serverUrl}, not ${expectedServerUrl}`,
    }
  }

  // Check nonce (prevent replay)
  if (isNonceUsed(token.nonce)) {
    return { valid: false, reason: 'Nonce already used (replay detected)' }
  }
  markNonceUsed(token.nonce, token.expiresAt)

  // Verify signature (requires shared secret or public key)
  if (!verifyTokenSignature(token)) {
    return { valid: false, reason: 'Invalid signature' }
  }

  return { valid: true }
}

Comparison: Before and After

Property Before (raw boolean) After (signed token)
Replay protection None Nonce + expiry
Server binding None -- flag works against any server Bound to specific serverUrl
Time limit None -- session lives forever 1-hour maximum lifetime
Audit trail None requestedBy, requestedAt, signature
Interceptability Boolean is trivially reusable Token is time-limited and nonce-protected

16.6 Rate Limiting Permission Bypass Requests

Even with all the above controls, an attacker who gains access to the local machine could repeatedly create bypass sessions. Rate limiting provides a backstop:

interface RateLimitConfig {
  maxBypassSessionsPerHour: number
  maxBypassSessionsPerDay: number
  cooldownAfterRejection: number  // milliseconds
}

const DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT: RateLimitConfig = {
  maxBypassSessionsPerHour: 5,
  maxBypassSessionsPerDay: 20,
  cooldownAfterRejection: 60_000,  // 1 minute cooldown after rejection
}

class BypassRateLimiter {
  private timestamps: number[] = []

  canCreateBypassSession(config: RateLimitConfig = DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT): {
    allowed: boolean
    reason?: string
    retryAfterMs?: number
  } {
    const now = Date.now()
    const oneHourAgo = now - 3600_000
    const oneDayAgo = now - 86400_000

    // Clean old entries
    this.timestamps = this.timestamps.filter(t => t > oneDayAgo)

    const hourCount = this.timestamps.filter(t => t > oneHourAgo).length
    const dayCount = this.timestamps.length

    if (hourCount >= config.maxBypassSessionsPerHour) {
      const oldestInHour = this.timestamps
        .filter(t => t > oneHourAgo)
        .sort()[0]
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Hourly limit (${config.maxBypassSessionsPerHour}) reached`,
        retryAfterMs: oldestInHour + 3600_000 - now,
      }
    }

    if (dayCount >= config.maxBypassSessionsPerDay) {
      return {
        allowed: false,
        reason: `Daily limit (${config.maxBypassSessionsPerDay}) reached`,
        retryAfterMs: this.timestamps[0] + 86400_000 - now,
      }
    }

    this.timestamps.push(now)
    return { allowed: true }
  }
}

16.7 Restricting dangerouslySkipPermissions to Non-Production

The strongest control for enterprise environments: block dangerouslySkipPermissions entirely in production.

Environment-Based Restriction

function isDangerouslySkipPermissionsAllowed(): {
  allowed: boolean
  reason?: string
} {
  // Check managed settings (enterprise policy)
  const managedPolicy = getManagedSettings()
  if (managedPolicy?.disablePermissionBypass === true) {
    return {
      allowed: false,
      reason: 'Permission bypass disabled by organization policy',
    }
  }

  // Check environment markers
  const env = process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development'
  const isProduction = env === 'production' ||
    process.env.CI === 'true' ||
    process.env.CLAUDE_PRODUCTION === 'true'

  if (isProduction &&
      !process.env.CLAUDE_ALLOW_PRODUCTION_BYPASS) {
    return {
      allowed: false,
      reason: 'Permission bypass is not allowed in production environments. ' +
        'Set CLAUDE_ALLOW_PRODUCTION_BYPASS=true to override (not recommended).',
    }
  }

  return { allowed: true }
}

Enterprise Policy Integration

{
  "managedSettings": {
    "disablePermissionBypass": true,
    "requireMFA": true,
    "auditAllSessions": true,
    "maxSessionDuration": 28800
  }
}

When disablePermissionBypass is set in managed settings (distributed via MDM or configuration management), no user on the machine can create bypass sessions, regardless of command-line arguments or environment variables. This provides organizational control over the most dangerous capability in the system.

16.8 Testing the Permission Control System

The six-layer defense requires comprehensive testing because each layer interacts with the others. A gap in any layer changes the security properties of the entire system.

Unit Tests for Localhost Restriction

describe('isLoopbackAddress', () => {
  test('127.0.0.1 is loopback', async () => {
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('127.0.0.1')).toBe(true)
  })

  test('127.0.0.2 is loopback (entire /8 range)', async () => {
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('127.0.0.2')).toBe(true)
  })

  test('::1 is loopback (IPv6)', async () => {
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('::1')).toBe(true)
  })

  test('localhost resolves to loopback', async () => {
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('localhost')).toBe(true)
  })

  test('10.0.0.1 is NOT loopback', async () => {
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('10.0.0.1')).toBe(false)
  })

  test('hostname resolving to mixed IPs is NOT loopback', async () => {
    // Mock: resolves to both 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.5
    mockDns.resolve('tricky.local', ['127.0.0.1', '10.0.0.5'])
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('tricky.local')).toBe(false)
  })

  test('DNS failure is NOT loopback', async () => {
    mockDns.reject('nonexistent.local', 'ENOTFOUND')
    expect(await isLoopbackAddress('nonexistent.local')).toBe(false)
  })
})

Integration Tests for the Token Lifecycle

describe('PermissionBypassToken', () => {
  test('token is accepted when valid', () => {
    const token = createPermissionBypassToken(
      'user-123', 'http://localhost:8080', 3600_000
    )
    const result = validateBypassToken(token, 'http://localhost:8080')
    expect(result.valid).toBe(true)
  })

  test('expired token is rejected', () => {
    const token = createPermissionBypassToken(
      'user-123', 'http://localhost:8080', -1  // Already expired
    )
    const result = validateBypassToken(token, 'http://localhost:8080')
    expect(result.valid).toBe(false)
    expect(result.reason).toContain('expired')
  })

  test('token bound to wrong server is rejected', () => {
    const token = createPermissionBypassToken(
      'user-123', 'http://localhost:8080'
    )
    const result = validateBypassToken(token, 'http://evil.com:8080')
    expect(result.valid).toBe(false)
    expect(result.reason).toContain('bound to')
  })

  test('replayed nonce is rejected', () => {
    const token = createPermissionBypassToken(
      'user-123', 'http://localhost:8080'
    )
    // First use succeeds
    const first = validateBypassToken(token, 'http://localhost:8080')
    expect(first.valid).toBe(true)

    // Second use (replay) fails
    const second = validateBypassToken(token, 'http://localhost:8080')
    expect(second.valid).toBe(false)
    expect(second.reason).toContain('replay')
  })

  test('tampered signature is rejected', () => {
    const token = createPermissionBypassToken(
      'user-123', 'http://localhost:8080'
    )
    const tampered = { ...token, expiresAt: token.expiresAt + 86400_000 }
    const result = validateBypassToken(tampered, 'http://localhost:8080')
    expect(result.valid).toBe(false)
    expect(result.reason).toContain('signature')
  })
})

End-to-End Test Scenario

describe('Remote permission bypass flow', () => {
  let server: TestServer

  beforeEach(async () => {
    server = await startTestServer({ port: 0 })
  })

  afterEach(async () => {
    await server.close()
  })

  test('local bypass session succeeds with all checks passing', async () => {
    const session = await createDirectConnectSession({
      serverUrl: `http://127.0.0.1:${server.port}`,
      cwd: '/tmp/test',
      dangerouslySkipPermissions: true,
      token: 'test-token',
    })

    expect(session.permissionMode).toBe('skip')
    expect(session.skipExpiresAt).toBeDefined()
    expect(session.skipExpiresAt! - Date.now()).toBeLessThanOrEqual(3600_000)
  })

  test('remote bypass session is rejected at client', async () => {
    await expect(createDirectConnectSession({
      serverUrl: 'https://remote-server.example.com:8080',
      cwd: '/tmp/test',
      dangerouslySkipPermissions: true,
      token: 'test-token',
    })).rejects.toThrow('restricted to localhost')
  })

  test('rate limiter blocks after hourly limit', async () => {
    const limiter = new BypassRateLimiter()

    // First 5 succeed
    for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      expect(limiter.canCreateBypassSession().allowed).toBe(true)
    }

    // 6th is blocked
    const result = limiter.canCreateBypassSession()
    expect(result.allowed).toBe(false)
    expect(result.reason).toContain('Hourly limit')
  })
})

Fuzzing the Loopback Check

The loopback address check is a critical security boundary. Edge cases in IP parsing can create bypasses:

Input Expected Risk if Wrong
0x7f000001 Loopback (127.0.0.1 in hex) Attacker bypasses remote check with hex IP
2130706433 Loopback (127.0.0.1 in decimal) Attacker bypasses with decimal IP
0177.0.0.1 Loopback (127.0.0.1 in octal) Attacker bypasses with octal notation
127.0.0.1.evil.com NOT loopback (DNS resolves) Loopback check passes but connects to attacker
[::ffff:127.0.0.1] Loopback (IPv4-mapped IPv6) IPv6 notation bypasses IPv4-only check
127.1 Loopback (short form of 127.0.0.1) Some platforms expand, others reject

The isLoopbackAddress() function must handle all these representations. Using Node.js's net.isIP() for initial classification, then DNS resolution for hostnames, ensures consistent handling:

test('handles exotic IP representations', async () => {
  // These should all be handled without security bypass
  expect(await isLoopbackAddress('0x7f000001')).toBe(false)  // Not a valid IP for net.isIP
  expect(await isLoopbackAddress('2130706433')).toBe(false)   // Not a valid IP for net.isIP
  expect(await isLoopbackAddress('0177.0.0.1')).toBe(false)   // Octal not recognized
  expect(await isLoopbackAddress('127.0.0.1.evil.com')).toBe(false) // DNS resolves to attacker
})

The defense strategy: treat only addresses that pass net.isIP() validation as literal IPs. Everything else goes through DNS resolution, which resolves the actual target. This prevents octal/hex/decimal representation tricks.

16.9 Attack Scenario: CI/CD Pipeline Exploitation

The most realistic attack scenario for remote permission bypass targets CI/CD pipelines. These environments have unique properties that amplify the risk:

  1. Non-interactive: No human is present to read warning prompts or type confirmations
  2. Credential-rich: Build environments contain deployment keys, NPM tokens, cloud credentials
  3. Network-accessible: Build servers are reachable from the corporate network
  4. Script-driven: Configuration is in code (.yml, .toml, .env), not interactive setup

The Attack Chain

graph TD
    A1["Step 1: Attacker compromises<br/>a dependency or build script"] --> A2["Step 2: Modify CI config to set<br/>CLAUDE_SERVER_URL=attacker.com"]
    A2 --> A3["Step 3: CI pipeline runs with<br/>dangerouslySkipPermissions=true"]
    A3 --> A4["Step 4: Bypass session created<br/>on attacker's server"]
    A4 --> A5["Step 5: Attacker's server<br/>executes arbitrary tools"]
    A5 --> A6["Step 6: Exfiltrate secrets,<br/>inject backdoors, pivot"]

    style A1 fill:#fce4ec
    style A6 fill:#fce4ec

How Each Defense Layer Mitigates This

Layer Effect on CI/CD Attack
Environment check If NODE_ENV=production or CI=true, bypass is blocked unless explicitly overridden
Warning prompt Non-interactive -- falls through to env var check (CLAUDE_CONFIRM_SKIP_PERMISSIONS)
Localhost check Blocks the attack -- attacker.com is not localhost
Rate limit Limits damage if localhost check is somehow bypassed
Signed token Token bound to server URL -- cannot be replayed against different server
Server validation Attacker's server would need to implement the validation protocol

The localhost check is the primary defense for CI/CD attacks. Even if the attacker controls the CLAUDE_SERVER_URL, the client refuses to send permission bypass tokens to non-loopback addresses. The CI pipeline can still use Claude Code with standard permission mode (where each tool call requires explicit allow rules in configuration), but it cannot create permissionless sessions against remote servers.

The full defense against remote permission bypass has six layers:

Backward Compatibility

The transition from raw boolean to signed token requires coordination between client and server:

  1. Phase 1: Server accepts both old format (dangerously_skip_permissions: true) and new format (permission_bypass_token: {...}). Log deprecation warning when old format is used.
  2. Phase 2: CLI update pushed to all clients, generating signed tokens instead of raw booleans.
  3. Phase 3: Server rejects old format. Only signed tokens accepted.

This three-phase approach ensures that no client-server version mismatch causes a service disruption. The deprecation window should be at least 4 weeks, with prominent warnings in the CLI output when the old format is still in use.

As discussed in Chapter 15, the sandbox system prevents MCP servers from exceeding their declared capabilities. This chapter applies similar principles to the remote session boundary: no component should receive more privilege than it needs, privilege escalation must require explicit authorization, and every authorization decision must be auditable.

Chapter 17: WebSocket & Network Security

Chapter 16 addressed how the dangerouslySkipPermissions flag crosses the network boundary to remote servers. This chapter broadens the scope to the entire network attack surface of Claude Code. Three findings from the security audit converge here: WebSocket origin validation (Finding 21, CWE-346), SSRF via DNS rebinding (Finding 17, CWE-918), and CA bundle download without certificate pinning (Finding 18, CWE-295). Together, they represent the network trust model -- how Claude Code establishes, validates, and maintains the integrity of its network connections.

Claude Code makes network connections in three contexts: the API connection to Anthropic's servers (streaming responses, session management), the WebSocket connection for remote sessions and real-time event delivery, and the WebFetch tool for user-directed HTTP requests. Each context has a different trust model, a different attack surface, and a different set of defenses that must be implemented.

17.1 WebSocket Origin Validation

The Missing Origin Check

Finding 21 identifies a medium-severity vulnerability (CVSS 5.5): SessionsWebSocket.ts establishes WebSocket connections with Authorization: Bearer headers but no explicit Origin validation. The isSessionsMessage() type guard accepts any object with a string type field, providing minimal message validation.

The data flow in the audit finding:

Malicious web page -> JavaScript opens WebSocket to
wss://api.anthropic.com/v1/sessions/ws/{id}/subscribe ->
if token is accessible (e.g., via XSS) -> connection succeeds ->
attacker receives session messages

While the audit notes this is low probability (the token is stored in keychain/file, not cookies), the defense should not rely on the absence of other vulnerabilities. If token theft ever becomes possible -- through a future XSS in a web-based interface, through environment variable exposure, or through an MCP server that reads the credential file -- the missing Origin validation becomes a direct exploitation path.

How WebSocket Hijacking Works

sequenceDiagram
    participant Victim as Victim's Browser
    participant Evil as evil-site.com
    participant WS as Claude WebSocket Server

    Victim->>Evil: Visits evil-site.com
    Evil->>Victim: Returns page with JavaScript

    Note over Victim: JavaScript executes in browser

    Victim->>WS: new WebSocket("wss://api.anthropic.com/v1/sessions/ws/...")
    Note over WS: Browser automatically sends:<br/>- Cookies (if any)<br/>- Origin: evil-site.com

    alt No Origin Validation
        WS-->>Victim: Connection accepted
        WS-->>Evil: Session events forwarded
        Note over Evil: Attacker reads session data
    end

    alt With Origin Validation
        WS-->>Victim: 403 Forbidden<br/>Origin not in allowlist
        Note over Evil: Attack blocked
    end

In the standard WebSocket hijacking scenario, the browser sends cookies automatically with the WebSocket handshake. Claude Code does not use cookies for WebSocket authentication -- it uses Authorization: Bearer headers. This means the browser-based attack requires the attacker to already possess the token. However, the Origin header validation provides defense-in-depth against scenarios where token theft happens through other means.

Client-Side Origin Enforcement

The client should set the Origin header explicitly and validate the server's response:

import WebSocket from 'ws'

interface SecureWebSocketOptions {
  url: string
  token: string
  expectedServerIdentity: string
  allowedOrigins: string[]
}

function createSecureWebSocket(
  options: SecureWebSocketOptions
): WebSocket {
  const { url, token, expectedServerIdentity, allowedOrigins } = options

  // Set explicit Origin header
  const origin = 'claude-code-cli'  // Not a web origin -- CLI identifier

  const ws = new WebSocket(url, {
    headers: {
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`,
      'Origin': origin,
      'X-Client-Version': getClientVersion(),
      'X-Session-Id': getSessionId(),
    },
    // TLS options
    rejectUnauthorized: true,
    // Connection timeout
    handshakeTimeout: 10_000,
  })

  // Validate server identity on upgrade response
  ws.on('upgrade', (response: IncomingMessage) => {
    const serverIdentity = response.headers['x-server-identity']

    if (serverIdentity !== expectedServerIdentity) {
      ws.close(4001, 'Server identity mismatch')
      throw new SecurityError(
        `WebSocket server identity mismatch. ` +
        `Expected: ${expectedServerIdentity}, Got: ${serverIdentity}`
      )
    }
  })

  return ws
}

Server-Side Origin Validation

The server must validate the Origin header on every WebSocket upgrade request:

const ALLOWED_ORIGINS = new Set([
  'claude-code-cli',
  'claude-code-vscode',
  'claude-code-jetbrains',
])

function handleWebSocketUpgrade(
  request: IncomingMessage,
  socket: Socket,
  head: Buffer
): void {
  const origin = request.headers['origin'] ?? ''

  // Reject unknown origins
  if (!ALLOWED_ORIGINS.has(origin)) {
    socket.write(
      'HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden\r\n' +
      `X-Rejection-Reason: Origin "${origin}" not allowed\r\n` +
      '\r\n'
    )
    socket.destroy()

    logSecurityEvent({
      event: 'websocket_origin_rejected',
      origin,
      ip: socket.remoteAddress,
      timestamp: Date.now(),
    })
    return
  }

  // Proceed with upgrade
  wss.handleUpgrade(request, socket, head, (ws) => {
    wss.emit('connection', ws, request)
  })
}

Message Validation Hardening

Beyond origin validation, the isSessionsMessage() type guard should be strengthened from a minimal type check to a full structural validation:

// BEFORE: Minimal check (vulnerable)
function isSessionsMessage(data: unknown): data is SessionsMessage {
  return typeof data === 'object' &&
    data !== null &&
    'type' in data &&
    typeof (data as Record<string, unknown>).type === 'string'
}

// AFTER: Structural validation
import { z } from 'zod'

const SessionsMessageSchema = z.discriminatedUnion('type', [
  z.object({
    type: z.literal('session_created'),
    sessionId: z.string().uuid(),
    createdAt: z.number(),
  }),
  z.object({
    type: z.literal('tool_result'),
    toolUseId: z.string(),
    content: z.array(z.object({
      type: z.enum(['text', 'image', 'document']),
    })),
  }),
  z.object({
    type: z.literal('session_ended'),
    sessionId: z.string().uuid(),
    reason: z.enum(['completed', 'timeout', 'error', 'user_cancel']),
  }),
  z.object({
    type: z.literal('heartbeat'),
    timestamp: z.number(),
  }),
])

function validateSessionsMessage(
  data: unknown
): z.infer<typeof SessionsMessageSchema> | null {
  const result = SessionsMessageSchema.safeParse(data)
  if (!result.success) {
    logSecurityEvent({
      event: 'invalid_ws_message',
      errors: result.error.issues,
      rawData: JSON.stringify(data).slice(0, 200),
    })
    return null
  }
  return result.data
}

The Zod schema ensures that: - Only known message types are accepted - Each message type has the expected fields with correct types - UUIDs are formatted correctly - Enum values are from the allowed set - Unknown properties are stripped

17.2 SSRF via DNS Rebinding

The WebFetch SSRF Vulnerability

Finding 17 (CVSS 5.9) identifies a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the WebFetch tool. The tool validates URLs at the application level but does not validate the IP address that DNS resolves to before making the connection.

// Current implementation -- VULNERABLE
export function isPermittedRedirect(
  originalUrl: string,
  redirectUrl: string
): boolean {
  const stripWww = (hostname: string) =>
    hostname.replace(/^www\./, '')
  return originalHostWithoutWww === redirectHostWithoutWww
}

This redirect check verifies hostname equivalence but does not check the resolved IP address. The key finding from the audit: "The ssrfGuardedLookup is only used for HTTP hooks, not for the WebFetch tool."

DNS Rebinding Attack Flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as Claude Agent
    participant DNS as DNS Server (attacker)
    participant Fetch as WebFetch Tool
    participant Meta as AWS Metadata<br/>169.254.169.254

    Agent->>Fetch: WebFetch("https://attacker.com/api")
    Fetch->>DNS: Resolve attacker.com
    DNS-->>Fetch: A: 203.0.113.50 (public IP)<br/>TTL: 0
    Fetch->>Fetch: IP 203.0.113.50 is public ✓

    Note over Fetch: First request succeeds<br/>Response includes redirect

    Fetch->>DNS: Resolve attacker.com (again, TTL=0)
    DNS-->>Fetch: A: 169.254.169.254 (metadata service!)
    Fetch->>Meta: GET /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
    Meta-->>Fetch: {"AccessKeyId": "AKIA...", "SecretAccessKey": "..."}

    Note over Agent: Agent now has AWS credentials<br/>in conversation context

The attack exploits DNS TTL: the attacker's DNS server returns a public IP on the first query (passing validation) and then switches to a private/metadata IP on subsequent queries (exploiting the rebind). Because the WebFetch tool does not re-validate the resolved IP on each connection, the second resolution to 169.254.169.254 is used for the actual HTTP request.

The ssrfGuardedLookup Solution

The fix is to apply the existing ssrfGuardedLookup function -- currently only used for HTTP hooks -- to all WebFetch requests:

import { lookup as dnsLookup, LookupAddress } from 'node:dns'
import { isIP } from 'node:net'

// IP ranges that should never be contacted by WebFetch
const BLOCKED_RANGES: Array<{
  cidr: string
  start: bigint
  end: bigint
  description: string
}> = [
  { cidr: '127.0.0.0/8', start: ipToBigInt('127.0.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('127.255.255.255'), description: 'Loopback' },
  { cidr: '10.0.0.0/8', start: ipToBigInt('10.0.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('10.255.255.255'), description: 'Private (RFC 1918)' },
  { cidr: '172.16.0.0/12', start: ipToBigInt('172.16.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('172.31.255.255'), description: 'Private (RFC 1918)' },
  { cidr: '192.168.0.0/16', start: ipToBigInt('192.168.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('192.168.255.255'), description: 'Private (RFC 1918)' },
  { cidr: '169.254.0.0/16', start: ipToBigInt('169.254.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('169.254.255.255'), description: 'Link-local / Cloud metadata' },
  { cidr: '0.0.0.0/8', start: ipToBigInt('0.0.0.0'),
    end: ipToBigInt('0.255.255.255'), description: 'Current network' },
  { cidr: 'fc00::/7', start: ipv6ToBigInt('fc00::'),
    end: ipv6ToBigInt('fdff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff'),
    description: 'IPv6 ULA' },
  { cidr: '::1/128', start: ipv6ToBigInt('::1'),
    end: ipv6ToBigInt('::1'), description: 'IPv6 loopback' },
  { cidr: 'fe80::/10', start: ipv6ToBigInt('fe80::'),
    end: ipv6ToBigInt('febf:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff'),
    description: 'IPv6 link-local' },
]

function isBlockedIp(ip: string): { blocked: boolean; reason?: string } {
  const ipBigInt = isIPv4(ip) ? ipToBigInt(ip) : ipv6ToBigInt(ip)

  for (const range of BLOCKED_RANGES) {
    if (ipBigInt >= range.start && ipBigInt <= range.end) {
      return {
        blocked: true,
        reason: `IP ${ip} is in blocked range ${range.cidr} (${range.description})`,
      }
    }
  }

  return { blocked: false }
}

DNS Resolution Caching with Pinning

To prevent DNS rebinding, the resolved IP address must be pinned for the duration of the request:

interface PinnedDnsEntry {
  hostname: string
  resolvedIp: string
  resolvedAt: number
  ttl: number
}

class SsrfSafeDnsCache {
  private cache = new Map<string, PinnedDnsEntry>()
  private readonly MIN_TTL_MS = 30_000  // Minimum 30s TTL regardless of DNS

  async resolve(hostname: string): Promise<string> {
    // Check cache first
    const cached = this.cache.get(hostname)
    if (cached && Date.now() - cached.resolvedAt < cached.ttl) {
      return cached.resolvedIp
    }

    // Perform DNS resolution
    const addresses = await dnsResolveAll(hostname)

    if (addresses.length === 0) {
      throw new SsrfError(`DNS resolution failed for ${hostname}`)
    }

    // Validate ALL resolved addresses
    for (const addr of addresses) {
      const check = isBlockedIp(addr.address)
      if (check.blocked) {
        throw new SsrfError(
          `SSRF blocked: ${hostname} resolved to ${addr.address}. ` +
          check.reason
        )
      }
    }

    // Pin the first valid address
    const pinnedIp = addresses[0].address
    const ttl = Math.max(this.MIN_TTL_MS, (addresses[0].ttl ?? 30) * 1000)

    this.cache.set(hostname, {
      hostname,
      resolvedIp: pinnedIp,
      resolvedAt: Date.now(),
      ttl,
    })

    return pinnedIp
  }
}

Integrating SSRF Protection into WebFetch

const dnsCache = new SsrfSafeDnsCache()

async function secureFetch(
  url: string,
  options: RequestInit = {}
): Promise<Response> {
  const parsed = new URL(url)

  // Step 1: Resolve hostname with SSRF check
  const resolvedIp = await dnsCache.resolve(parsed.hostname)

  // Step 2: Create a custom agent that connects to the pinned IP
  const agent = new https.Agent({
    lookup: (hostname, opts, callback) => {
      // Override DNS: always use the pre-validated, pinned IP
      callback(null, resolvedIp, isIPv4(resolvedIp) ? 4 : 6)
    },
    // Verify the TLS certificate against the original hostname
    servername: parsed.hostname,
    rejectUnauthorized: true,
  })

  // Step 3: Make the request with the pinned agent
  const response = await fetch(url, {
    ...options,
    // @ts-expect-error -- Node.js fetch supports agent
    agent,
    redirect: 'manual',  // Handle redirects ourselves
  })

  // Step 4: Validate redirects
  if (response.status >= 300 && response.status < 400) {
    const redirectUrl = response.headers.get('location')
    if (redirectUrl) {
      return handleSecureRedirect(url, redirectUrl, options)
    }
  }

  return response
}

async function handleSecureRedirect(
  originalUrl: string,
  redirectUrl: string,
  options: RequestInit,
  depth: number = 0
): Promise<Response> {
  // Prevent infinite redirects
  if (depth >= 5) {
    throw new SsrfError(`Too many redirects (${depth}) from ${originalUrl}`)
  }

  const redirectParsed = new URL(redirectUrl, originalUrl)

  // Validate redirect destination
  const redirectIp = await dnsCache.resolve(redirectParsed.hostname)
  const check = isBlockedIp(redirectIp)
  if (check.blocked) {
    throw new SsrfError(
      `SSRF blocked: redirect from ${originalUrl} to ${redirectUrl} ` +
      `resolved to blocked IP ${redirectIp}. ${check.reason}`
    )
  }

  // Follow the redirect with the same security checks
  return secureFetch(redirectUrl, options)
}

SSRF Protection Summary

Attack Vector Defense Location

DNS rebinding (TTL=0) Minimum 30s TTL, IP pinning SsrfSafeDnsCache
Redirect to internal IP Redirect target IP validation handleSecureRedirect()
IPv6 mapped IPv4 (::ffff:127.0.0.1) Both IPv4 and IPv6 blocklists BLOCKED_RANGES
DNS returning multiple IPs ALL addresses validated dnsCache.resolve()

17.3 CA Bundle Certificate Pinning

The Unpinned CA Download

Finding 18 (CVSS 5.9) identifies that downloadCaBundle() fetches a CA certificate from the API server and concatenates it with the system CA bundle. The downloaded CA is then used to validate all HTTPS connections going through the upstream proxy.

// Current implementation -- VULNERABLE
const resp = await fetch(
  `${baseUrl}/v1/code/upstreamproxy/ca-cert`,
  { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) }
)
const ccrCa = await resp.text()
const systemCa = await readFile(systemCaPath, 'utf8').catch(() => '')
await writeFile(outPath, systemCa + '\n' + ccrCa, 'utf8')

The data flow: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL -> fetch CA cert -> concatenate with system CA -> write to ~/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt -> used as SSL_CERT_FILE for all subprocesses.

Why This Matters

If an attacker can MITM the initial HTTPS connection to the API server (using a valid certificate for the API domain -- possible via a compromised CA, a corporate proxy, or a state-level attacker), they can provide a rogue CA certificate. Once the rogue CA is added to the bundle, the attacker can MITM all subsequent HTTPS connections from Claude Code and its subprocesses.

graph TD
    subgraph "Normal Operation"
        N1["CLI fetches CA from API server"]
        N2["API returns legitimate CA"]
        N3["CA added to bundle"]
        N4["All HTTPS validated correctly"]
        N1 --> N2 --> N3 --> N4
    end

    subgraph "MITM Attack"
        A1["CLI fetches CA from API server"]
        A2["MITM intercepts, returns rogue CA"]
        A3["Rogue CA added to bundle"]
        A4["Attacker can MITM ALL HTTPS<br/>from CLI and subprocesses"]
        A1 --> A2 --> A3 --> A4
    end

    style A2 fill:#fce4ec
    style A4 fill:#fce4ec
    style N4 fill:#e8f5e9

Implementing Certificate Pinning

The fix uses public key pinning: the client knows the expected public key hash of the CA certificate before downloading it. Even if an attacker provides a certificate with the correct subject name, it will have a different public key.

import { createHash, X509Certificate } from 'node:crypto'

// Known CA public key hashes (base64-encoded SHA-256 of SubjectPublicKeyInfo)
const PINNED_CA_HASHES: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  // Primary CA
  'sha256/YLh1dUR9y6Kja30RrAn7JKnbQG/uEtLMkBgFF2Fuihg=',
  // Backup CA (for rotation)
  'sha256/sRHdihwgkaib1P1gN7akICObfQ0XY1oqEv8xCZH4Dns=',
])

interface CaPinningResult {
  valid: boolean
  downloadedHash: string
  reason?: string
}

function validateCaCertificate(
  certPem: string,
  pinnedHashes: ReadonlySet<string> = PINNED_CA_HASHES
): CaPinningResult {
  try {
    const cert = new X509Certificate(certPem)

    // Extract SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) and hash it
    const spki = cert.publicKey.export({
      type: 'spki',
      format: 'der',
    })
    const hash = 'sha256/' +
      createHash('sha256').update(spki).digest('base64')

    if (pinnedHashes.has(hash)) {
      return { valid: true, downloadedHash: hash }
    }

    return {
      valid: false,
      downloadedHash: hash,
      reason: `CA certificate public key hash ${hash} ` +
        'does not match any pinned hash. ' +
        'This may indicate a MITM attack or a CA rotation. ' +
        'If this is expected, update the pinned hashes.',
    }
  } catch (error) {
    return {
      valid: false,
      downloadedHash: 'PARSE_ERROR',
      reason: `Failed to parse CA certificate: ${(error as Error).message}`,
    }
  }
}

Secure CA Download with Pinning

async function downloadCaBundleSecure(
  baseUrl: string,
  outPath: string,
  systemCaPath: string
): Promise<void> {
  // Step 1: Fetch the CA certificate
  const resp = await fetch(
    `${baseUrl}/v1/code/upstreamproxy/ca-cert`,
    {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
      // Use system CA for this initial fetch
      // (this is the bootstrap trust problem)
    }
  )

  if (!resp.ok) {
    throw new Error(`CA download failed: ${resp.status} ${resp.statusText}`)
  }

  const ccrCa = await resp.text()

  // Step 2: Validate the certificate against pinned hashes
  const pinResult = validateCaCertificate(ccrCa)

  if (!pinResult.valid) {
    logSecurityEvent({
      event: 'ca_pin_mismatch',
      downloadedHash: pinResult.downloadedHash,
      reason: pinResult.reason,
      baseUrl,
      timestamp: Date.now(),
    })

    throw new SecurityError(
      'CA certificate pinning validation failed. ' +
      pinResult.reason +
      '\n\nThe downloaded certificate will NOT be used. ' +
      'If you are behind a corporate proxy, contact your IT team.'
    )
  }

  // Step 3: Validate the certificate is actually a CA
  const cert = new X509Certificate(ccrCa)
  if (!cert.ca) {
    throw new SecurityError(
      'Downloaded certificate is not a CA certificate (basicConstraints.cA is false). ' +
      'This may indicate a MITM attack.'
    )
  }

  // Step 4: Check certificate dates
  const now = new Date()
  if (now < new Date(cert.validFrom) || now > new Date(cert.validTo)) {
    throw new SecurityError(
      `CA certificate is not currently valid. ` +
      `Valid from: ${cert.validFrom}, Valid to: ${cert.validTo}`
    )
  }

  // Step 5: Read system CA and concatenate
  const systemCa = await readFile(systemCaPath, 'utf8').catch(() => '')

  // Step 6: Write the validated bundle atomically
  const tmpPath = `${outPath}.tmp.${process.pid}`
  await writeFile(tmpPath, systemCa + '\n' + ccrCa, 'utf8')
  await chmod(tmpPath, 0o644)
  await rename(tmpPath, outPath)  // Atomic rename

  logSecurityEvent({
    event: 'ca_bundle_updated',
    caHash: pinResult.downloadedHash,
    baseUrl,
    timestamp: Date.now(),
  })
}

Certificate Pin Rotation

Pins must be rotatable. If Anthropic rotates their CA, the CLI must be able to accept the new CA without requiring a code update. The solution: include backup pins and a pin update mechanism.

interface PinSet {
  primary: string[]     // Currently active pins
  backup: string[]      // Pre-staged backup pins for rotation
  version: number       // Pin set version
  updatedAt: string     // ISO timestamp of last update
}

async function fetchPinSet(
  baseUrl: string
): Promise<PinSet> {
  // Fetch the pin set over HTTPS (validated by system CA)
  const resp = await fetch(
    `${baseUrl}/v1/code/upstreamproxy/pin-set`,
    {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
      headers: {
        'X-Current-Pin-Version': String(getCurrentPinVersion()),
      },
    }
  )

  const pinSet: PinSet = await resp.json()

  // Verify the pin set itself is signed
  if (!verifyPinSetSignature(pinSet)) {
    throw new SecurityError('Pin set signature verification failed')
  }

  // The pin set must always include at least one primary
  // and one backup pin
  if (pinSet.primary.length === 0 || pinSet.backup.length === 0) {
    throw new SecurityError('Pin set must have primary and backup pins')
  }

  return pinSet
}

The Bootstrap Trust Problem

Certificate pinning has a chicken-and-egg problem: the initial HTTPS connection to download the CA uses the system's default TLS validation. If the system's CA store is compromised (corporate proxy, malicious CA), the initial fetch is already MITM'd, and the pinning check validates against the attacker's certificate.

Defense Layer What It Protects Against What It Does Not Protect Against
TLS (system CA) Network-level eavesdroppers Compromised CA in system store
Certificate pinning Rogue CAs, CA compromise First-connection MITM before pins are cached
Pin set versioning Downgrade attacks (old pins) First-ever connection (no cached pins)
Backup pins CA rotation All pins compromised simultaneously

The practical mitigation: ship initial pins as compile-time constants in the Claude Code binary. The first connection does not need to download pins -- it uses the embedded pins. Subsequent connections can update the pin set through the secure channel established by the initial pinned connection. This is the same approach used by Chrome's certificate pinning (HPKP predecessor) and Certificate Transparency logs.

17.4 TLS Configuration Hardening

Beyond certificate pinning, the TLS configuration itself must be hardened to prevent downgrade attacks and weak cipher usage.

Minimum TLS Version

import { Agent as HttpsAgent } from 'node:https'

function createSecureAgent(): HttpsAgent {
  return new HttpsAgent({
    // Minimum TLS 1.2, prefer TLS 1.3
    minVersion: 'TLSv1.2',
    maxVersion: 'TLSv1.3',

    // Reject connections that don't verify
    rejectUnauthorized: true,

    // Cipher suite ordering (prefer AEAD ciphers)
    ciphers: [
      'TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384',
      'TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256',
      'TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256',
      'ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384',
      'ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384',
      'ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256',
      'ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256',
    ].join(':'),

    // ECDH curves
    ecdhCurve: 'X25519:P-256:P-384',

    // Session tickets (for TLS 1.2 resumption)
    sessionTimeout: 300,
  })
}

TLS Configuration Audit Table

Setting Current Recommended Rationale

Max TLS version Not set (defaults to TLS 1.3) TLS 1.3 Already optimal

17.5 WebSocket Connection Security

Beyond origin validation (Section 17.1), the WebSocket connection has additional security requirements.

Connection Lifecycle Security

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Connecting: new WebSocket(url)
    Connecting --> TLSHandshake: TCP established
    TLSHandshake --> CertValidation: TLS negotiated
    CertValidation --> Upgrading: Certificate valid
    CertValidation --> Failed: Certificate invalid
    Upgrading --> OriginCheck: HTTP upgrade request
    OriginCheck --> Connected: Origin validated
    OriginCheck --> Failed: Origin rejected
    Connected --> Authenticated: Bearer token verified
    Authenticated --> Active: Session events flowing
    Active --> Heartbeat: Periodic health check
    Heartbeat --> Active: Response received
    Heartbeat --> Stale: No response in 30s
    Stale --> Reconnecting: Close + reconnect
    Reconnecting --> Connecting: With backoff
    Active --> Closed: Clean close
    Failed --> [*]
    Closed --> [*]

Heartbeat and Stale Connection Detection

WebSocket connections can become stale without either side detecting it (half-open connection due to network failure, firewall timeout, or server crash). Without detection, the client continues operating under the assumption that the server is receiving its messages.

class SecureWebSocketConnection {
  private ws: WebSocket
  private heartbeatInterval: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | null = null
  private lastPongAt: number = Date.now()
  private readonly HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS = 15_000  // 15 seconds
  private readonly PONG_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000  // 30 seconds

  startHeartbeat(): void {
    this.heartbeatInterval = setInterval(() => {
      // Check if the last pong is too old
      if (Date.now() - this.lastPongAt > this.PONG_TIMEOUT_MS) {
        this.handleStaleConnection()
        return
      }

      // Send ping
      if (this.ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
        this.ws.ping()
      }
    }, this.HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS)

    this.ws.on('pong', () => {
      this.lastPongAt = Date.now()
    })
  }

  private handleStaleConnection(): void {
    logSecurityEvent({
      event: 'websocket_stale_connection',
      lastPongAt: this.lastPongAt,
      staleDurationMs: Date.now() - this.lastPongAt,
    })

    // Close and reconnect
    this.ws.terminate()  // Hard close (no close frame)
    this.reconnectWithBackoff()
  }

  private async reconnectWithBackoff(): Promise<void> {
    const maxRetries = 5
    for (let attempt = 0; attempt < maxRetries; attempt++) {
      const delay = Math.min(1000 * Math.pow(2, attempt), 30_000)
      await sleep(delay)

      try {
        await this.connect()
        return
      } catch (error) {
        logSecurityEvent({
          event: 'websocket_reconnect_failed',
          attempt: attempt + 1,
          error: (error as Error).message,
        })
      }
    }

    throw new ConnectionError(
      `WebSocket reconnection failed after ${maxRetries} attempts`
    )
  }
}

Message Size Limits

WebSocket messages should have size limits to prevent memory exhaustion:

const MAX_WS_MESSAGE_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024  // 10 MB

ws.on('message', (data: Buffer) => {
  if (data.length > MAX_WS_MESSAGE_SIZE) {
    logSecurityEvent({
      event: 'websocket_oversized_message',
      size: data.length,
      limit: MAX_WS_MESSAGE_SIZE,
    })
    ws.close(4002, 'Message exceeds size limit')
    return
  }

  // Process normally
  handleMessage(data)
})

Testing SSRF Defenses

SSRF defenses require specific test scenarios:

describe('SSRF protection', () => {
  test('blocks direct metadata IP', async () => {
    await expect(secureFetch('http://169.254.169.254/latest/'))
      .rejects.toThrow('SSRF blocked')
  })

  test('blocks IPv6 mapped IPv4 loopback', async () => {
    await expect(secureFetch('http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/'))
      .rejects.toThrow('SSRF blocked')
  })

  test('blocks redirect to internal IP', async () => {
    // Mock server returns 302 to http://10.0.0.1/
    mockServer.onGet('/redirect').reply(302, '', {
      location: 'http://10.0.0.1/admin',
    })
    await expect(secureFetch(mockServer.url + '/redirect'))
      .rejects.toThrow('SSRF blocked')
  })

  test('respects minimum DNS TTL', async () => {
    // First resolution: public IP
    mockDns.resolve('rebind.example.com', '203.0.113.50', { ttl: 0 })
    await secureFetch('https://rebind.example.com/page1')

    // Second resolution: would return private IP
    mockDns.resolve('rebind.example.com', '169.254.169.254', { ttl: 0 })
    // But cache has not expired (minimum 30s TTL)
    // Still uses pinned 203.0.113.50
    const resp = await secureFetch('https://rebind.example.com/page2')
    expect(resp.ok).toBe(true)
  })

  test('validates all DNS responses', async () => {
    // Hostname resolves to both public and private IPs
    mockDns.resolveMulti('dual.example.com', [
      '203.0.113.50',    // Public
      '169.254.169.254', // Metadata
    ])
    await expect(secureFetch('https://dual.example.com/'))
      .rejects.toThrow('SSRF blocked')
  })
})

This chapter completes Part VI (Bridge & Remote Session Hardening). Together with Chapter 16's remote permission controls, the network security controls ensure that Claude Code's external connections are authenticated, validated against SSRF, protected by certificate pinning, and monitored for anomalies. The network boundary is where local security controls meet the hostile internet -- and every connection crossing that boundary must justify its trust.

Chapter 18: Debug Log Sanitization

Chapters 16 and 17 hardened the bridge and network layers -- the channels through which Claude Code communicates with remote servers. This chapter shifts focus to what those channels inadvertently carry outward: debug log output. Every debugging statement that includes token material, session identifiers, or organizational metadata creates a data exfiltration surface that persists long after the session ends. Log files get collected by centralized logging infrastructure, shipped to SIEMs, stored in S3 buckets with overly broad access policies, and indexed by full-text search engines. A single token.slice(0, 15) in a debug message can turn an entire logging pipeline into a credential exposure vector.

The audit identified four distinct instances of token prefix logging (V-32, V-41, V-43, V-47), one instance of organizational UUID exposure in URL parameters (V-42), and a systemic absence of structured log redaction across the debug utility layer. This chapter implements comprehensive log sanitization -- not by trying to detect and remove sensitive data after the fact, but by establishing an allowlist architecture where only explicitly approved data fields can appear in log output.

18.1 The Anatomy of Debug Log Exposure

Why Token Prefixes Matter

A common misconception in security engineering is that partial token exposure is harmless. The reasoning goes: if the full token is 128 characters, showing the first 15 characters reveals only 12% of the entropy, leaving the remaining 88% as the security barrier. This reasoning is wrong for three reasons.

First, token prefixes reveal the token type. Claude Code's authentication tokens use the sk-ant-si- prefix, which consumes 10 of those 15 characters. The remaining 5 characters of actual secret material reduce the search space from the full token entropy to a much smaller universe. An attacker who knows 5 characters of a base62-encoded token has reduced the brute-force space from 62^n to 62^(n-5) -- a factor of approximately 916 million.

Second, token prefixes enable correlation attacks. If the same prefix appears in multiple log entries across different systems, an attacker can link sessions, identify users, and map access patterns without ever obtaining the full token. This is particularly damaging in enterprise environments where logs from multiple Claude Code instances aggregate into shared infrastructure.

Third, token prefixes in logs create compliance violations. PCI DSS Requirement 3.4 mandates rendering PANs unreadable anywhere they are stored. SOC 2 CC6.1 requires protection of confidential information in all forms. While these frameworks were written for payment card data and customer information, the principle applies universally: secret material in logs is secret material at rest, subject to the same protection requirements as the original credential.

The Four Instances

The audit identified four specific locations where token material appears in debug output:

Finding CVSS Location Vulnerable Code Data Exposed
V-32 4.3 (MEDIUM) bridge/jwtUtils.ts:112 token.slice(0, 15) in JWT decode error Token type + 5 chars of secret
V-41 3.1 (LOW) bridge/jwtUtils.ts:110 token.slice(0, 15) in refresh log Same prefix on different code path
V-43 2.7 (LOW) utils/debug.ts:221 No redaction in logForDebugging() Any data passed through debug utility
V-47 2.4 (INFO) services/analytics/metadata.ts:291 Tool input in telemetry File paths, URLs, command args

The first two findings (V-32 and V-41) represent the same anti-pattern applied in two code paths within jwtUtils.ts. The third (V-43) is the systemic root cause -- the debug utility itself lacks any redaction capability. The fourth (V-47) extends the pattern into the telemetry layer, where tool inputs containing sensitive data flow to analytics endpoints.

The Org UUID Exposure

Finding V-42 (CWE-598, CVSS 3.1 LOW) represents a different class of log exposure: organizational metadata in URL parameters.

// VULNERABLE: remote/SessionsWebSocket.ts:109
const baseUrl = getOauthConfig().BASE_API_URL.replace('https://', 'wss://')
const url = `${baseUrl}/v1/sessions/ws/${this.sessionId}/subscribe?organization_uuid=${this.orgUuid}`
logForDebugging(`[ws] Connecting to ${url}`)

The organization UUID is not a secret in the authentication sense -- it cannot be used to gain access. But logging the full URL including the organization UUID violates the principle of data minimization. When these logs reach centralized infrastructure, the UUID enables:

  • Mapping which organizations use Claude Code
  • Correlating organization IDs across different log sources
  • Identifying enterprise deployments for targeted attacks
  • Building organizational profiles from usage patterns
